title: Chemistry of niobium(V) in alkaline aquatic carbonated systems containing Ca: Solubility phenomena and formation of ternary Ca-Nb(V)-O/OH solid phases
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Nils Huber, Krassimir Garbev, Rosa Ester Guidone, Xavier Gaona, Florian Bocchese, Stéphane Brassinnes, Marcus Altmaier, Horst Geckeis
abstract: Comprehensive solubility experiments with niobium(V) were conducted from oversaturation conditions in weakly alkaline, carbonated solutions equilibrated with calcite and carbonated cement. These conditions are expected in advanced degradation stages of cement, and are representative of cementitious environments as those foreseen in underground and near-surface repositories for short-lived low- and intermediate-level radioactive wastes (L/ILW-SL). Moderate niobium concentrations ([Nb]aq ≈ 10−6 M) were quantified at short contact times (t 10 days), a further decrease in solubility ([Nb]aq ≤ 10−8 M) is observed, which evidences the formation of a sparingly soluble secondary phase transformation. Comparison of solubility data determined in this work with previous studies in carbonate-free systems support that Nb(V)-carbonate complexes can be neglected in the investigated range of carbonate concentrations (≈10−3–10−4 M). Systematic characterization of the resulting solid phases by means of Raman spectroscopy and powder X-ray diffraction unequivocally point towards the predominance of hydrated Ca-Nb(V) solid phase/s of rather amorphous character and small (sub-nm) particle size. A conclusive assignment of the stoichiometry of this/these solid phase/s is not feasible at this stage, although available evidence points towards a Ca: Nb ratio clearly below 1.

title: Source-to-Sink Pathways of Sediments in the Taiwan Strait: Sr and Nd isotopic evidence
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Hao-Wei Huang, Fang-Yu Hu, Chuan-Hsiung Chung, Chen-Feng You
abstract: The Taiwan Strait (TS), a shallow marine channel separating the southeastern Chinese mainland and Taiwan, receives significant sediment input from rivers draining both sides of the strait, making it an ideal site for reconstructing regional climate evolution. This study analyzes the major element composition and Sr-Nd isotopic signatures of TS surface sediments to trace sediment sources. The Ca/Na and Ca/Mg ratios reveal two distinct sediment sources: western Taiwan and mainland China rivers. The heterogeneity in Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of riverine sediments further differentiates TS sediment sources, with samples near river mouths primarily influenced by local riverine inputs, while those along the path of the Zhe-Min Coastal Current (ZMCC) exhibit significant contributions from ZMCC-derived sediments, originating from the Changjiang and Korean rivers. Our findings provide a spatial distribution of Sr-Nd isotopic compositions in TS sediments and identify their primary sources, offering key locations for reconstructing regional climate evolution and studying past variations in current strength.

title: Arsenic behavior and release from mine tailings in tropical semiarid region: insights from geochemistry, mineralogy, and texture
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Ondra Sracek, Ondřej Bábek, Bohdan Kříbek, Vojtěch Ettler, František Veselovský, Michal Čurda, Jan Filip, Jaroslav Kapusta, Martin Mihaljevič, Aleš Vaněk, Tereza Zádorová, Vít Penížek, Zibisani Bagai
abstract: Patterns of weathering and arsenic release from As-rich mine tailings heap at Mupane, northeastern Botswana, were studied through grain size and quantitative color analysis, mineralogy, and geochemistry of solids and water in nearby ponds. Arsenic is contained mostly in arsenopyrite, and Fe-oxyhydroxides. Sand fraction is mainly deposited at margins, and clayey silt at the center of the heap. A pink colored, oxidized zone enriched in Fe-oxyhydroxides, mainly goethite and hematite, and strongly depleted in S, and As, is developed at the surface of the heap, to about 110 cm depth. The center of the heap is oxidized to lower depth than its margins due to coarser grain size and lower water content of the latter. Some arsenopyrite and pyrrhotite grains show oxidation rims at the margin of the heap. Iron sulfides predominate at greater depths of the heap. The Ca-arsenate with composition close to arseniosiderite, Ca2Fe3O2(AsO4)3·3H2O, was found at the central profile. The weathering of arsenopyrite releases large amounts of As. The Acid Base Accounting indicates no or very little risk of acid mine drainage. Water leachates are alkaline (pH > 9.0) and have high As concentrations, consistently with water chemistry in nearby ponds, with As concentration up to 1.077 mg/L. High As concentrations are caused by desorption of arsenate at high pH. At the beginning of rainy period, the mine tailings can be source of As rich seepage with high As concentration, but the site is far from human settlements. Findings of this study are applicable to many alkaline mine tailings in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Pb isotope fingerprints and legacy contribution of historical mine tailings to downstream river sediments in the Nacozari district, northern Mexico
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Verónica Moreno-Rodríguez, Aracely Leyva-Haro, Sergio Adrián Salgado-Souto, René Loredo-Portales, José Luis Aguirre-Noyola, Lucas Ochoa-Landín, Rafael Del Rio-Salas
abstract: The dispersion of potentially toxic elements (PTE) related to historical mine sites has been a concerning issue due to its legacy impact on environmental media. Samples from the three historical mine tailings (MT) from Nacozari de García town (Nacozari mining district in northwestern Mexico), along with the downstream river sediments (up to 30 km away) from the Moctezuma River, were studied to determine Pb contents and isotope compositions. Pb isotope systematics is a powerful geochemical tool for discriminating and tracing Pb dispersion. Differences in the Pb isotope composition of the tailings impoundments were detected. MT-I and MT-III display similar and partially overlapping less radiogenic compositions (206Pb/204Pb = 18.580-18.856), while MT-II is slightly more radiogenic (206Pb/204Pb = 18.952-19.133), which is relevant for environmental assessments. The Pb isotope compositions of downstream sediments show closer isotopic affinities with MT-I and MT-III than with MT-II. Bayesian mixing modeling supports this interpretation, estimating contributions of 75.6% from geogenic sources, 11.9% from MT-I, 1.6% from MT-II, and 10.8% from MT-III. Determining the Pb isotope composition of historical mine tailings enables discrimination among individual tailings deposits and between geogenic and anthropogenic Pb sources. This information establishes a Pb isotopic baseline for future environmental monitoring and source identification.

title: Metal transport through century-old waste rock
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Andrew Hicks, Colleen O. Harper, Richard T. Amos
abstract: The potential for waste rock from mining activities to leach poor quality drainage has been well documented. However, despite the potential for leaching to occur over many decades or centuries, few studies have investigated the relevant geochemical processes over long timescales. This study looks at the porewater geochemistry from a ∼10 Ktonne waste-rock pile at an abandoned prospecting property, the Ore Chimney mine, that has been in place for approximately 100 years. Waste-rock samples were collected at 0.5 m intervals from three trenches that transected the ∼5 m depth of the pile; samples were centrifuged to extract porewaters and analyzed for standard geochemical parameters, anions, cations, and metals. The geochemical modelling software PHREEQC was used to explore possible secondary controls on porewater chemistry. The results indicate near-neutral pH throughout the depth of the waste rock and abundant alkalinity (average: 58.6 mg/L CaCO3), indicating that carbonate buffering is still active within the waste rock. Zn concentrations, as high as 87.5 ppm (16.5 ppm on average), accounted for 92% [M] of heavy metals and is attributed to the oxidative dissolution of sphalerite, the primary sulfide mineral in the waste rock. The preferential weathering of sphalerite over pyrite produces less acidity and plays a large role in maintaining carbonates and neutral pH in the system. Despite the long period of weathering within the Ore Chimney waste rock, weathering processes are similar to those observed in other waste-rock studies and differences in geochemical parameters are largely ascribed to differences in lithology, principally sulfide mineralogy and carbonate content, rather than the age of the waste-rock. High alkalinity levels suggest that the dissolution of calcite and dolomite controlpH, and Pb, Zn, Cd, and Cu concentrations in the porewaters. Results from this study indicate that the source lithology of sulfides plays a strong role in weathering. This study shows that a detailed understanding of in situ solid- and aqueous-phase geochemistry is required to delineate waste-rock weathering as a function of long-term exposure.

title: From rock to fins: A multi-catchment study of 87 Sr/ 86 Sr transfer across the lithosphere–hydrosphere–biosphere interface and constraints for broader application
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Filip Scheiner, Lucie Vaňková, Martin Svojtka, Lukáš Ackerman, Kateřina Soukalová, Ondřej Slavík, Jan Kubečka
abstract: Freshwater fish otolith 87Sr/86Sr microchemistry holds considerable promise for animal provenance assignment and mobility reconstruction, yet its application requires both a geochemically distinct isotopic landscape and a clear understanding of species-specific recording fidelity. We exploited the exceptional lithological diversity of the Bohemian Massif (Czech Republic) to sample five catchments spanning contrasting bedrock, land-use, and hydrology, combining bedrock, stream water, and otolith measurements into an integrated provenance framework. Despite pervasive bedrock–water decoupling, driven in most catchments by preferential mineral-phase weathering, each system yields a temporally reproducible dissolved 87Sr/86Sr signature, and most can be discriminated at the third to fourth decimal place. Recording fidelity, however, is not a fixed property of species: while Cottus gobio, Barbatula barbatula, and resident Salmo trutta m. fario faithfully track ambient water and are recommended as baseline recorders, Gobio gobio records the local signal in one catchment yet is systematically offset in another, showing that fidelity depends on ecological context and must be verified per-system. Mobile cyprinids and perch carry movement-integrated signals; the dispersal inferred for Squalius cephalus was independently corroborated by targeted river water sampling. Rather than establishing an already-known tracer, these results define the conditions under which otolith 87Sr/86Sr can be applied reliably in Central European fluvial systems, and highlight the need for expanded catchment-scale Sr isotopic mapping and systematics and per-system validation of species-specific recording behaviour.

title: Siderophore-mediated immobilization of thorium, uranium, and cerium on acid birnessite
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Lucy Hunley, Wilfredo I. Rivera Rodriguez, Alexander Humbert, Skyler Moe, Mismel Ruiz-Garcia, Brandon Jones, Vasileios Anagnostopoulos
abstract: The geochemical behavior of radionuclides is governed by complicated interactions between aqueous speciation, ligands, and mineral surfaces. This study considers the role of siderophores, specifically desferrioxamine B (DFOB) and its analog, desferrioxamine D (DFOD), in modulating the retention and migration of heavy metals, uranium and thorium, and cerium, on acid birnessite, a highly reactive manganese oxide. While siderophores are traditionally viewed as agents that enhance metal mobility through solubilization, this research demonstrates that they can also promote actinide immobilization via ligand-mediated co-retention. Batch experiments conducted at pH 3, 6, and 8 revealed that at pH 3, the addition of DFOB increased thorium removal from the aqueous phase from approximately 70% to nearly 100%. Comparative studies with DFOD confirmed that secondary amide groups, in addition to the terminal amine of DFOB, facilitate association with the mineral surface. Overall, the evidence suggests that siderophore complexes in manganese-rich environments may enhance actinide retention, whereas the opposite would be true in the absence of birnessite minerals. This work underscores the need to consider mineralogical and biological context in remediation frameworks, as microbial ligands can significantly alter predicted contaminant transport at mining and legacy nuclear sites.

title: Molecular-level understanding of natural organic matter-nuclide interactions: unraveling the complexation and aggregation mechanisms
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Lei Huang, Haozhe Ma, Zhiyu Zhou, Ranran Cui, Meng Chen, Chi Zhang, Hanzhong Jia
abstract: Understanding molecular-scale interactions between natural organic matter (NOM) and nuclide species is essential for predicting contaminant fate and designing effective remediation strategies in aquatic environments. Molecular simulations were used to investigate the complexation and aggregation behaviors of four representative nuclide species (UO2 2+, Sr2+, Cs+, and TcO4 −) with NOM under environmentally relevant aqueous conditions. A clear hierarchy in binding affinity was observed (UO2 2+ > Sr2+ > Cs+ ≈ TcO4 −), with distinctly ion-specific complexation mechanisms. UO2 2+ predominantly forms stable, multidentate inner-sphere complexes with oxygen-containing functional groups of NOM, whereas Sr2+ mainly exhibits monodentate inner-sphere coordination. In contrast, Cs+ shows weak, predominantly outer-sphere association, while TcO4 − is electrostatically excluded, leading to unfavorable association with NOM. The resulting free-energy profiles elucidate the thermodynamic controls governing these ion-specific interactions. Furthermore, background Ca2+ promotes NOM aggregation, which may alter effective nuclide retention in a nuclide-dependent manner, enhancing immobilization of strongly complexing cations while providing limited attenuation for weakly interacting species. These findings highlight the role of NOM as a selective geosorbent and scavenger in aquatic systems and emphasize the need for nuclide-specific risk assessments that explicitly consider ambient water chemistry when predicting nuclide mobility.

title: Geochemical baseline, potentially toxic element contamination, and ecological risks in stream sediments of the northern Vazante-Paracatu Belt, Brazil
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Gabriela Rodrigues Caitano, Eduardo Duarte Marques, Débora Silvano Moreira, Emmanoel Vieira Silva-Filho
abstract: The Vazante-Paracatu Mineral Province, located within the Brasília Fold Belt on the western margin of the São Francisco Craton in Minas Gerais, Brazil, extends about 250 km and hosts significant gold and zinc mineralization. In this study, we evaluated concentrations and spatial distribution of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in the province's northern portion and discussed geogenic influences and potential anthropogenic contributions. We analyzed about 2198 stream sediment samples to establish geochemical baseline values for nine PTEs across four geological units. Methodological comparison showed that a robust, median-based statistical approach yielded more consistent anomaly thresholds than a method based on data structure. Environmental indices were used as screening-level indicators of relative enrichment, sediment contamination, and potential ecological risk. Contamination factor (CF) analysis showed the highest proportions of considerable to very high contamination for Cd and As, followed by Co, Zn, Mo, and Cr. The median for each geological unit better represented its geochemical characteristics. The modified degree of contamination and the potential ecological risk index identified an area with high contamination levels and high potential ecological risk in the southeastern portion of the study area, with values decreasing toward the northwest. The spatial patterns of PTEs are consistent with lithological and mineralization-related controls, while mining activities and the application of fertilizers and soil amendments may also contribute locally. This study delineates priority areas for environmental management and highlights areas of elevated PTE enrichment and potential ecological risk in this mineralized region.

title: Geochemically constrained hierarchical co-simulation for modeling Cu–Au associations in mine tailings
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Alikhan Ibraimov, Nasser Madani, Mohammad Maleki, Annika Parviainen
abstract: Accurate modeling of geochemical element distributions in mine tailings is essential for evaluating resource recovery potential and mitigating environmental risks. Metal mine tailings may contain economically valuable elements, such as copper and gold, whose spatial variability and geochemical relationships must be reliably characterized to support reprocessing decisions. However, conventional Gaussian co-simulation methods may fail to preserve important bivariate relationships between geochemical variables, leading to unrealistic joint distributions and potentially biased interpretations of metal co-enrichment. To address this limitation, this study proposes a dual-linearity-constrained acceptance–rejection hierarchical co-simulation approach (DLC-AR-HCOSIM). The method incorporates an acceptance–rejection sampling procedure to enforce both lower and upper linear constraints between Cu and Au during hierarchical co-simulation. The proposed method was applied to a historical Cu–Au tailings deposit in Southwest Finland and compared with four alternative approaches: conventional hierarchical sequential Gaussian co-simulation without constraints (C-HSGCOSIM), upper-bound acceptance–rejection hierarchical co-simulation (UB-AR-HCOSIM), lower-bound acceptance–rejection hierarchical co-simulation (LB-AR-HCOSIM), and projection pursuit multivariate transform with linear model of coregionalization (PPMT-LMC). The results show that all methods provide reasonable reproduction of global statistics and cutoff-based responses. However, important differences were observed in the reproduction of the Cu–Au bivariate relationship. The conventional C-HSGCOSIM and PPMT-LMC methods tended to overestimate the Cu–Au correlation, producing Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.74 and 0.78, respectively, compared with 0.62 in the original dataset. In contrast, the proposed DLC-AR-HCOSIM reproduced the rank correlation more accurately, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.61, while also respecting the empirically defined lower and upper Cu–Au constraint boundaries. The one-sided constraint methods reduced violations on either the upper or lower side but were less effective in reproducing the full admissible bivariate domain. Overall, the proposed dual-constraint approach provides a more controlled and geochemically consistent framework for simulating Cu–Au tailings, supporting more reliable assessment of resource recovery potential and environmental risk.

title: The influence of abandoned coal mines on the spatial and temporal variability in metal concentration and distribution in an Appalachian stream
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Annika Dudik, David M. Singer, Chloe Pearson, Allyson C. Tessin
abstract: Coal mine drainage (CMD) is produced from untreated and/or abandoned coal mining operations and can release toxic metals into the environment long after the cessation of coal production. Streams impacted by CMD can transport these metals throughout the affected watershed, with the aqueous and suspended sediment phases influencing the transportation and removal of the metals present. To better understand the behavior of these fractions and the influence of CMD on watersheds, monthly water sampling took place over the course of a year at four sites in the Huff Run Watershed, Ohio (USA), one upstream of historical coal mining within the watershed and three below. Field-based measurements included discharge, dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature, and electrical conductivity. Laboratory-based analyses included the separation of the water samples into the aqueous (Maq) and acid extractable metals from solids (MAE-solid) as a proxy for labile metal associated with the suspended sediments and analyzed via inductively coupled plasma optical emissions spectroscopy (ICP-OES). Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) analyses of powders and selected samples prepared as thin sections were conducted to examine the external and internal composition and morphology of suspended sediments. Metal concentrations in the stream were found to vary spatially and temporally and were grouped into the following categories: (1) Na, K, Al, and Si, which did not exhibit a large change in concentrations between Sites 1 (above coal mining in the watershed) and the other sites; (2) Mg, S, and Ca, which exhibited a large increase in concentrations starting at Site 2 and were dominated by the Maq fraction; (3) Mn, Co, and Ni which also exhibited a large increase in concentration at Site 2 and were partially associated with the MAE-solid fraction; and (4) Fe and Zn which exhibited a large increase in concentration at Site 2 and were dominated by (Fe) or strongly associated with (Zn) MAE-solids. Seasonal variation in concentration occurred, corresponding to changes in discharge, with a majority of elements exhibiting a dilution behavior, with the notable exception of Feaq at Site 4 (mobilization) and Znaq and ZnAE-solild (chemostatic or mobilization) at all sites. These results indicate that although the abandoned coal mines have been reclaimed, they are continuing to influence stream chemistry with an influx of high metal concentrations including labile metals associated with suspended sediments. These particles also include chemically and physically heterogeneous and complex phases in redox disequilibrium, with the potential for transport of labile metal-bearing phases beyond the watershed. The data presented here shows the importance of understanding metal concentrations and distribution over both time and space to better understand how metals are being transported, removed, and remobilized in response to various hydrogeochemical conditions. Watershed managers can use the data collected here to better predict how CMD-impacted metals will travel through streams, and design treatment plans in response.

title: Geochemical exploration of concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits beneath thick granitoid overburden: Insights from conventional soil geochemical methods and geoelectrochemical extraction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Jianting Li, Meilan Wen, Panfeng Liu, Wen Gao, Yuxiong Jiang, Xiaohan Zhang
abstract: In South China, thick granitoid overburden is widespread and hosts substantial mineral exploration potential. However, as mineral exploration increasingly shifts toward deep-seated and concealed orebodies, reliable and appropriate exploration techniques are required. Geoelectrochemical extraction, a typical deep-penetrating geochemical method, has proven effective for identifying concealed orebodies. This paper uses the concealed Luobuling porphyry Cu–Mo deposit as a case study to compare the exploration performance of conventional soil geochemical methods and geoelectrochemical extraction beneath thick granitoid overburden. The results show that ore-related elemental anomalies revealed by conventional soil geochemical methods merely reflect surficial geochemical patterns and cannot effectively delineate deep concealed orebodies. Further results of Tessier sequential extraction reveal that ore-forming elements in soils are predominantly hosted in stable phases including organic-sulfide bound and residual fractions. The high geochemical background generated by these stable fractions masks weak deep mineralization signals, which is the fundamental cause of the limitations of conventional soil geochemical methods in the study area. In contrast, Cu anomalies revealed by geoelectrochemical extraction are strongly correlated with concealed orebodies, indicating that this technique effectively overcomes surficial overprinting and directly reflects deep-seated mineralization. Based on the results of geoelectrochemical extraction, a set of integrated prospecting indicators for concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits has been established, enabling rapid delineation of favorable exploration targets. Overall, compared with conventional soil geochemical methods, geoelectrochemical extraction is an effective exploration tool for concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits beneath thick granitoid overburden in South China.

title: Lithium occurrence in brines and clay-bearing strata of the Salt Range, Pakistan: Insights from hydrogeochemistry and mineralogy
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Muhammad Hussain, Muhammad Jabran, Dawar Abbas, Muhammad Nadeem, Abbas Ali
abstract: Lithium is a critical raw material supporting clean-energy technologies and Sustainable Development Goals 7, 9 and 13. Despite extensive Neoproterozoic evaporites and saline brines, the lithium potential of Pakistan's Salt Range remains unassessed. This study presents the first hydrogeochemical and mineralogical baseline for lithium in Salt Range brines and clay-bearing strata. Nine brines from mine galleries, a surface stream and two boreholes across the Kalabagh, Warchha and Khewra sectors, together with 26 clay, marl and clastic rock samples, were analyzed for physicochemical parameters, major ions and lithium by atomic absorption spectrometry; representative lithium-rich clays by X-ray diffraction. Data were interpreted using Piper, Durov, Schoeller and Gibbs diagrams, ionic ratios, correlation and principal component analysis. The brines are predominantly Na–Cl waters with total dissolved solids of 3–275 g/L, and salinity tracks the mapped extent of the Salt Range Formation, indicating that evaporite dissolution and water–rock interaction supply most solutes, with evaporative concentration a further control on the most saline waters. Without Br/Cl and stable-isotope data, halite-dissolution and seawater-derived brines cannot be uniquely distinguished. Lithium was detected only in the Kalabagh brines (270–280 mg/L; Mg/Li 4.3–10.6), all others below the 10 mg/L detection limit. Solid samples contain 124–859 mg/kg Li in the western sector against under 40 mg/kg elsewhere, and the lithium-rich clays examined are dominated by illite. Equally saline Khewra brines carry no measurable lithium, showing that lithium distribution is supply-limited rather than salinity-controlled, and identifying Kalabagh as the most prospective target.

title: Halotrichite-group sulfates as mineralogical and spectral indicators of Cu, Co and As enrichment in mining environmental liabilities
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): J. Gerding, J. Morales, J. Alvarez, J. Perez, C. Sandoval-Muñoz
abstract: This study evaluates the potential of halotrichite-group minerals as mineralogical and geochemical indicators of critical metals in mining environmental liabilities. Synthetic halotrichite, pickeringite and apjohnite were produced under experimental evaporative conditions designed to reproduce semi-arid environments, using solutions containing Cu, Co and As to assess metal uptake during sulfate crystallization. The resulting phases were characterized by X-ray diffraction, ICP-OES, SEM–EDS, LIBS and VNIR–SWIR spectroscopy, and were compared with natural efflorescent sulfate salts collected from abandoned tailings deposits in the Coquimbo Region, Chile. The results show that the dominant structural cation strongly controls both phase stability and trace-metal uptake. Halotrichite, the Fe–Al end-member, displayed the highest affinity for Cu, Co and As, whereas pickeringite showed intermediate uptake, particularly for Cu, and apjohnite showed limited incorporation. Alunogen did not show significant association with the evaluated trace metals. Natural samples from the Delirio and Barraza tailings were dominated by pickeringite-bearing sulfate assemblages and contained high Cu and Co concentrations, supporting the environmental relevance of the experimental results. VNIR–SWIR spectra showed distinguishable responses among sulfate assemblages containing halotrichite-group phases under laboratory conditions, with absorption features mainly related to water and sulfate-bearing molecular groups. These spectral differences support further evaluation of VNIR–SWIR spectroscopy as a complementary tool for the proximal recognition of sulfate-rich assemblages, while remote sensing applications require scale-specific validation. Overall, the study proposes halotrichite and pickeringite as potential mineralogical indicators for early-stage assessment of critical-metal enrichment and environmental risk in oxidized mining residues developed under semi-arid climatic conditions.

title: pH-dependent catechol oxidation by Mn oxides: Insights from Mn(III)
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Hui Li, Mingjing Sun, Tao Wen
abstract: Manganese (Mn) oxides are keystone minerals in the terrestrial ecosystems that regulate the long-term stability of soil organic matter (SOM) through their versatile roles in associating with and oxidizing SOM. Despite their importance, the underlying mechanisms, particularly the roles of Mn(III), in these processes remain poorly understood, partly due to their low stability in soil solution. Here, we used catechol as a model polyphenol to investigate its oxidation by two structurally distinct Mn oxides—cryptomelane (tunnel structure) and birnessite (layered structure) under environmentally relevant pH conditions (6 and 8). Pyrophosphate (PP) was further introduced to complex and probe the roles of Mn(III) formed during birnessite-catechol interactions. Overall, cryptomelane had a higher oxidation capability than birnessite, but they formed similar products. pH had a strong influence on the product composition, with alkaline condition favoring polymerization to larger products. PP addition increased the reaction rate but markedly suppressed larger polymers, particularly under acidic conditions. When introduced as a direct Mn source, dissolved Mn(III)-acetate in the presence of PP readily oxidized catechol, however, with a simpler product composition than mineral systems and inhibited accumulation of larger polymers at acidic pH. These findings demonstrate a pH-controlled abiotic oxidation system of polyphenol, enabled by both structural Mn(III/IV) in Mn oxides and dissolved Mn(III). This work provides new insights into the complex roles of Mn in organic transformation, highlighting the importance of Mn(III) beyond mineral surface reactivity. These findings have implications for understanding the potential role of Mn redox cycling in regulating soil carbon persistence.

title: Tracing Groundwater–Seawater exchanges using geochemical tracers (radon, radium, stable isotopes of water) in a seasonally frozen beach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Laísa Peixoto Ramos, Antoine Biehler, Pieter van Beek, Pascal Bernatchez, Gwénaëlle Chaillou
abstract: Groundwater–seawater exchanges remain poorly documented in subarctic and arctic regions, particularly during winter, when coastal ice alters hydrogeology conditions and limits sampling opportunities. This study investigates winter groundwater dynamics at a seasonally frozen beach by combining the use of various geochemical tracers. Stable water isotopes (δ2H and δ18O) were used to identify the origin of the water, whereas short-lived radioisotope tracers (222Rn, 223Ra, 224Ra) were used to trace subsurface geochemical processes along the groundwater flow path, from the upper beach to the discharge zone. Three sampling campaigns were conducted in 2023 along a 2.5 km sandy beach on Québec's coastline, covering frozen (February), thawing (April), and pre-freeze (October) conditions. Along the flow path, two distinct groundwater sources were identified, including i) fresh, terrestrial groundwater emerging from coastal cliffs upstream of the beach, and ii) seawater circulating within permeable sediments that mixes with terrestrial groundwater along the beach, thus yielding a salinity gradient corresponding to the subterranean estuary (STE). In this zone, δ2H and δ18O analyses indicate that fresh groundwater contributes from 10% to 42% of the mixed groundwater throughout the three periods. As expected, the fresh groundwater contribution increases markedly during the thawing season, largely sustained by local snowmelt inputs. 222Rn and 224Raex activities exhibited strong spatial variability likely driven by geomorphological features and the presence of ice, which influenced the permeability and thus groundwater flow within the beach aquifer. Temperature may also influence the release and mobility of Ra and Rn in porewater (e.g., recoil, diffusion and desorption processes). These patterns supported a persistent west-east activity gradient across the different seasons: low 222Rn and 224Ra activities were observed near a subsurface paleochannel structure, whereas activities up to two orders of magnitude higher were found in front of a high cliff structure. In the adjacent embayment, while 222Rn remained systematically undetectable in seawater, significant activities of 224Raex were detected, pointing to short-lived Ra inputs to the coastal ocean across all seasons, potentially including a contribution from beach groundwater discharge, whether from terrestrial freshwater or recirculated seawater within the permeable sediments, although a Ra input via diffusion from the sediment cannot be excluded. Taken together, these results indicate that groundwater–seawater exchanges may persist beneath the winter ice cover and that freshwater flow may remain active year-round despite freezing conditions. These findings provide novel insights into beach hydrogeology in cold regions and demonstrate the value of multi-tracer approaches for characterizing groundwater–seawater exchanges under challenging winter conditions.

title: Decoupling aeolian and hydrochemical element migration in closed arid basins: A τ–act–IER geochemical framework with interpretable machine learning
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Xiaomeng Cheng, Yuanli Qin, Honghong Ma, Min Peng, Zheng Yang, Shiqi Tang, Li Zhang, Chen Zhao, Yalong Zhou, Zijia Liu, Yu Zhao, Lingling Ma, Yang Shao, Yinfeng He, Hongli Hu, Hangxin Cheng
abstract: Element migration, fractionation, and accumulation in closed arid basins govern continental silicate weathering and evaporite formation, with direct implications for soil salinization, groundwater quality, and potash exploration in dryland regions. However, existing mass-balance and ion-ratio approaches have not quantitatively distinguished two fundamentally different transport modes: aeolian physical sorting of detrital minerals versus solute convergence through fluvial-hydrochemical pathways at the basin scale. To address this limitation, we develop a τ–act–IER geochemical framework that integrates mass transfer coefficients (τ), labile cation activation fractions (act), and ion equivalent ratios (IER). We validate this framework using a comprehensive multi-layer dataset from the Tarim Basin—a classic hyper-arid closed basin—comprising 16,198 surface soil samples, 3733 deep parent materials, and 6620 soluble ion extracts. A tripartite interpretable machine learning workflow (Geodetector–RF–SHAP) is further applied to identify nonlinear climatic and topographic thresholds controlling element partitioning. Two antithetical yet spatially coupled geochemical processes are identified: residual Si enrichment driven by long-term aeolian sorting in the desert interior, and evaporative accumulation of Na, Cl, and sulfate at the terminal playa. Spatial gradients of τ and IER jointly define a solubility-controlled precipitation sequence—Ca → S → Mg → Na → Cl—consistent with classical evaporite stratigraphy extended to continental basin scale, with the Ca gradient confirmed to be robust to correction methodology (Spearman ρ = 0.695, p < 0.001). Potassium exhibits a basin-wide steady state with near-zero net mass transfer, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence including mineralogical dilution and incipient feldspar alteration, the lowest labile K activation fraction among base cations, weak precipitation modulation, and balanced aeolian input versus fluvial export. SHAP analysis identifies three critical thresholds governing dryland element cycling: MAP (Mean Annual Precipitation) ≈ 20 mm, DEM (Digital Elevation Model) ≈ 1200 m, and MAT (Mean Annual Temperature) ≈ 11 °C. Correlations between τ and all act indices are negligible (R2 < 0.04), confirming that millennial-scale mass redistribution is statistically decoupled from instantaneous cation exchange reactivity. The τ–act–IER framework with interpretable machine learning provides a broadly applicable quantitative approach for distinguishing physical and chemical element transport in closed arid basins, advancing understanding of continental weathering cycles and evaporite deposit formation.

title: Environmental magnetism and geochemical screening of anthropogenic contamination in suburban university campus topsoil: lithogenic controls and localized ferrimagnetic enrichment in Querétaro, Mexico
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Alejandro Rodríguez-Trejo, Reneé González-Guzmán, Héctor E. Ibarra-Ortega, Harald Böhnel, Sara Solís-Valdez, Rodrigo Rodríguez, Gabriela Guzmán, Ana G. Castañeda-Miranda
abstract: Magnetic susceptibility (χ) is widely used as a rapid indicator of anthropogenic influence in urban soils; however, its interpretation can be complicated by heterogeneous lithogenic backgrounds. To this end, this study examines topsoil magnetic variability across the UNAM Campus Juriquilla (Querétaro, central Mexico), a suburban educational infrastructure underlain by basaltic andesite and affected by secondary carbonate inputs. Topsoil samples were collected and analyzed via integrated mineralogical, geochemical, and environmental magnetism approaches. To complement bulk magnetic susceptibility measurements, we conducted thermomagnetic analyses, hysteresis loops, and Day-plot domain-state characterization, together with X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM–EDS), portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF), X-ray fluorescence (XRF), and ICP–MS analyses. Mineralogical and geochemical results demonstrate that the soils are compositionally immature and derived primarily from mafic volcanic parent material. Variable contributions of secondary calcite locally dilute mass-specific magnetic signals. Furthermore, diffractograms, PAAS-normalized REE patterns, and other geochemical proxies support strong lithogenic inheritance modulated by weathering and organic matter accumulation. Magnetic data indicate that ferrimagnetic carriers are dominated by magnetite and low-Ti titanomagnetite, illustrating pseudo-single-domain behavior and mixed assemblages. Mass-specific susceptibility shows a positively skewed distribution, with discrete spatial clusters that exceed background variability. While spatial interpolation of χ and geochemical proxies underscores localized enrichments of χ, Fe, and Mn near buildings and internal circulation corridors, low-χ sectors align with green areas and carbonate-rich soils. The analytical results demonstrate dual control on the campus magnetic signal: (i) a heterogeneous volcanic–carbonate lithogenic baseline and (ii) localized ferrimagnetic enrichment consistent with near-surface anthropogenic inputs. This study develops a robust campus-scale baseline and demonstrates the value of combining environmental magnetism, geochemistry, and geospatial modeling as a screening framework for determining priority areas for targeted urban soil contamination assessments.

title: Removal of arsenic using Fe-modified biochar and Carbo-Iron® materials
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Mingyu Feng, Laura A. Richards, Ariette Schierz, Katrin Mackenzie, James M. Byrne, David A. Polya, Jonathan R. Lloyd
abstract: Arsenic (As) mobilization in aquifers poses potential threats to global human health and ecosystems. The adsorption performance and stability of pristine biochar, Fe-modified biochars, and Carbo-Iron for As removal from water were evaluated to investigate feasibility for potential remediation applications. The Fe-modified biochars included ferrihydrite-containing biochar (FH + BC; 155 mg/g Fe) and magnetite-containing biochar (M + BC; 86 mg/g Fe). SEM and XRD indicated aggregated Fe phases in FH + BC and partially crystallized Fe with readily soluble Fe in M + BC. Adsorption over 24 h (initial As 100 μg/L, dosage 5 g/L) showed that all Fe-containing materials achieved substantially higher As(V) removal than pristine biochar. The pH dependence was biochar-specific: FH + BC favoured As adsorption under acidic conditions, M + BC displayed largely pH-dependent adsorption, and Carbo-Iron demonstrated consistently high adsorption with limited sensitivity to equilibrium pH range of 3.5 – 7.4. Under circumneutral conditions, the three materials showed broadly comparable performance, while Carbo-Iron demonstrated a significantly higher adsorption than M + BC, consistent with Carbo-Iron > M + BC in adsorption isotherm modelling. Performance of adsorption extended over six months (initial As 100 μg/L, initial pH 5.0 – 8.0) showed marked differences in long-term As retention. Pristine biochar supported negligible As(V) removal, while FH + BC exhibited declining performance with aqueous As(III/V) exceeding 30 μg/L. In contrast, both M + BC and Carbo-Iron maintained aqueous As(V) and As(III) concentrations below 1.4 μg/L after 27 days, with Carbo-Iron achieving this level within 24 h. These findings highlight the role of biochar- or activated carbon-supported Fe phases in remediating As and identify M + BC and Carbo-Iron as potentially effective materials for mitigating low As contaminated waters over timescales of up to six months.

title: Geochemical modeling of H 2 storage in a sandstone reservoir: Sensitivity analysis of abiotic H 2 S and CO 2 gas formation
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Robin Hintzen, Jeroen Snippe, Tim Tambach, Roland Hellmann, Laurent Truche, Kevins Rhino, Julia F. van Winden
abstract: Hydrogen storage in geologic reservoirs is a promising technology for storing surplus renewable energy, but the H2 gas quality may be compromised by fluid-rock-gas interactions. Using redox-decoupled, kinetically-controlled, abiotic 0D batch models, this study simulates the 30-year geochemical evolution of a sandstone reservoir (117 °C, 150 bar P total, 98 mol% H2) and quantifies the temporal evolution of gas concentrations (H2, CO2, H2S). The models reveal two concurrent reaction regimes: initial perturbation of the pre-existing carbonate-fluid-gas equilibrium, causing CO2 degassing (∼4.2 mol%) and siderite dissolution, and long-term pyrite reductive dissolution with secondary pyrrhotite precipitation. Leaching of Fe2+ from Fe-chlorite enhances sulfide scavenging via pyrrhotite formation, stabilizing H2S(gas) at 26-28 ppm. Sensitivity analyses (40-140 °C, 5-250 bar P total, 0.001-2.0 vol% pyrite) demonstrate that the reservoir geochemistry is governed by a reaction feedback loop involving: i) sulfide release from reductive pyrite dissolution, ii) aqueous sulfide removal by pyrrhotite precipitation, and iii) secondary Fe2+-mobilization from ferrous minerals. An Fe-mineral buffer sequence (Fe-chlorite → siderite → ankerite) determines the geochemical impact on the reservoir. Siderite alteration notably increases dilution of the H2 storage gas mixture by CO2. Under storage-relevant conditions (T ≤ 120 °C, P total ≥ 50 bar), our batch models indicate H2S(gas) concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 80 ppm at H2(gas) concentrations from 85 to 98 mol%. At temperatures ≤ 80 °C, the mineral reaction kinetics are slow enough to significantly reduce gas contamination, with abiotically-derived concentrations > 97 mol% H2. Our gas estimates are conditional, but stress the importance of non-sulfide Fe-minerals to prevent excessive H2S accumulation.

title: Effects of weathering and secondary carbonate precipitation on carbon cycling across different erosion rates in the Yarlung Tsangpo River Basin
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Haofei Zhang, Fusheng Guo, Ming Luo
abstract: Rock weathering is a key process controlling riverine carbon cycling, while secondary carbonate precipitation during river transport can alter dissolved solute compositions and thereby affect estimates of weathering fluxes and carbon budgets. We compiled published hydrochemical data, Sr concentrations, runoff data, and 10Be erosion rates for the Yarlung Tsangpo River Basin. Catchment average steepness indices were calibrated against 10Be erosion rates and used to estimate erosion rates at hydrochemical sampling sites. Ca2+ loss associated with secondary carbonate precipitation was corrected using a three dimensional Sr/Ca, Na/Ca, and SO4/Ca relationship. A constrained multi-endmember inversion with one integrated evaporite endmember was then applied to quantify solute sources, source specific fluxes, and CO2 budgets. Riverine solutes were dominated by carbonate weathering, silicate weathering, and evaporite dissolution, with mean contributions of 53.2%, 21.5%, and 15.7%, respectively, while geothermal input and atmospheric precipitation contributed 5.3% and 4.3%. Source specific fluxes varied nonlinearly with erosion rate and were generally highest at intermediate erosion rates. Secondary carbonate precipitation related CO2 release was low for most samples but reached the order of 103 μmol L−1 at several main stem and tributary sites. Most samples acted as CO2 sinks when weathering alone was considered, whereas inclusion of secondary carbonate precipitation shifted some weak sinks to weak sources. Over longer timescales, silicate weathering remained the dominant control on the carbon budget. These results highlight the need to jointly consider erosion rate, lithology, and secondary carbonate precipitation when evaluating weathering related carbon budgets in lithologically complex river basins.

title: Differential effects of continuous rainfall on iron-bound organic carbon within subtropical red soil aggregates
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 211 Author(s): Qianyu Long, Degen Zhu, Weizhi Chen, Xiang Liu, Jiyuan Cai, Hu Wang, Yuanlong Li, Wenlin Wu, Liankai Zhang
abstract: Climate change has increased the frequency of persistent extreme rainfall events in subtropical regions, altering red-soil aggregate structure and carbon cycling. Fe-bound organic carbon (Fe-OC) contributes to the long-term stabilization of soil organic carbon (SOC) in red soils, but extreme rainfall may alter Fe-OC stability. We combined continuous rainfall simulations with δ13C isotope tracing, synchrotron radiation Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (SR-FTIR), and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) to investigate Fe-OC stability in red soil aggregates under continuous rainfall. Continuous rainfall reorganized soil structure and reduced the proportion of macroaggregates by 12.38%. Fe-OC showed size-dependent differences, increasing by 102.53% in macroaggregates but decreasing by 28.02% in microaggregates. Feo increased by 5.08% in macroaggregates and 5.36% in microaggregates. SR-FTIR and SEM-EDS indicated that continuous rainfall promoted associations between Fe oxides and OC in macroaggregates but weakened them in microaggregates. δ13C tracing showed that the added carbon source increased Fe-OC formation in silt + clay and improved aggregate stability. These results indicate contrasting aggregate responses: Fe-OC stabilization was maintained in macroaggregates but declined in microaggregates. External carbon input may therefore enhance SOC stability by promoting Fe-OC formation in the fine fraction. This study provides a new mechanistic perspective for understanding the formation and stabilization of organic carbon in red soils under the combined effects of extreme rainfall and external carbon input in the context of global climate change.

title: A mineral-centric framework for predicting arsenic behaviour in lithium mine wastes
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Quentin Bollaert, Quentin Dehaine, Fernando Prado Araujo, Sonja Lavikko, Hugh O'Brien, Olivier Mathon, Valérie Cappuyns
abstract: The expansion of lithium mining in Europe is essential for securing strategic raw materials, but it raises increasing challenges for long-term tailings management. Arsenic (As), present at trace levels in lithium ores, can partition into mine wastes during beneficiation, yet its mineral hosts and solid-phase speciation remain poorly constrained due to low concentrations and diffuse distribution. This limits predictions of arsenic behaviour during processing, leaching, and storage, while current assessments often rely on bulk data that overlook key mineralogical controls. Here, we combine quantitative mineral deportment with As K-edge XANES to characterise arsenic distribution and speciation in ores and residues from three major European lithium projects. Arsenic is hosted in minor As-rich phases, such as sulfarsenides and sulfides, but it also occurs at trace levels within more abundant phases such as silicates, oxides, and phosphates. Sulfarsenides are dominated by As(–I), whereas other phases show mixed speciation (As(–I), As(III), As(V)). Linear combination fitting indicates overall dominance of As(–I) and As(V), with As(III) minor and sample-specific. XANES of leaching residues reveal the oxidation of arsenic released during arsenopyrite dissolution to As(V), followed by its immobilisation under specific pH conditions, demonstrating that arsenic leaching behaviour at disposal sites is strongly controlled by weathering conditions. Coupled with traditional leaching approaches, this mineral-centric framework quantifies the contribution of As-bearing phases to the release of arsenic under different environmental conditions, supporting more targeted tailings management and improved environmental strategies for lithium production.

title: Interfacial redox processes of plutonium with iron phases and organic ligands in repository-relevant brine systems
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Ugras Kaplan, Adrianne E. Navarrette, Phillip G. Hammer, Jandi L. Potter, Valery N. Bliznyuk, Brian A. Powell, Juliet Swanson, Jeremiah Beam
abstract: The redox behavior and solubility of plutonium (Pu) were investigated in complex, high-ionic-strength brines containing the organic ligands ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), oxalate, citrate, and acetate and the iron phases magnetite and zero-valent iron (Fe0) under an inert atmosphere. Long-term batch solubility experiments were conducted using an undersaturation approach to evaluate Pu oxidation-state distribution and the solid phases controlling solubility under reducing, alkaline conditions relevant to some deep geologic repositories. A novel dual-sampling strategy was implemented to simultaneously determine Pu oxidation states in (i) Pu-bearing precipitates and (ii) Pu associated with iron phases after long-term reaction periods of up to 1300 days, providing a realistic, interface-resolved view of redox processes in saline environments. Pu LIII-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) revealed that Pu(III) dominates in Fe0 systems, whereas Pu(IV) predominates in magnetite systems, independent of organic ligands. The ligands caused only minor shifts in oxidation state and did not substantially alter overall solubility trends. Pu LIII-edge EXAFS indicated predominantly inner-sphere Pu–Fe coordination, with only minor PuO2-like contributions. Bulk powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) showed no detectable bulk structural alteration or measurable bulk phase transformation of either metallic iron or magnetite over the three-year equilibration period. Plutonium solubility varied by up to two orders of magnitude (10−5–10−8 M) across pCH + 7–10. Small organic-induced changes in Pu oxidation state were not accompanied by significant changes in solubility. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was consistent with XANES, showing the same oxidation-state trends and confirming Pu(III) and Pu(IV) dominance in Fe0-and magnetite-bearing systems, respectively, under the investigated conditions. Scanning electron microscopy-energy dispersive X-ray (SEM–EDX) mapping demonstrated a clear spatial association between Pu and Fe on particle surfaces, supporting close Pu–Fe coupling within the interfacial microstructure. Overall, this long-term dataset provides direct experimental evidence for stable, metallic Fe0 and magnetite-dependent Pu redox partitioning within the specific brine compositions, iron materials, and experimental conditions investigated and highlights the critical role of surface-mediated redox interactions in controlling Pu speciation and solubility. These findings inform long-term safety assessments of salt-based repositories and may also be relevant to other geological disposal concepts in high-salinity groundwater environments.

title: Application of large community sorption datasets to surface complexation and ion exchange model development: Uranium sorption to montmorillonite
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Luis Eguiguren, Haruko Wainwright, Mavrik Zavarin
abstract: The safe disposal of nuclear waste depends critically on robust predictions of radionuclide mobility in subsurface environments, where sorption to mineral surfaces is a key retardation mechanism. Mechanistic models, such as surface complexation (SC) and ion exchange (IE), offer improved predictive capability over empirical (Kd) partitioning approaches but are hindered by a lack of internally consistent, comprehensive reaction constant databases. This study leverages the LLNL Surface Complexation/Ion Exchange (L-SCIE) database—an open-source, FAIR-compliant repository containing over 100,000 sorption data—to optimize SC/IE reaction constants for uranium(VI) sorption to montmorillonite, a common clay mineral proposed as nuclear waste repository backfill. Using automated workflows and the CrunchFlow geochemical modeling engine, we tested the non-electrostatic SC/IE models of Bradbury and Baeyens (2005) and Marinich et al. (2025) against 2585 U(VI)-montmorillonite community sorption data spanning a broad range of pH, ionic strength, mineral source, and solution conditions. These published U(VI)-montmorillonite models were originally calibrated to much smaller datasets and failed to simulate the larger community data. However, the published reactions constants could be readily adjusted to more effectively capture the large set of community data, underscoring the benefit of large, accessible community datasets in model calibration. A separate reaction/parameter optimization scheme revealed that as few as four reactions (three SC, one IE) can effectively reproduce the community data. Inclusion of ternary carbonate surface complexes did not improve model calibration under the tested non-electrostatic model framework. Importantly, different sources of montmorillonite (Arizona vs. Wyoming) were also found to yield statistically equivalent fitted parameters which is critical to addressing data transferability. This work establishes a scalable, transparent methodology for SC/IE database development to support data-driven performance assessment and safety case modeling for nuclear waste repositories. Future efforts will build on this approach to grow the L-SCIE FAIR community database and develop comprehensive self-consistent SC/IE reaction databases to advance the reliability of reactive transport simulations in complex geochemical environments.

title: Discriminatory power of 204 Pb-inclusive Pb isotope systematics for seasonal variability in atmospheric Pb: evidence from western Japan
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Yu Saitoh, Yu Umezawa, Kazuaki Kawamoto, Masaharu Tanimizu, Tsuyoshi Ishikawa
abstract: Lead (Pb) isotope ratios are widely used to trace atmospheric aerosol sources, but most atmospheric Pb studies continue to rely on isotope ratios among the radiogenic isotopes 206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb. Ratios including 204Pb can provide a broader isotope-ratio space, yet their statistical advantage for resolving atmospheric aerosol populations has rarely been evaluated quantitatively. Here, we analyzed aerosol samples collected at Omura, western Japan, from June 2011 to August 2012 and compared conventional 204Pb-exclusive isotope ratios (206Pb/207Pb and 208Pb/207Pb) with 204Pb-inclusive ratios (206Pb/204Pb, 207Pb/204Pb, and 208Pb/204Pb). Seasonal classes were defined a priori using calendar-based intervals. Air-mass backward trajectories, residue titanium (Ti) concentrations, and previously reported strontium (Sr)-neodymium (Nd) isotope compositions supported the interpretation of the seasonal groups as contrasting transport regimes. Selected sample-level comparisons showed that the positions in 204Pb-inclusive isotope space were broadly consistent with independently calculated regional transport pathways. In particular, samples associated with transport over or near southern China plotted toward the S-China reference field in 204Pb-inclusive space, whereas this relationship was not clearly resolved using conventional ratios because the N-China and S-China reference fields overlapped. All Pb isotope ratios showed significant seasonal variability, but multivariate statistics indicated stronger discrimination using the 204Pb-inclusive system. MANOVA and pairwise MANOVA resolved more seasonal contrasts with 204Pb-inclusive ratios, and PERMANOVA showed higher seasonal explanatory power that persisted after variable standardization. These isotope and trajectory relationships should be interpreted as evidence for transport-related Pb isotope variability rather than deterministic source apportionment because regional reference fields overlap. These results demonstrate that 204Pb-inclusive Pb isotope ratios provide modest but consistent improvement in resolving seasonal atmospheric Pb variability and indicate the need for broader acquisition of 204Pb-inclusive atmospheric and source reference data.

title: Groundwater quality and vulnerability assessment in flood-prone areas of the Ikopa watershed, Antananarivo, Madagascar: an integrated hydrogeochemical and statistical approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Voary Rajoelina, Geneviève Bordeleau, Naivo Rabesiranana, Joël Rajaobelison, Voahirana Ramaroson, Emma Mamifarananahary, Christian Ulrich Rakotomalala, Falintsoa Fanantenana Asombola Razafitsalama
abstract: This study evaluates groundwater quality and contamination risk in flood-prone areas of the Ikopa watershed in Antananarivo, Madagascar, where rapid urbanization, inadequate sanitation, and recurrent flooding threaten shallow hand-dug wells used for drinking water. The objectives were to characterize groundwater quality, identify major contaminants and their sources, and evaluate the influence of hydrogeological conditions and local well protection measures on contamination risk. A total of 35 water samples, including groundwater from 26 hand-dug wells and 9 river sites, were collected during the rainy season and analyzed for major ions, trace elements, hydrocarbons, and microbiological indicators. Multivariate statistical analyses, including principal component analysis and hierarchical cluster analysis, identified three hydrochemical groups reflecting differences in mineralization, redox conditions, and anthropogenic influences. High concentrations of nitrate, hydrocarbons, and fecal indicators (Escherichia coli, total coliforms, and intestinal enterococci) were detected, frequently exceeding drinking water guidelines. Nitrate contamination was mainly attributed to manure and septic waste sources based on dual isotope analysis (δ15N, δ18O), with evidence of denitrification in some samples. Groundwater vulnerability was assessed using the DRASTIC method, while an integrated contamination risk classification considered land use, flood exposure, and well protection conditions. Results showed that well protection measures were associated with reduced bacterial contamination but had limited effects on nitrate and hydrocarbon pollution. These findings highlight that protecting wells alone is insufficient and that integrated interventions targeting sanitation, flood management, land-use planning, and groundwater protection are needed to safeguard drinking water resources in rapidly urbanizing flood-prone regions.

title: Organic matter in CO 2 -rich mineral waters of the Lastochka reservoir, Russia
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): V.A. Poturay, E.V. Zippa, E.A. Vakh
abstract: The study of organic impurities composition in natural waters, particularly CO2-rich mineral waters, is an important aspect of geochemical research. It provides an understanding of transformation mechanisms and migration of organic matter and also allows researchers to identify organic pollutants and their distribution pathways. The study objects include mineral waters with high concentrations of mantle CO2, as well as surrounding groundwaters and surface waters. The solid-phase extraction method was used in situ to concentrate semi-volatile organic compounds. Qualitative analysis of these compounds was carried out using capillary gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) was identified using a high-temperature catalytic oxidation method. The DOC concentration ranged from 0.5 mg/L in the groundwaters to 9.1 mg/L in the river waters. A total of 133 semi-volatile organic compounds were identified in the studied waters. The saturated, branched and aromatic hydrocarbons dominated in the deep CO2-rich mineral waters. Similar components were also predominant in the shallow mineral and fresh waters, together with terpenes and phthalates. It was established that the relative concentration of n-alkanes, alkenes and arenes is higher in the mineral waters than in the fresh waters. In contrast, the relative content of isoalkanes, heteroaromatic hydrocarbons, esters, alcohols and terpenes is higher in the fresh waters than in the mineral well. The mineral waters contained range of arenes and naphthenes that were absent from the fresh waters. Conversely, the fresh waters contained a greater variety of isoalkanes, esters, heteroaromatic hydrocarbons and terpenes than mineral waters. The possible origin of organic matter was attributed to bacterial activity and interaction with sedimentary deposits, whereas the influence of plant residues appeared to be less significant. In our opinion, the mantle CO2 may extract naphthenes and arenes from sediments in the deep mineral waters. In addition, phthalates, Cl-hydrocarbons and several other compounds were detected in the studied waters and were interpreted as anthropogenic pollutants. Therefore, the studied waters appear to be susceptible to anthropogenic contamination.

title: Elemental and isotope geochemistry of Smackover Formation brines in Alabama and Arkansas: Implications for fluid mixing and water-rock interaction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Kelly Kreitzer, Ming-Kuo Lee, Haibo Zou, Yang Wang, Andrew L. Masterson, Ann Sullivan Ojeda, Zeki M. Billor, Natalia Malina, Gregory M. Guthrie, Bonnie McDevitt, Ann Arnold, Demi Durham
abstract: This study investigates the geochemical characteristics of brines within the Upper Jurassic Smackover Formation in Alabama and Arkansas through elemental and isotopic analyses and geochemical modeling to reveal the extent and nature of fluid mixing and water-rock interactions. Smackover Formation brines exhibit Na-Cl-Ca hydrogeochemical facies and sulfate depletion relative to seawater. Lower sulfate concentrations, coupled with high H2S concentrations in some brines (0-364 mg/L) at temperatures >80°C, suggest that thermochemical sulfate reduction occurred. Cl/Br and Na/Br ratios indicate that salinity was controlled by the mixing of meteoric water with evaporated seawater that had reached halite saturation, rather than by halite dissolution. The δ18O and δ2H values of the brines also suggest mixing between meteoric water and evaporated seawater that had reached gypsum and halite saturation. Geochemical modeling of seawater evaporation predicts a Cl-Na or Cl-Mg facies after halite saturation, contrasting with the observed Cl-Ca dominance of the Smackover Formation brines. The Ca-enriched brines may have evolved from Cl-Mg-dominated evaporated seawater through dolomitization of limestone. The 87Sr/86Sr ratios range from 0.70740 to 0.71048, higher than the average of Jurassic seawater (0.707). The non-linear relationship between 87Sr/86Sr and 1000/Sr suggests alteration of brine geochemistry by fluid mixing or by inputs from Sr and 87Sr-enriched rock sources. Lithium concentrations are positively correlated with 87Sr/86Sr ratios and TDS in brines enriched in these constituents. These correlations suggest deeper-seated geogenic sources and have implications for Li exploration in the northern Gulf Coast basin. Normal faults associated with the pre-Jurassic topography may have provided potential pathways for brine migration into the Smackover Formation under the influence of overpressure or thermohaline convection in the Gulf Coast.

title: Molecular compositions and source identification of organic aerosols in the highly polluted city: Dhaka, Bangladesh
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Mosammat. J. Fardus Jui, Md Mozammel Haque, Mohammad Lokman Hossain, Masum Billah, Md Farhan Ahmed, S.M. Mostahidul Hasan, Abul Kalam M. Lutfor Rahman
abstract: Organic aerosol (OA) represents a fundamental component of atmospheric particulate matter and is widely acknowledged as a critical contributor to ambient air degradation and climate change. Dhaka, among the most polluted cities globally, experiences alarmingly poor air quality. Aerosol samples collected in Dhaka, Bangladesh, during the winter of 2020 (from 10 January to 10 February), were examined to determine their carbonaceous fractions, organic constituents, and stable carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) isotopic compositions of total carbon (TC) and total nitrogen (TN) in fine particulate matter (PM2.5). The measured organic content, calculated as the sum of all quantified target organic compound concentrations (n-alkanes, PAHs, hopanes, and steranes), was considerably higher at night (avg. 768 ± 501 ng m−3) compared to the daytime (349 ± 506 ng m−3). This disparity is likely attributable to the presence of atmospheric inversion layers and elevated nighttime emissions from heavy-duty vehicles. N-Alkanes were the prevalent compounds (mean total: 454 ng m−3), followed by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) (80.4 ng m−3), hopanes (9.38 ng m−3), and steranes (2.61 ng m−3). The low carbon preference index (CPI) of n-alkanes (mean: 1.30) indicates a predominantly anthropogenic origin. The PAH profile was primarily composed of high molecular weight (HMW) PAHs (4-ring and 5-ring compounds), constituting over 75% of the total, emphasizing the significant health risks posed by Dhaka's aerosols. Diagnostic ratios (DRs) suggest that HMW PAHs were primarily associated with fossil fuel combustion, and hopanes were linked to traffic emissions. The δ13C and δ15N isotopic signatures suggest that human-related activities, particularly the combustion of fossil-based fuels, including coal and petroleum products, and biomass burning, are the predominant sources of carbonaceous and nitrogenous aerosols. Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) was applied to identify and quantify the key sources of PM2.5 in the study area, revealing significant contributions from coal combustion, traffic, and biomass burning emissions. The health risk assessment highlights a substantial carcinogenic threat from airborne PAHs, with risk levels far exceeding the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended standards. These findings point out the urgent need for local and regional pollution control measures to reduce excessive anthropogenic aerosol emissions in South Asia.

title: Galena as a recorder of metal sourcing and sulfur evolution in a rift-related sediment-hosted Pb–Zn system: Insights from the Gunga deposit, Pakistan
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Muhammad Amar Gul, Huishan Zhang, Mohamed Faisal, Zahid Imran Bhatti, Nosheen Akhtar, Rizwan Sarwar Awan, Xiaoyong Yang
abstract: Galena is one of the most robust recorders of ore-fluid Pb isotope compositions in sediment-hosted Pb–Zn systems; however, coupled sulfur–lead isotope systematics in galena remain underexplored in many deposits. This study presents the first integrated major-element and in situ sulfur–lead isotope dataset for galena from the Gunga Pb–Zn deposit, a rift-related sediment-hosted system developed along the western margin of the Indian Plate. Galena from the Lower Mineralization Zone (LMZ) and Upper Mineralization Zone (UMZ) is chemically homogeneous and close to ideal PbS stoichiometry, with Pb 85.6–87.2 wt% and analytical totals of 99.06–99.87 wt%. These features are consistent with precipitation from low-temperature basinal brines and indicate effective preservation of primary compositions. Galena defines a remarkably narrow Pb isotope field (206Pb/204Pb = 18.541–18.554; 207Pb/204Pb = 15.682–15.692; 208Pb/204Pb = 38.705–38.727; n = 32), consistent with a compositionally homogeneous or well-mixed upper-crustal Pb reservoir. In contrast, sulfur isotope compositions vary strongly with mineralogy and stratigraphic position. Galena ranges from −1.0 to +4.9‰ overall, whereas sphalerite ranges from −10.5 to −0.7‰ in the LMZ and +3.0 to +5.6‰ in the UMZ, and pyrite ranges from −15.0 to +20.0‰ and −23.5 to +26.2‰, respectively. The apparent zone-scale δ34S difference between sphalerite and galena changes from −5.7‰ in the LMZ to +3.1‰ in the UMZ. Inter-mineral sulfur isotope relationships indicate pronounced disequilibrium in the LMZ, consistent with open-system fluid flow and kinetically controlled sulfide precipitation. In the UMZ, restoration of the expected sphalerite > galena ordering indicates a greater approach toward isotopic equilibration under more focused and chemically buffered conditions. Together, the narrow galena Pb-isotope field and zone-dependent sulfur-isotope patterns reveal a clear contrast between comparatively homogeneous metal-source information and evolving sulfur-system conditions during mineralization. These results demonstrate that galena provides a robust quantitative record of primary ore-fluid Pb isotope signatures and, when interpreted with coexisting sulfides, offers critical insight into sulfur evolution in multi-stage sediment-hosted Pb–Zn systems.

title: Modeling the sorption of palladium onto a natural bentonite under highly saline and alkaline conditions: Kinetics, mechanism, competition
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Jan Jakob Langer, Aaron Haben, Ralf Kautenburger
abstract: In proposals for clay-based repositories for high-level nuclear waste (HLW), bentonite is a crucial component within a multi-barrier system. For robust safety assessments of a HLW disposal site, knowledge about geochemical interactions between bentonite and HLW elements is of great importance. HLW contains palladium occurring as 107Pd (t1/2 = 6.5 · 106 years), but to this date, reliable data on its sorption behavior towards bentonite remains scarce, especially under alkaline conditions. In this study, we investigated palladium’s sorption behavior onto a natural, untreated bentonite (Calcigel®) as a function of time, pH, ionic strength (emulating Northern German porewater) and concentration in batch experiments, quantifying retention via ICP-QQQ. In the kinetic studies, we showed that a high ionic strength delays the formation of the sorption equilibrium. Retention itself is not impacted by it, but decreases with excess calcium. Based on the experimental results, we modeled Pd(II) sorption using the 2 site protolysis non-electrostatic surface complexation/cation exchange (2SPNE SC/CE) model, while accounting for divalent competition by Mg(II) and Ca(II) which are naturally contained in bentonite. We identified four Pd(II) surface complexes, alongside two surface complexes each for Mg(II) and Ca(II), with an overall good agreement with experimental data across all conditions investigated. Based on experimental data and model values of the concentration dependence studies, we applied sorption isotherms, resulting in excellent correlations (R2 > 0.95). The Freundlich isotherm predicted a near linear sorption behavior at trace Pd(II) concentrations, while the Langmuir fit (based on model values) estimated a realistic q max of 3.13 · 10−4 mol kg−1.

title: The performance of PHREEQC databases for modelling the solubility of CO 2 , N 2 , CO 2 -N 2 mixtures, calcite and barite at elevated temperatures, pressures and electrolyte concentrations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Knud Dideriksen, Hanne Dahl Holmslykke, Bi Yun Zhen-Wu, Jakob Molander, Claus Kjøller
abstract: Modelling of geochemical reactions in the deeper subsurface can provide valuable insight into the state and dynamics of a system where processes are complicated to observe. In addition, it allows prediction of the outcome of interventions, such as geothermal exploitation or CO2 injection. The degree to which the modelling portrays reality depends in part on the ability of the thermodynamic data to describe solubility of gases and solids accurately. For most modelling software, the thermodynamic data is typically compiled in databases, which have been tested to some extent. However, the capabilities of the databases to accurately calculate solubility over a wide range of conditions are most often not well defined. This study tests the performance of 13 PHREEQC databases, benchmarking them against an empirical dataset with 3147 measurements of the solubility of CO2(g), N2(g), CO2(g) - N2(g) mixtures, calcite, and barite at variable temperature, pressure, and electrolyte concentration. Our work shows that the databases employing the Peng-Robinson equation of state and molar volume changes of reaction are generally capable of correctly describing experimental values of solubility at higher pressure as intended. Databases relying on the Pitzer approach for description of activity coefficients often provide reasonably accurate calculations of solubility at an extended range of electrolyte concentrations at variable temperature and pressure. For many databases, including those based on Pitzer equations, calculations substantially deviate from measured values at conditions that are unexpected based on general expectations to database performance. This is particularly true for simulations of calcite solubility. Identifying these deviations requires tests such as the one given here. Our approach allows selection of databases based on the objective criterion that calculations should match empirical data at or near the modelled conditions as closely as possible. We exemplify the use of our results for database selection for the simulation of calcite scaling in a model geothermal well. To enable users and developers of databases to conduct tests of performance themselves, the supplementary information contains experimental data, input files and Python code for calculations.

title: Removal of dissolved zinc using zero-valent iron: Aqueous geochemistry, XANES, and EXAFS analyses
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Lingyi Kong, Heather K. Shrimpton, Jane Eagling, Ning Chen, Y. Zou Finfrock, Carol J. Ptacek, David W. Blowes
abstract: Zinc is an essential micronutrient for the health of humans and other organisms. However, high Zn concentrations, such as those associated with mining wastewater and urban runoff, can be harmful. Zero-valent iron (ZVI) has been used as a remediation material in permeable reactive barriers (PRBs) to reduce Zn concentrations in water. This study used laboratory batch experiments employing two Zn-bearing solutions (made from ZnCl2 and ZnSO4) with varying alkalinity (0 and 10 mg L−1 CaCO3) to evaluate Zn removal mechanisms associated with ZVI. X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analyses of the solid ZVI at the end of the experiment (288 h) indicated the coordination number of Zn changed from six in the initial solutions to four on solid ZVI. The primary mechanisms removing Zn from solution were precipitation as ZnO and Zn(OH)2 and adsorption on ferrihydrite. These results help characterize the removal mechanism of Zn by ZVI under different chemical conditions and have implications for the long-term sequestration of Zn in ZVI remediation systems.

title: Lake sediment trace-element and strontium isotope data reveals spatiotemporal changes and anthropogenic influence: Implications for archaeological provenance studies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 210 Author(s): Sander Jegorov, Rasmus Andreasen, Bent Vad Odgaard, Erik Thomsen, Stéphane Bodin
