Target-site observations from 2021 to 2022 were subsampled to simulate sparse monitoring during model development. Data from 2023 were reserved for independent testing, with target-site observations used only for performance evaluation. Across the four variables, the data-driven model improved Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) by 4.2–27.4 % relative to the mechanistic model. Transport-consistency regularization provided a further 1.5–7.4 % improvement over the data-driven baseline, with the largest gain for ammonia nitrogen. The physics-guided model also showed lower performance variability and lower sensitivity to independent Gaussian perturbations of adjacent-station inputs. These results support the use of physics-guided virtual sensing to extend river water-quality monitoring coverage where continuous target-site measurements are unavailable.

title: A prototype multi-hazard early warning system integrating flood and landslide forecasting: application in the upper Garonne River Basin
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Flavio Alexander Asurza, Marcel Hürlimann, Vicente Medina, Francis Nieto
abstract: Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (MHEWS) are essential for disaster risk management, yet operational implementation remains limited by challenges in hazard integration, forecast uncertainty, and computational requirements. This study develops and evaluates a fast and lightweight prototype MHEWS integrating fluvial flooding and shallow landslide forecasting. The MHEWS couples snow-hydrological modeling (SNOW-17 and CREST) with a slope stability approach (infinite slope and Random Forest models) driven by bias-corrected Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) meteorological forecasts. Quantile mapping bias correction substantially improves precipitation and temperature forecast performance, reducing variability errors and enhancing distributional agreement. Applied in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Spanish Pyrenees) using 24-hour lead time forecasts, multi-hazard analysis for 2010–2020 reveals asymmetric coupling between hazards: flood warnings respond rapidly to rainfall intensity, while landslide warnings depend on cumulative subsurface conditioning and antecedent soil moisture, with high-level warnings rarely coinciding. Evaluation of multiple forecast lead times (24, 48, 72 h) for June 2013 demonstrates systematic performance degradation with increasing lead time, reflecting amplified uncertainty propagation. This degradation is further compounded by the limitations of the quantile mapping approach; while it effectively aligns marginal statistics, it fails to preserve temporal autocorrelation or event persistence. This introduces residual biases in cumulative dynamics that disproportionately affect landslide prediction compared to flood estimation. The fully automated prototype, designed to be scalable and transferable, and built on open-source software and cloud infrastructure, demonstrates operational feasibility for real-time early warning applications across hydro-meteorologically complex environments.

title: Hydrological diagnosis of preferential seepage and internal erosion in embankment dams and levees: From transient forcing to uncertainty-aware decisions
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Zhiwen Xie, Liang Chen, Hanxuan Luo, Ruiyang Liu, Ding Sang
abstract: Preferential seepage becomes evidence of internal erosion only when the hydraulic response can be linked to particle detachment and transport. This critical review examines that distinction in embankment dams and levees, considering how transient loading, storage, and geological structure affect both the physical process and its observation. Hydraulic records establish the response to changing loads, while thermal and geophysical surveys help constrain possible pathways. Particle sampling and investigation of sediment sources provide evidence of material loss that these indirect observations cannot establish alone. Joint interpretation of lag, attenuation, hysteresis, recession, and spatial coherence helps distinguish regional groundwater and bank-storage responses from localized seepage. The comparison of sensing and inverse methods shows why resolution, uncertainty, and verification must be assessed for the particular question being asked. We propose an evidence hierarchy and an observation-conditioned event tree to connect these interpretations with engineering decisions. For learned models and digital twins, testing on unseen events and assets, independent physical checks, and the consequences of false and missed alarms are central to evaluating practical benefit. The review emphasizes physically grounded, site-specific interpretation and verification as the basis for diagnosis and warning.

title: Projected droughts readily trigger vegetation decline
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Zixu Jia, Tao Lin, Xiangzhong Guo, Faith Ka Shun Chan, Lichang Yin, Hongkai Geng, Yicheng Zheng, Junmao Zhang, Yuan Chen, Meixia Lin, Jing Lin, Yuqin Liu
abstract: Drought is intensifying under a warming climate, while the lag of vegetation response and the drought trigger thresholds for relative vegetation loss remain insufficiently quantified. Here we provide a global assessment of vegetation responses to the Terrestrial Water Storage Drought Severity Index (TWS_DSI) under historical and future climate scenarios. Using five vegetation indicators, including Leaf Area Index (LAI), Fraction of Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FPAR), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (kNDVI), and Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), we quantified their lagged responses to drought during the historical period. The mean optimal lag times ranged from 8.20 months for LAI to 10.59 months for NDVI, with FPAR (8.78 months), GPP (9.80 months), and kNDVI (10.42 months) showing intermediate lag responses. Based on future LAI simulations under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, the mean lag varied from 5.15 to 10.48 months. At predefined vegetation loss levels (≤40th, ≤30th, ≤20th, ≤10th), we identified the drought trigger thresholds for vegetation decline and mapped their spatial variability. Compared to the historical baseline, the average drought trigger thresholds increased by 30.0%, 36.3%, and 35.3% under the SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios, respectively, indicating heightened vulnerability whereby even milder drought conditions in the future could trigger vegetation decline. Our findings characterize the temporal lags, threshold behavior, and projected changes of vegetation responses to terrestrial water deficits, providing a scientific basis for assessing ecosystem vulnerability and informing targeted ecological conservation and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Using stable isotope to depict 3 typical tree species’ water use in a subtropical forest through three consecutive hydrological years
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Xiong Xiao, Yong Zhang, Xinping Zhang, Jinzhao Liu
abstract: Against global climate change, more frequent extreme droughts have profoundly altered water cycling and plant water use strategies in the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum (SPAC). The subtropical monsoon region suffers frequent droughts despite abundant precipitation. Based on in-situ observations (June 2022 ∼ May 2025) covering a centennial extreme drought, we analyzed δ2H and δ18O in precipitation, xylem water of three dominant tree species, 0 ∼ 20 cm soil water, and 20 ∼ 100 cm weathered layer water in a subtropical secondary forest in Hunan, China, while plant water sources were quantified using the MixSIAR model. Our results showed that extreme drought enhanced non-equilibrium fractionation in the SPAC, markedly lowering the soil and xylem water line slope. In summer and in the extreme drought year, shallow and desiccated 0 ∼ 20 cm soil forced plants to rely heavily on the weathered layers as a “lifesaving water source”, with utilization of 20 ∼ 60 cm strongly weathered layer exceeding 35% and 60 ∼ 100 cm weakly weathered layer exceeding 20% for all three species. Under drought stress, species exhibited divergent strategies: the evergreen broad-leaved tree C. camphora showed flexible “opportunistic” water use; the deciduous broad-leaved tree L. formosana combined deep water uptake and leaf abscission for drought resistance; the evergreen coniferous tree P. massoniana suffered the highest physiological vulnerability and widespread mortality due to rigid hydraulic structure and cavitation risk. Extreme drought was a key driver reshaping plant water niches, with stronger impacts on water use depths, interspecific competition, and community stability than ordinary seasonal drought. Conservation should optimize stand structure, mitigate soil erosion, and apply targeted interventions during extreme drought events.

title: A coupled optical-thermodynamic framework for predicting freezing onset in unsaturated saline silty clay
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Haojin Zhang, Haihua Zhang, Xianfeng Ma, Jiangu Qian, Eiji Fukuzawa
abstract: The onset of ice formation in unsaturated saline porous media controls frost heave, water redistribution and hydrothermal property changes in cold-region soils, yet it remains difficult to define because pore water freezes progressively rather than at a single temperature. Here we combine polymer optical fiber (POF) sensing with thermodynamic modelling to identify and predict the ice-formation onset temperature in silty clay. The exposed optical fiber segment responds to abrupt changes in refractive index and scattering caused by pore-ice formation, providing an optical criterion that is distinct from the conventional temperature-plateau method. Cooling experiments on three silty clays show that, under salt-free conditions, the onset temperature increases with water content, whereas addition of NaCl produces a further depression that increases with salt concentration. These trends indicate that freezing onset is governed by coupled pore-scale confinement, adsorption/capillary pressure and solution thermodynamics. We therefore develop a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron model that integrates the Gibbs–Thomson curvature effect, adsorption/capillary pressure and water activity, while accounting for pore-size distribution and unsaturated pore filling through a critical water-filled pore radius and an effective pore radius. The model reproduces the measured onset temperatures across different water contents and NaCl concentrations. This optical–thermodynamic framework provides a physically consistent criterion for ice-formation onset in unsaturated saline soils and improves the prediction of phase-transition thresholds that regulate water redistribution, salt migration and hydrothermal connectivity in cold-region hydrological systems.

title: Distributed modeling reveals the evolution of supraglacial lakes: a multi-basin study on the Greenland ice sheet
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jiake Wu, Lei Zheng, Qi Liang, Teng Li, Quan Zhou, Chuyue Peng, Baojuan Huai, Zhuoqi Chen, Xiao Cheng, Fengming Hui
abstract: Supraglacial lakes (SGLs) on the Greenland Ice Sheet play a critical role in modulating surface energy balance and meltwater storage, thereby influencing ice-sheet mass balance and hydrological processes. Accurately characterizing the evolution of SGLs is essential for elucidating the mechanisms governing lake behavior and for predicting the timing and conditions of lake drainage events. However, characterizing SGL evolution remains challenging because most existing SGL models either provide one-dimensional representations of vertical lake evolution or neglect vertical lake deepening altogether. Here, we present GlacierLake_v3, a distributed SGL model that simulates lake evolution in horizontal and vertical dimensions by explicitly resolving runoff generation, transport, loss, and accumulation across the ice-sheet surface. Meltwater losses occur during transport processes including retention, refreezing, evaporation, and drainage into crevasses, which are commonly neglected in previous models and are here collectively represented using a constant meltwater loss rate parameter. This parameter is calibrated for each catchment using satellite observations from different years. Validation across different basins demonstrates that GlacierLake_v3 accurately reproduces lake areas and volumes, with maximum R2 values of 0.89 and 0.95, respectively. The model also successfully captures the two-dimensional distribution of lake depth and its temporal evolution, showing close agreement with satellite-derived retrievals. Our results further show that daily and cumulative runoff from regional climate models (RCMs) were 14–79% and 6–122% higher, respectively, than the lake-volume-based estimates. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating more comprehensive meltwater losses into RCMs to improve their representation of supraglacial hydrology.

title: Trends in the frequency and duration of high flow events across climates
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Amee Huang, Mercy Gijima, Caleb Dykman, Rory Nathan, Conrad Wasko
abstract: Flood events play a critical role in infrastructure design, floodplain management, water supply and natural ecology. While large floods are a risk to life and infrastructure, smaller flood events, here termed high flow events, are essential for maintaining biodiversity of wetlands and filling our water supplies. With climate change altering extreme rainfall magnitude, frequency, and timing there is a need to understand the impact of these changes on catchment flow response. Globally, studies have generally focused on changes in flood magnitude, and the drivers of these changes, and there remains a gap in understanding the historical changes in the frequency and duration of high flow events – those critical for sustaining ecosystem health and water supply. Here, using a set of 476 long record streamflow gauging stations across the continent of Australia, which span a wide range of climate zones, we investigate the trend in the frequency of high flow events and their duration. We find that, across most arid and temperate regions, the frequency of high flow events has decreased and their duration shortened, suggesting a reduction in water availability. In the tropics, there have been increases in the frequency of high flow events. Testing the robustness of the historical trends to the assumptions made in the analysis, we find that the rarer the event, the more likely it is to be increasing in frequency. These results provide some evidence that climate change is impacting both streamflow magnitude and frequency, which has significant implications for water supply, as well as the health of our ecological and environmental systems.

title: Rising risk of carbon sink-source transition in China’s terrestrial ecosystems under compound drought-heat extremes
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Wenwen Guo, Shengzhi Huang, Shikun Sun, Deliang Chen, Qiang Huang
abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of compound drought-heat events pose a growing threat to terrestrial ecosystems, yet the carbon sink-source transition risks and dynamics under such combined stress remain poorly quantified. Here, we develop a risk assessment framework to evaluate historical and future carbon sink-source transition risks across terrestrial ecosystems in China, along with identifying the key drivers underlying their spatiotemporal evolution. Our results show that the warm temperate deciduous broad-leaved forest region in eastern China and southwestern China have historically exhibited elevated transition risks, with high-risk areas projected to expand southeastward under future climate scenarios. From the historical period to the SSP585 scenario, the national mean transition risk trend is projected to increase by approximately 1.69-fold relative to the historical level. Driver attribution indicates that precipitation is the dominant contributor to transition risk during the historical period (35.4%), followed by air temperature (13.4%) and vapor pressure deficit (11.3%). Notably, the influence of potential evapotranspiration and soil moisture on risk dynamics has intensified over time. Regions characterized by limited increases in precipitation combined with pronounced warming are projected to experience the largest increases in transition risks in the future. Overall, this study provides a systematic framework for assessing ecosystem carbon stability under compound climate extremes, offering critical insights for regional carbon management and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Dynamic-programming-based subwaveform retracking with along-track constraints for inland river water level retrieval from Sentinel-3 altimetry
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Mengran Tang, Lihua Xiong
abstract: Sentinel-3 radar altimetry provides an important data source for inland water level monitoring, yet accurate retrieval over rivers remains difficult because contaminated waveforms complicate subwaveform identification. This study proposes a dynamic-programming-based subwaveform retracking (DPSR) method, which transforms conventional footprint-wise retracking into an along-track global optimization problem, enabling the selection of physically consistent subwaveforms from contaminated observations for river water level retrieval. DPSR is evaluated over the Amazon basin with 78 gauge-virtual station (VS) pairs and the Poyang Lake basin with 39 gauge-VS pairs, and is compared with several existing retracking methods. The results indicate that DPSR outperforms all benchmark methods, yielding a median RMSE of 0.41 m, which decreases by 0.02–1.2 m compared with other methods, while improving data availability by about 39% relative to benchmark retrackers. Moreover, DPSR performs particularly well in narrow rivers. The proposed method highlights the value of integrating spatial constraints into subwaveform interpretation and offers a robust solution for satellite altimetry retrieval of river water levels in complex environments.

title: Quantifying dynamic ponding–detention effects of microtopography in low-relief plains: insights from field-scale hydrological monitoring
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Pengxuan Zhao, Gang Chen, Chuanhai Wang, Pingnan Zhang, Reinhard Hinkelmann, Jiale Gao, Yixiao Qian
abstract: Microtopography in low-relief plains exerts significant regulatory influences on surface hydrological responses. Yet its chaotic and nested configuration gives rise to highly dynamic ponding–detention processes that remain poorly understood. Based on field hydrological monitoring, this study proposed a process-based framework for quantifying microtopographic ponding–detention effects, comprising an elementary microtopographic unit (EMU)-based representation of hydrological connectivity, a microtopographic detention curve (MDC), and a microtopography-informed hydrological model (MIHM). The framework was evaluated using eighteen rainfall–runoff observations from two experimental plots together with high-resolution topographic data from seven representative sites. The EMU-based representation transformed intricate microtopographic configurations into an ordered topological network, enabling explicit characterization of the complex evolution of hydrological connectivity and ponding–detention processes. It reduced the number of units required for connectivity analysis by approximately one to two orders of magnitude while preserving the hierarchical organization of microtopography. The MDC effectively captured the nonlinear ponding–detention relationship, with mean R2 of 0.990 across seven study sites and 0.965 across 213 river-network polygons in the Taihu Basin. It exhibited scale dependence and strong transferability across DEM resolutions and spatial scales. Compared with the Taihu Basin Model–Plain Hydrological Module (TBM–PHM), the MIHM improved hydrograph simulations, increasing the mean NSE and KGE by 0.04 and 0.15, respectively, while reducing the relative total runoff error by 14.9% and the peak timing error by 2.5 min during validation. It was further incorporated into a hydrological–hydrodynamic modeling framework and applied across the Taihu Basin, demonstrating its applicability from field-scale plots to regional-scale river-network polygons. This study establishes a transferable framework for quantitatively describing microtopographic ponding-detention effects and advances understanding of hydrological mechanisms driven by microtopography in low-relief plains.

title: External source restructuring activates legacy sediment phosphorus cycling and delays recovery in a shallow plateau lake
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Ziteng Wang, Fuhong Sun, Qingjun Guo, Aoping Mao, Royngfei Wei, Jingfu Wang, Fengchang Wu
abstract: Legacy phosphorus (P) stored in lake sediments can delay water quality improvement after external inputs decline, but the historical transition from external P enrichment to persistent sedimentary feedback remains poorly resolved. Here, we combined two dated sediment cores from Dianchi Lake, China, with sequential P fractionation, sediment inferred lake water total phosphorus (SI-TP), phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18OPO4), structural equation modelling, and Bayesian source apportionment. SI-TP increased from 0.10 ± 0.02 mg L−1 during 1825–1870 to 0.32 ± 0.12 mg L−1 during 1990–2022. This increase was accompanied by a decline in the relative contribution of mineral associated HCl-P, expansion of NaHCO3-P and NaOH-P pools, and a 225.8% increase in net sediment P burial flux relative to Stage I. Disequilibrium of δ18OPO4 values increased most clearly in the labile NaHCO3-P fraction, indicating progressively stronger nonequilibrium processing associated with changes in P sources and sedimentary biogeochemical processes. Bayesian mixing models further indicated increasing contributions from fertilizer and industrial wastewater after 1960. Across the reconstructed time series, anthropogenic pressure and sedimentary P indicators were strongly associated with lake water TP, whereas climatic effects were predominantly indirect. Together, these results show that historical external P enrichment was recorded not only as greater sediment P accumulation but also as a reorganization toward more reactive P pools. This durable increased P burial flux and reorganisation are consistent with a legacy P feedback that may sustain eutrophication risk after external loading is reduced.

title: Land-use controls on soil hydraulic functioning: the role of pore organization and gravel distribution in an agricultural catchment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Leandro Dalbianco, Jean Paolo Gomes Minella, Gizachew Ayalew Tiruneh, Maria Cândida Moitinho Nunes, José Miguel Reichert
abstract: Soil hydraulic functioning in headwater catchments reflects interactions among pore organization, land use, and coarse-fragment distribution, but the relative importance of these controls remains uncertain when point measurements are interpreted at broader spatial scales. This study evaluated how near-surface soil permeability and water storage varied among land-use and tillage systems and whether those variations were associated with soil structure and gravel distribution in a 1.19 km2 agricultural headwater catchment in southern Brazil. Physical and hydraulic properties were measured in the 0–0.05 m layer at 69 sampling points (414 undisturbed cores), including bulk density, pore-size distribution, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), air permeability (Ka), water retention across matric potentials, gravel content, texture, and soil organic carbon (SOC). Planned contrasts, Pearson correlations, and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to evaluate group differences and multivariate associations. Natural forest had lower bulk density and greater permeability-related attributes than grazed grassland, whereas conservation tillage increased water retention and plant-available water relative to conventional tillage without a consistent increase in Ksat. Gravel abundance was positively associated with macroporosity, Ka, and Ksat and negatively associated with water retention near field capacity, but these correlations do not establish a causal pathway. Land-use differences in water retention were strongest near saturation and diminished at higher suctions. The first two PCA axes explained 49.3% of total variance and separated transmission-related attributes (Ksat, Ka, macroporosity, total porosity, and saturated water content) from denser, storage-related conditions, while substantial variability remained in higher components. Overall, near-surface hydraulic functioning was more closely associated with pore organization and coarse-fragment abundance than with texture or SOC. Because the study represents only the surface layer of one catchment and did not explicitly model spatial autocorrelation or deeper pedogenetic discontinuities, extrapolation to profile- and catchment-scale flow should be made cautiously.

title: Physics-constrained deep learning for evapotranspiration estimation by integrating process-model information and observations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yong Bo, Kai Liu, Shudong Wang, Long Li, Guoxu Li, Xueke Li
abstract: Accurate estimation of evapotranspiration (ET) is essential for characterizing regional water cycle dynamics and informing sustainable agricultural water management. However, conventional physics-based ET models are often hindered by complex parameterizations and uncertainties in forcing inputs, while purely data-driven approaches frequently suffer from weak physical consistency. This study develops a physics-constrained deep learning (PCDL) framework for generating high-resolution (daily, 100 m) ET by incorporating process-model information into a neural network learning architecture. The framework first constructs a consistent high-resolution dataset of land surface variables through multi-source data fusion. Building on this dataset, a baseline artificial neural network (ANN) is established using remotely sensed variables and in-situ eddy covariance observations, and is subsequently extended into a physics-constrained model by incorporating information derived from surface energy balance and vegetation biophysical processes. The framework is evaluated in the Middle Heihe River Basin during 2012–2016. Results show that PCDL outperforms the ANN model in cross-site transfer experiments, reducing root mean square error (RMSE) by ∼20% on average and by up to 32%. Compared with physics-based benchmark models, PCDL achieves an overall RMSE reduction of ∼30–40% and maintains an accuracy better than 0.7 mm/d. In addition, PCDL reduces large prediction errors by approximately 48% and demonstrates stable performance under limited training samples. Energy-balance-based diagnostics further show that PCDL consistently reduces physical inconsistencies across all evaluated sites, indicating greater consistency with the observed surface-energy balance. Overall, our work demonstrates that incorporating physical information into deep learning could provide an effective pathway for high-resolution ET estimation.

title: Tracing soil–water signatures from contrasting land uses in low-flow streamwater of a mixed headwater catchment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Zhixiang Sun, Junfang Cui, Xiangyu Tang, Lei Chen, Zhenyao Shen, Mohammad Sadegh Askari, Jialiang Tang
abstract: Baseflow sustains water delivery from headwater catchments during non-event conditions and low flows. However, in mixed land-use headwater catchments, how land-use-related soil–water storage signatures are represented in low-flow streamwater and vary seasonally remain poorly understood. To address this gap, a two-year study involving monthly monitoring of a hilly purple-soil headwater catchment was conducted. We employed a combination of dissolved organic matter (DOM) fluorescence, stable water isotopes, and Bayesian mixing analysis to characterize source composition in low-flow streamwater, characterize temporal variation in dominant source signatures, and assess depth-related soil–water signatures under baseflow-dominated conditions. This study showed that orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters formed the main source-signature group, with a summed mean posterior attribution of 62.9% across the 19 retained samples, and summed monthly posterior-median attributions ranging from 52.7% to 72.8%, compared with a mean attribution of 10.7% to sampled valley shallow groundwater (monthly posterior-median range: 4.7%-26.1%). The dominant-source pattern showed seasonal variation among orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters, with estimated layer attributions favoring shallow layers (10 cm) in orchard and sloping farmland and middle layers (20–30 cm) in paddy; exploratory analyses indicated associations with bulk density and DOC. The findings indicate that different land-use types are associated with distinct soil–water storage signatures in low-flow streamwater, providing a basis for evaluating how future land-use changes may influence low-flow hydrological functioning.

title: Hydrological regulation of patchy soil salinization: The role of soil profile structure
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Chenggong Liu, Lidong Ren, Xuan Yu, Xiaoxu Jia
abstract: Salt-affected croplands often exhibit strong spatial heterogeneity in soil salinity, forming localized salt patches adjacent to vegetated areas with lower salinity. Although such patchiness is common, the role of soil-profile structure and horizon-specific hydraulic properties in regulating salt-patch formation remains poorly understood. This study compared representative salt-patch and vegetation-patch profiles in the Yellow River Delta, China, using electrical resistivity tomography, soil physical and hydraulic measurements, infiltration experiments, pore-size analysis, and HYDRUS-1D simulations. The results showed that soil water content did not differ significantly between the two patch types, whereas soil salt content was consistently higher in salt patches and was significantly associated with the observed resistivity differences. Salt patches exhibited greater penetration resistance at 27.5–35 cm, lower saturated hydraulic conductivity and higher bulk density in the plow layer, weaker sustained infiltration, fewer surface macropores, and greater subsoil micropore volume. Under identical atmospheric and groundwater forcing, simulations showed annual net upward water and salt fluxes across the 20-, 60-, and 120-cm interfaces in all three scenarios. The bare salt-patch profile showed 15–46% greater net upward water flux than the bare vegetation-patch profile. Together with its higher antecedent salinity, this resulted in 2.79–3.90 times greater net upward salt flux. Within the modeled scenarios, the contrast between the two bare-soil profiles was greater than the change produced by adding crop transpiration and root water uptake to the vegetation-patch profile, indicating that differences in profile hydraulic configuration exerted a stronger influence on simulated water and salt redistribution than the vegetation processes represented in the model. These findings suggest that future salt-patch management should emphasize profile-structure adjustment to enhance downward salt removal and limit groundwater-supported upward salt accumulation.

title: Nonlinear sea level rise and storm surge interactions amplify future coastal flood hazards in the world’s largest urban delta
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Haoxuan Du, Liang Gao, Limin Zhang, Lishu Xu
abstract: Tropical-cyclone (TC)-induced coastal water-level hazards are expected to intensify as sea level rises and TC climatology responds to anthropogenic forcing. We develop a probabilistic framework for the Pearl River Delta (PRD) that combines SSP-conditioned CHIPS-CMIP6 synthetic TCs, the Joint Probability Method with Optimal Sampling and Bayesian Quadrature (JPM-OS-BQ), stochastic regional sea-level-rise (SLR) projections, and high-resolution hydrodynamic modeling. For SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5 during 2070–2100, JPM-OS-BQ selects 80 weighted storm-SLR combinations from the PRD-filtered candidate ensemble, reducing required hydrodynamic simulations by approximately 95%. The optimized subsets retain the principal marginal and pairwise statistical structures of the input parameter space. Response-level performance is further evaluated against the complete 2,351-event SSP5-8.5 hydrodynamic ensemble, showing good representation of the broad hazard structure but increasing site-specific discrepancies toward the far return-period tail. Relative to SSP2-4.5, the area-averaged event-maximum total water level under SSP5-8.5 is approximately 1.1 m (29%) higher at the 100-year return period and 1.7 m (43%) higher at the 1000-year return period. At Hong Kong and Macao, 100-year total water levels increase from approximately 2.4 and 3.5 m under SSP2-4.5 to 4.2 and 5.2 m under SSP5-8.5. Paired simulations reveal a spatially heterogeneous nonlinear SLR residual: total water levels are suppressed by up to about 0.2 m along parts of the open coast but amplified by a similar magnitude in some interior distributary channels. These results show that linear addition of SLR to baseline water levels can misrepresent future hazards in complex deltas and support adaptive flood-risk management.

title: Satellite-derived nutrient reconstruction reveals the drivers of eutrophication risk in a subtropical estuary
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Qiqi Wei, Shaohua Lei, Pengfei Wang, Yunfeng Tian, Yifei Fan, Feifei Wang, Wenzhi Cao
abstract: Monitoring the dynamics of estuarine nutrients, specifically dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and silicate (DSi), is essential for assessing the ecological health of nearshore waters; however, traditional sampling methods struggle to provide the high-frequency temporal data and broad spatial coverage required for comprehensive assessment. Here, we developed a robust “two-step inversion” remote sensing framework (R2 > 0.70) that bridges the gap between remote sensing reflectance and salinity, subsequently linking salinity to DIN and DSi concentrations. By applying this model to the Jiulong River Estuary, we achieved a high-frequency, large-scale, and accurate reconstruction of surface DIN and DSi concentrations over the past decade. Both DIN and DSi exhibited a distinct land-to-sea gradient and significant seasonal fluctuations, characterized by higher concentrations in winter and lower concentrations in summer. The dissolved silicate-to-dissolved inorganic nitrogen molar ratio (Si/N ratio) remained stable between 1.27 and 1.34 over the long term but displayed marked spatial heterogeneity during the summer. Nutrient dynamics are influenced by salinity-driven mixing, biogeochemical processes, climatic variability, and human activities. Salinity-driven mixing primarily affects large-scale spatial patterns, whereas climatic factors are linked to seasonal variability. Furthermore, socioeconomic development and pollution control measures can affect long-term changes in nutrient levels. Our framework is an effective tool for monitoring non-optically active substances and has implications for eutrophication early-warning systems and integrated basin management.

title: Hydrometeorological and hydrogeological trends and drought dynamics in a cold-humid, coastal region
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): A. Motamedi, N.K. LeRoux, A.M.R. Hill, R.C. Jamieson, L.D. Somers, B.L. Kurylyk
abstract: Quantifying groundwater response to droughts remains challenging, as aquifers typically respond to meteorological conditions with delays, and long-term groundwater records remain limited. This study investigated statistical relationships among meteorological, hydrogeological, and hydrological datasets in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. Standardized Groundwater Index (SGI) values were calculated using daily groundwater level data (2009–2025) from 32 observation wells and compared with meteorological (Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index, SPEI) and hydrological (Standardized Base Flow Index, SBFI) drought indicators. To complement the statistical analyses of drought dynamics, geospatial drought layers were used to examine spatiotemporal patterns in drought severity and distribution. In most groundwater systems, SGI exhibited short ( 0.5 on average) with both SPEI and SBFI, suggesting the atmosphere-aquifer-stream hydrologic continuum patterns are strongly associated. Trend analysis revealed that the fall season is experiencing the most significant and persistent negative trends across the hydrological cycle (net precipitation, baseflow, and groundwater level). Significant negative fall trends were identified in 67% of net precipitation records, 60% of streamflow records, 40% of baseflow records, and 25% of groundwater level records. Kernel density analyses for summer and fall indicated significant shifts toward drier SPEI, SGI, and SBFI distributions (p < 0.05) after 2016. The geospatial drought layer analysis reveals that more intensive droughts are becoming more frequent and spatially extensive. Collectively, the results yield a better understanding of drought characteristics in a cold, coastal region, an essential step towards evaluating ongoing climate change impacts in similar environments worldwide.

title: Constrained differentiable hybrid hydrologic modeling across multiple process backbones: accuracy gains and risks to physical consistency
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jiaoyang Li, Guoqiang Tang, Jun Xia
abstract: Differentiable parameter learning (dPL) has emerged as a promising strategy for integrating process-based hydrological models with deep learning, but its applicability across hydrological model structures remains unclear. Moreover, in hybrid models where process-based modules are jointly optimized without explicit module-level constraints, strong final streamflow performance does not necessarily imply that the process-based module remains hydrologically meaningful or contributes substantially to the final prediction. Here, we investigate these issues across eight conceptual hydrological models using the CAMELS dataset and develop a constrained differentiable hybrid framework to mitigate the degradation of the process-based module during joint training. Our results show that dPL is strongly backbone-dependent. Under a single-component configuration, it generally does not outperform traditional CMA-ES calibration, and its gains under a multi-component configuration vary markedly across model structures. More importantly, in unconstrained hybrid models, the final streamflow accuracy can remain high even when the process-based module is poorly calibrated, indicating that the post-processing LSTM may partially bypass the physical backbone. To address this failure mode, we introduce a constrained joint objective that explicitly incorporates the streamflow loss of the process-based module. This strategy substantially improves the realism of the process-based module while maintaining or improving overall predictive skill. The best-performing constrained hybrid model achieves a median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.742, exceeding that of the baseline LSTM (0.724). In arid basins, the constrained hybrid model with the MOPEX2 backbone attains a median NSE of 0.505, compared with 0.394 for the LSTM. Overall, this study identifies a key failure mode in differentiable hybrid hydrologic modeling and provides practical guidance for improving runoff prediction without hollowing out the physical backbone.

title: Aquifer settings and interflow dynamics across continental flood basalts: A synthesis of hydro-geophysical evidence
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Lohithkumar Kethavath, Sahebrao Sonkamble, Madhusudan Rao
abstract: Continental flood basalts (CFBs), spanning over ∼75,000 line-km globally, offer exceptional opportunities to advance the understanding of aquifer settings and interflow dynamics across their margins, where distinct stratigraphic heterogeneity, variable weathering, fracturing, and complex hydrochemical processes create a dynamic and diverse hydroenvironment. This study applies an integrated hydro-geophysical methodology to characterize aquifer settings and dynamics along ∼115 line-km lateral margin of basalt-granite (B-G) in the Deccan Volcanic Province (DVP). Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) with forward simulations was utilised to construct detailed litho-hydrogeological models, while steady-state numerical modelling quantified aquifer dynamics. The laterally constrained inversion (LCI) of ERT data enabled sharper delineation of the B-G vertical contact (nonconformity) by clearly distinguishing the low-resistive (10–200 Ωm) ferromagnesium-rich basaltic flow from the underlying high-resistive (>1000 Ωm) quartz-feldspar-rich granitic base. These geophysically derived layers were incorporated into numerical groundwater modelling to understand strata-specific aquifer dynamics. The resulting annual discharge (Q) estimates for basalt (QB = 273 MCM), B-G contact (QB-G = 580 MCM), and granite (QG = 296 MCM) aquifers revealed the order QB-G > QG > QB, indicating a preferential flow path and higher aquifer potentiality of the B-G contact. Hydrochemical evaluation across the B-G contact reveals mixed facies confirming dissolution of both basaltic and granitic minerals. Synthesizing the multidisciplinary approach, this study significantly reduces the inherent ambiguities of aquifers across B-G contact by quantitatively demonstrating the hydraulic dominance of the B-G contact and offers an adaptable framework with methodological insights and quantitative evidences for future comparative studies across CFBs worldwide.

title: Pilot point-based geostatistical parameterization with deep learning models
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Wei Ling, Behnam Jafarpour
abstract: Calibration of subsurface flow models in geologically complex environments with non-Gaussian spatial patterns remains a significant challenge in hydrology. A central difficulty is conditioning complex geological representations on nonlinear flow data (e.g., pressure and saturation) while preserving geological realism and spatial continuity. Traditional pilot point–based parameterization (PPM) provides an intuitive and physically meaningful calibration framework, but its applicability is limited when the underlying geostatistical interpolation or conditional simulation cannot adequately reproduce complex, non-Gaussian spatial patterns. To address this limitation, we propose a practical PPM extension that replaces the interpolation step with a multi-channel U-Net trained on channelized facies realizations. The U-Net generates facies distributions conditioned on sparse pilot points and hard data, retaining the interpretability of pilot points while learning non-Gaussian spatial structure from a training image, and is coupled with the Ensemble Smoother with Multiple Data Assimilation (ES-MDA) for iterative calibration. Reconstruction quality improves systematically with pilot-point density, and a controlled benchmark against Multiple-Point Statistics (MPS) across matched conditioning scenarios shows that the proposed approach outperforms MPS in facies reconstruction accuracy, with the advantage becoming most pronounced at higher conditioning densities. The framework is demonstrated on binary fluvial channel systems and provides a practical pathway for pilot point–based calibration where classical interpolation cannot reproduce non-Gaussian spatial structure.

title: Tracking hydrological drought propagation in river networks: an event-based framework
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Alex Crespillo López, S.M.Vicente Serrano, L. Gimeno
abstract: Hydrological droughts are dynamic phenomena that evolve across space and time, propagating through river networks under the influence of climatic forcing, catchment properties, and human regulation. Despite substantial progress in drought research, most existing approaches rely on aggregated indicators or statistical relationships, limiting their ability to explicitly characterise how individual drought events propagate within connected river systems. This study introduces a novel event-based framework to analyse the spatiotemporal propagation of hydrological droughts along river networks. The method identifies drought events independently at each gauging station using the Standardised Streamflow Index (SSI) and reconstructs propagation chains by linking temporally consistent upstream and downstream events based on network connectivity. A set of propagation metrics is then derived to quantify the spatial extent, timing, and severity of drought propagation processes. The framework is applied to daily streamflow data from 33 gauging stations in the Ebro River basin (Spain) over the period 1961–2020, and it illustrates the substantial variability that may characterise the propagation dynamics, with events ranging from localised sub-basin responses to basin-wide droughts involving a large proportion of the upstream network and with timescales that vary from rapid responses to delayed, multi-annual processes. To support reproducibility and facilitate application in other basins, the methodology has been implemented in an open and modular computational workflow, enabling transparent replication and extension of the analysis. The proposed framework provides a process-orientated perspective on hydrological droughts, generating a propagation-chain catalogue that offers a new data foundation for characterising basin-specific drought dispersal regimes. Beyond its methodological contribution, the framework characterises upstream drought signals and cumulative downstream deficits, providing a reproducible basis for future research and for the development of early-warning applications following prospective validation.

title: Goal-oriented Bayesian experimental design for variable-density seawater intrusion: Adjoint expected information gain for joint monitoring and managed-aquifer-recharge placement
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Dulian Zeqiraj
abstract: Coastal alluvial aquifers are increasingly threatened by seawater intrusion (SWI), and their protection requires both monitoring networks and active controls such as managed aquifer recharge (MAR). Existing SWI design relies largely on heuristic simulation–optimization without a goal-oriented information measure, and where observation and control are linked it is through a two-stage adaptive loop rather than through one objective; meanwhile, adjoint goal-oriented optimal experimental design (OED), now mature for single-density and generic PDE-constrained problems, has not been brought to variable-density SWI physics. This paper presents what is, to the author’s knowledge, the first adjoint-based goal-oriented expected information gain (EIG) framework for steady variable-density (Henry-class) seawater intrusion. The method derives a goal-oriented information operator from the coupled flow–transport adjoint and assembles one objective, the expected information gain about the management target under a facies-conditional prior net of cost, which places monitoring wells and MAR infrastructure jointly rather than in sequence. The discrete adjoint reuses an existing validated forward solver without modification, assembling the required Jacobian from its residual evaluator. It further establishes a poolability phase boundary: parameterizing the facies-stratified prior by a single cross-facies correlation ρ F , a facies-blind design becomes provably suboptimal below a critical value ρ c . In a linear-Gaussian synthetic study, ρ c ≈ 0.76 , with the goal-information loss exactly zero above ρ c (a “dead zone”) and reaching ≈ 19 % of the pooled-design information below it; the threshold is structurally invariant across problem sizes. On a Henry-class variable-density benchmark, the discrete adjoint reproduces forward sensitivities to a relative error of 4.4 × 10 - 9 , and the same solve places the mid-isochlor toe, taken at half the seawater concentration, at 0.696 of the cell length, within one per cent of an independent finite-element solution of the same problem. Application to the Tirana–Fushë-Kuqe–Lezhë coastal aquifer (Albania) recommends 5 monitoring and 3 MAR locations and gains about 10% of goal information over a facies-blind baseline (0.595 vs. 0.537 nats); the site lies marginally above the critical threshold, so facies-blind sampling is borderline admissible there. A reference MATLAB implementation is openly available (https://github.com/dulianzeqiraj/swi-goal-oed).

title: Flood modeling incorporating spatially heterogeneous rainfall and nonlinear routing mechanisms
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jing Feng, Keke Zhou, Jianzhu Li, Hongdong Song, Benlong Zhao, Hao Wang
abstract: The spatial heterogeneity of rainfall and nonlinear catchment routing are important factors affecting the accuracy of flood simulation, yet they remain inadequately represented in conventional conceptual models. This study proposes an integrated flood simulation framework that employs Ensemble Rainfall-Runoff Analysis (ERRA) to identify rainfall-runoff response characteristics, correct spatially heterogeneous rainfall inputs, and construct rainfall-intensity-dependent unit hydrographs. The framework was applied and validated in the XDY catchment, a 4420 km2 basin located in a semi-arid-semi-humid region. First, linear and nonlinear net rainfall-surface runoff response functions were derived using ERRA, and mean areal precipitation was corrected using spatial response efficiency weights. The identified response functions were then incorporated into the Nash Instantaneous Unit Hydrograph (Nash IUH) to represent nonlinear routing under different rainfall intensities. The improved routing scheme was further coupled with the SCS-CN runoff generation module and a subsurface flow simulation module to establish an integrated flood simulation model. For five independent validation flood events, the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) ranged from 0.89 to 0.95, the relative error in peak discharge ranged from −8.93% to 23.31%, the relative error in runoff volume ranged from 1.81% to 18.91%, and the peak timing error ranged from −3 to 2 h. Scenario comparisons showed that both the spatial rainfall correction and the ERRA-based refinement of the unit hydrograph improved model performance. The proposed model provides a parsimonious and potentially applicable approach for flood simulation in medium-sized catchments.

title: From end-of-pipe detention to source–process regulation: multi-objective optimization of gray–green infrastructure for urban flood mitigation
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Haiyuan Ma, Wenqiu Tang, Hao Wu, Lei Chen, Haoran Zhu, Cheng Cheng, Jia Yan, Hongxiang Chai
abstract: Under climate change and rapid urbanization, urban flood risk has intensified, and traditional drainage systems are inadequate for extreme rainfall. To enhance the integrated regulation capacity of gray–green infrastructure (GGI) under intense rainfall and complex runoff processes, this study developed a multi-objective optimization framework for GGI. The framework coupled the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to analyze the effects of algorithm parameters and the diversion ratio of detention tanks on optimization performance. A runoff-path-based spatial hierarchical design (RSHD) strategy was introduced to explore the spatial configuration mechanisms of GGI, and joint optimization was performed under five rainfall return period scenarios ranging from 10 to 200 years. The entropy-weighted TOPSIS method was applied for scheme decision making. The results showed that: (1) the crossover and mutation distribution indices significantly affected convergence and solution diversity, while an appropriate diversion ratio facilitated hydraulic load matching between gray and green infrastructure, thereby improving regulation performance; (2) the RSHD strategy substantially altered the spatial configuration of facilities, increasing the minimum total node overflow reduction rate from 44% to 55%, the proportion of upstream detention tanks from 43.5% to 68.2%, and the proportion of high-frequency nodes from 47.8% to 77.3%. For representative schemes with nearly identical total node overflow reduction rates, the downstream overflow reduction rate increased by an average of 25.14%; and (3) with increasing rainfall return periods, gray infrastructure accommodated greater hydraulic loads by expanding detention capacity, whereas green infrastructure maintained a relatively stable source-control function, and the system gradually shifted toward full-chain coordination across source, process, and end-of-pipe stages. This study provides a basis for parameter selection and spatial guidance for GGI optimization in complex-terrain cities under climate change and offers theoretical support for the transition of urban stormwater management toward upstream-priority and coordinated regulation.

title: Hydrodynamic connectivity reveals priority locations for surface flow constructed wetland deployment in complex plain river networks
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jinyaxuan Huang, Wei He, Shiqiang Gao, Xiaoyi Shen, Xuetong Zhang, Hongwu Tang, Andrew Western
abstract: Surface flow constructed wetlands (SFWs) are a promising strategy for improving water quality, yet their regulatory mechanisms in complex plain river networks remain poorly understood. Based on five years of observed water-quality data from the urban river network of Suqian, China, a coupled modelling framework integrating runoff generation, drainage systems, river networks, and SFWs was established and validated. Building upon long-term observations and multi-scenario simulations, a Structure–Process–Response–Deployment (SPRD) framework integrating process-based indicators, contribution analyses, and causal pathway modelling was developed to quantify how river-network structure controls hydrodynamic transport and water-quality responses. Results showed that (1) SFWs drove a cascading effect regulating network-wide water quality by reshaping hydrodynamic connectivity and redistributing pollutant exposure, rather than acting as localised sinks. During the 30-mm rainfall event, SFWs induced only minor hydrodynamic alterations yet reduced cumulative ammonia nitrogen exposure by 4.81%, indicating that limited hydraulic perturbations can generate substantial water-quality benefits. These effects exhibited strong spatial heterogeneity, with the greatest improvements occurring within deployment zones. (2) Across rainfall depths of 10–100 mm, the response indicators exhibited distinct non-monotonic patterns: the relative changes in cumulative exposure and peak concentration reached optimal values at 30 mm, whereas the change in exceedance duration was optimal at 20 mm. Hydrodynamic connectivity was identified as the dominant process variable. Strategies targeting reaches with high current-flow betweenness (a network metric quantifying a reach’s role in mediating flow pathways) outperformed those targeting low-betweenness reaches under light-to-moderate rainfall (10–40 mm), whereas this performance divergence diminished under extreme events (100 mm). These findings demonstrate that current-flow betweenness provides a practical indicator for prioritising SFW deployment and maximising network-scale water-quality benefits.

title: StreamFormer: A multi-resolution transformer for scalable global river streamflow prediction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Jinyang Li, Hayato Ushijima-Mwesigwa, Kuolin Hsu, Soroosh Sorooshian
abstract: Data-driven streamflow models based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have achieved strong predictive skill but rely on long daily meteorological input sequences that impose substantial data storage and computational costs when scaled globally. We introduce StreamFormer (SF), a Transformer-based architecture that combines a hydrologically informed Multi-Resolution Scheme (MRS) and Dual-Scale Patching (DSP) to preserve short-term meteorological signals at high resolution while progressively compressing long-term history at coarser scales, substantially reducing both input storage and computational cost. Using data from over 6200 gauge stations worldwide, SF achieves an NSE of 0.753 and KGE of 0.757 under the multi-resolution scheme, comparable to the standard 365-day baseline but at substantially lower computational cost. Critically, SF maintains or improves performance with the shortened multi-resolution scheme while LSTM performance degrades, suggesting that attention-based models are better suited to heterogeneous temporal inputs. Stratified analysis reveals that catchments with high snow fraction and aridity benefit most from long-term context. SF also achieves faster training and inference, lower GPU memory, and reduced input storage compared to both the standard LSTM and vanilla Transformer baseline. The study demonstrates that hydrological domain knowledge can be used to compress inputs while preserving predictive accuracy at much lower computational cost, supporting scalable operational global hydrological modeling.

title: A large-scale molecular dynamics investigation of anisotropic hydraulic conductivity in compacted clay system
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yu Zhong, Annan Zhou, Jiapei Du, Ali Zaoui
abstract: This study developed a large-scale molecular dynamics framework to investigate anisotropic hydraulic conductivity by linking directional water transport to compaction state, platelet fabric, and surface chemistry. A total of 150 multi-particle nanoflow models were constructed across dry densities (ρ d) of 1.2–1.8 g·cm−3, orientational order parameters (S) of 0.60 to 0.92, and cation exchange capacities (CEC) of 0.11–97.44 cmol·kg−1. Simulated hydraulic conductivities ranged from 0.77 × 10-14 to 1.96 × 10-12 m·s−1, with 97.0% of available experimental measurements falling within this envelope. Mean horizontal hydraulic conductivity (k h) consistently exceeded mean vertical hydraulic conductivity (k v) by factors of approximately 2.4–5.6. Increasing dry density narrowed water-accessible pores, reduced independent spanning pathways and critical spanning diameters, and increased tortuosity, thereby decreasing both k h and k v. Platelet orientation differentiated the two flow directions by maintaining more direct horizontal pathways. Increasing CEC shifted pore water toward Na associated states and reduced the flux carried by interfacial only and free water, further lowering both k h and k v. Random Forest models achieved mean testing R 2 values of 0.92 for k h and 0.88 for k v and identified dry density as the dominant descriptor in both directions. Platelet orientation had a greater relative influence on vertical than horizontal conductivity, whereas CEC made a smaller but consistent contribution. Fixed-density sensitivity analysis showed that increasing dry density shifted the relative sensitivity weight from platelet orientation toward CEC, particularly for k v. These findings clarify the distinct structural and physicochemical controls on directional water transport and hydraulic anisotropy in compacted clay barriers.

title: Seasonal differences in Fe:P regulation of phosphorus source–sink dynamics in an urban shallow lake
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Baowen Liang, Wen Xiong, Cong Xiao
abstract: Internal phosphorus (P) release in urban shallow lake sediments is strongly coupled to iron (Fe) cycling, yet how the molar supply ratio of dissolved Fe(II) to phosphate-P (Fe:P) regulates P source‒sink dynamics remains unclear. Four seasonal field surveys in Nanhu Lake (Wuhan, China) and standardized low-oxygen incubations across Fe:P supply gradients were conducted to examine how Fe:P supply affects the timing and pathway of P transformation under contrasting seasonal sediment backgrounds. Field observations showed clear seasonal differences in Fe–P coupling at the sediment-overlying water interface, with higher aqueous P and Fe concentrations in summer and autumn, accompanied by a shift from HCl-extractable Fe(III) toward HCl-extractable Fe(II) in surface sediments. Under standardized low-oxygen conditions, winter- and summer-derived sediments exhibited contrasting P-transformation pathways. In winter-derived sediments, higher Fe:P supply accelerated early PO4 3- removal, but concentrations subsequently rebounded to 4.89-5.17 mg/L at 40 d, accompanied by transformation of reactive Fe pools. In summer-derived sediments, aqueous PO4 3- declined continuously to 0.06-0.14 mg/L at 40 d, with exchangeable P and organic P decreasing and Fe-bound P and authigenic P increasing. Metagenomic analysis indicated distinct microbial functional responses associated with these pathways, with Fe input being associated with lower functional potential for P solubilization and inorganic P transport. Overall, Fe:P supply modulated sediment P source–sink dynamics in association with coordinated, stage-dependent changes in reactive Fe pools, P fractions, and microbial functional potential rather than acting as a fixed threshold. These findings provide new insights into internal P risk assessment in urban shallow lakes.

title: Contiguous evolution and hydroclimatic drivers of compound drought–heatwave events across mainland China
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Hao Guo, Ying Cao, Xiangchen Meng, Yunqian Wang, Aminjon Gulakhmadov, Khusen Sh. Gafforov, Philippe De Maeyer
abstract: Compound drought–heatwave events (CDHEs) have intensified under global warming, yet the diversity of their contiguous evolution pathways and the hydroclimatic conditions associated with different evolution modes remain insufficiently understood. Distinguishing CDHEs according to their multidimensional propagation characteristics is therefore important for revealing process heterogeneity and identifying mode-specific hydroclimatic associations. In this study, contiguous CDHEs across mainland China during 1981–2024 were identified using a three-dimensional spatiotemporal algorithm based on the non-stationary Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (NSPEI) and daily maximum temperature. Event characteristics were quantified, evolution modes were classified using six process-related features, and their hydroclimatic associations were examined using XGBoost–SHAP. A total of 1,711 CDHEs were identified. Over the 44-year period, grid cells covering 89.1 % of mainland China experienced more than 80 CDHEs, indicating widespread recurrence. Annual event frequency increased by 0.33 events yr⁻1, while the overall intensification was characterized mainly by more frequent, longer-lasting, and more intense events rather than a sustained expansion of affected area. Northwest China showed the strongest intensification. Four major evolution modes were identified, differing primarily in duration, spatial extent, migration speed, and directional stability. Localized slow-moving events with variable propagation directions were the most common, whereas long-lasting, large-area events were less frequent but exhibited greater duration, spatial extent, and intensity. Vapor pressure deficit was the dominant driver across the four modes, while other hydroclimatic factors contributed differently among modes. These findings demonstrate diverse contiguous evolution pathways of CDHEs across mainland China and provide an event-based basis for risk assessment and impact mitigation.

title: A framework for simulating and assessing the spatiotemporal cumulative effects of multi-reservoir operation on streamflow
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yu Han, Ann van Griensven, Yiwen Wang, Xinyuan Qian, Zixin Song, Mengxue Ben, Ping-an Zhong
abstract: Accurately simulating multi-reservoir operation and assessing its spatiotemporal cumulative effects on streamflow remain major challenges in large-scale regulated basins. To address these challenges, this study develops a framework using the SWAT+ model, in which customized parameterized reservoir operation rules (CUS) are developed based on the seasonal operation patterns of reservoirs in the upper Yangtze River Basin. Results show that CUS reflects regional reservoir operation characteristics and improves streamflow simulations relative to the reference models at all control stations during both calibration and validation, with particularly good performance at the basin outlet. Evaluations of reservoir inflow, storage, and outflow further provide process-level validation of the model’s physical realism. Multi-reservoir operation shifts streamflow from the refill to the drawdown period, decreases high flows and increases low flows, and makes intra-annual distribution more uniform, whereas its impact on annual magnitude is limited. Spatial cumulative effects become more pronounced from tributaries to the mainstream and from upstream to downstream, controlled by the topology of the reservoir–river network. Temporal cumulative effects generally intensify across most streamflow indicators as the multi-reservoir system expands. The cumulative effects are dominated by mainstream reservoirs, particularly those in the lower Jinsha River and the Three Gorges Reservoir. Most streamflow indicators exhibit additive behavior, whereas low flow shows supra-additive behavior. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly and appropriately representing regional reservoir operation rules for hydrological modeling in large-scale regulated basin and advance understanding of the mechanisms governing the cumulative effects of multi-reservoir operation on streamflow.

title: A two-stage framework integrating information entropy and machine learning for rapid pollution source identification in looped river networks
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Lehao Zhao, Jiabiao Wang, Tongtiegang Zhao, Xiaohong Chen
abstract: Rapid source identification of sudden water pollution incidents in looped river networks remains challenging because of the complex connectivity, multiple transport pathways, and mixing at junctions. Pollution source identification has been widely studied in both surface water and groundwater systems, but studies focusing specifically on looped river networks remain limited. To address this gap, this study develops a two-stage framework integrating information entropy (IE) and machine learning (ML). Concentration and discharge time series measured at monitoring stations are first transformed into IE values, making the data more compact and easier to process. In the first stage, the IE values are used as inputs to ML models to identify the river containing the pollution source. In the second stage, the IE values are used to establish an IE-based empirical formula (IE-EF) that links IE to the exact source location in the identified river. The case study shows that the accuracy of river identification (RI) exceeds 98% in the first stage. In the second stage, the location identification (LI) error is generally less than 1 km. The proposed framework also demonstrates good stability and can support emergency water-quality management in looped river networks.

title: Characterization and quantification of compound drought-heatwaves events along with population exposure
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Ashesh Rudra Paul, Rajib Maity
abstract: Droughts and heatwaves each cause severe impacts on ecosystems, agriculture, and human health, but when they occur simultaneously their combined effects are far more devastating. These compound extremes, referred to as Drought-Heatwave Compound Events (DHCEs) amplify risks to water security, food systems and public health, creating cascading impacts that surpass those of individual events. Under climate change, DHCEs are projected to intensify worldwide, yet their combined consequences remain underexplored, particularly when population growth is considered. To address this gap, this study develops a methodological framework to assess DHCEs and their implications for human exposure. The framework is additionally evaluated using an alternative temporal concurrence criterion to assess the sensitivity of compound-event identification and population exposure estimates to the adopted definition of concurrence. Although adaptable to any geography, the methodology is applied here to Northeast India, including West Bengal, and Bangladesh (NEIB region), a climatically sensitive and densely populated zone, to demonstrate its efficacy. The findings reveal a marked intensification in DHCEs, with the regional maximum annual dry days rising from ∼5 to ∼35 days (about 7 times higher) towards the end of 21st century, while the regional maximum DHCE Magnitude Index (DMI) rises from 3.5 to 32 (about 9 times higher). Mean temperature of DHCE is projected to increase by 0.06 °C/year, highlighting intensifying dry and hot conditions. Across the NEIB region, the states Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Sikkim, and northeastern Bangladesh, are expected to experience the most pronounced changes post-2070. By integrating DHCE indicators with population density through Population Exposure Index (PExI), the identified exposure hotspot shifts towards more densely populated areas. Population exposure is projected to increase by roughly 3–6 times depending on the climate change scenario and parameters of the DHCE indices, i.e. magnitude, frequency, duration etc. Furthermore, a decomposition analysis suggests that the changes in climatic conditions account for the largest share of projected increases in population exposure, followed by population growth and interaction effect, especially in urbanized regions. These findings highlight strong spatial contrasts between climatic intensity and population exposure, underscoring the importance of jointly considering climate extremes and population distribution when assessing compound-event impacts under climate change.

title: Hysteretic response of water temperature and persistent thermal regime shift under extreme hydrological pulses
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yi Wang, Liqin Zhu, Baoshun Kan, Xiaolin Zhu, Haozhi Wang, Yongtao Zhu, Tao Wei, Xueping Huo, Peng Jiang
abstract: Unlike the gradual evolution of river water temperature under long-term climatic forcing, extreme floods impose high-intensity hydrological pulses that can rapidly alter river heat exchange and boundary conditions. Yet the abrupt cooling, delayed recovery and post-flood thermal anomalies induced by such pulses remain poorly constrained in ecohydrology. Here we use the July 2023 “23.7” extreme flood in the Haihe River Basin as a natural experiment. We analysed long-term water-temperature and meteorological records from 2009 to 2022, together with 2023 discharge and suspended-sediment data from the Yongding River Basin. We then combined an air-temperature baseline regression, lagged partial least-squares regression and a thermal recovery ratio (TRR) to quantify event-scale thermal responses and their drivers. The flood caused marked cooling within 24–48 h from the gorge reach to the downstream plain reach, with maximum decreases of 22.22–27.76% and cooling rates of 2.13–4.05 °C d−1. Relative to the non-flood meteorological baseline, discharge-related hydrodynamic changes, together with thermal inertia, explained most anomalous temperature fluctuations, whereas sediment-related contributions increased downstream. During recovery, river temperature shifted from upstream under-recovery to downstream over-recovery. TRR values at the downstream estuarine gate exceeded 1.3, and recovery-period temperatures were 1.9–3.1 °C higher than those in 2022. Google Earth Engine (GEE)-based evidence of post-flood changes in bank-zone wetness, vegetation condition and surface exposure further suggests that downstream over-recovery was associated with altered bank-zone and hydrological boundary conditions. These findings identify an event-scale sequence of abrupt cooling, delayed recovery and thermal over-recovery, providing evidence for assessing river thermal risk under intensifying hydrological extremes.

title: Evapotranspiration intensification will drive terrestrial water storage decline in the Turpan–Hami Basin
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Yanxin Su, Guojing Gan, Jingyi Bu, Yanchun Gao
abstract: In the hyper-arid Turpan–Hami Basin (THB) of northwestern China, where water availability critically constrains socio-ecological sustainability, reliable hydrological characterization is essential yet insufficient. This insufficiency stems from a notable scarcity of integrated modeling studies that employ fully coupled surface–subsurface frameworks to resolve the complex hydrological interactions of the region. Furthermore, conventional potential evapotranspiration (PET) estimators (e.g., Penman-Monteith (PM), Priestley-Taylor (PT)) exhibit systematic biases under extreme arid conditions, while model calibration is often limited by sparse observational data. To overcome these dual challenges, this study developed a bias-corrected, fully coupled CWatM–MODFLOW model for the Turpan–Hami Basin and introduced a novel multi–objective calibration scheme. This scheme jointly constrains the model by simultaneously assimilating GRACE/GRACE–FO observations of terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) and the PML–V2 evapotranspiration (ET) product, thereby significantly improving the simulation of regional water storage dynamics and flux partitioning and yielding more robust and physically consistent results. Based on this reliable modeling framework, the study further conducted an integrated assessment combining multi–objective calibration, scenario projection, and lag–based attribution analysis. Climate forcing data were obtained from the ISIMIP3b dataset, bias–adjusted to ERA5. We benchmark three potential PET schemes—PM, PT, and PT with α-tuning plus systematic bias correction and then diagnose 21st-century TWSA evolution under SSP scenarios, the sensitivities and contributions of precipitation (PRE) and ET to TWSA, lagged responses, and compound extremes. Results show: (1) Calibration (2003–2013) robustly reproduces basin-scale storage; while default PET schemes markedly underestimate ET (KGE = 0.016, NSE = − 1.05, PBIAS = − 97%), the PT-α and bias-corrected scheme substantially improves ET skill (KGE = 0.858, NSE = 0.707, PBIAS = 2.3%) without degrading TWSA performance (KGE = 0.783). (2) Validation (2014–2019) exhibits reduced TWSA skill, reflecting non-stationary hydroclimatic and anthropogenic drivers; the improved ET scheme maintains strong accuracy (KGE = 0.828, NSE = 0.690, PBIAS = − 3.1%), indicating good cross-period generalization. (3) Future meteorology features accelerated warming with scenario dependence and moderate increases in precipitation; Tmin rises faster than Tmax, implying a narrowing diurnal temperature range (DTR) and more warm nights. (4) Projected TWSA and ET reveal scenario-dependent storage declines, stronger under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5; polynomial trends indicate the fastest acceleration under SSP5-8.5. (5) Attribution and sensitivity analyses demonstrate that the annual responses of dS to PRE and ET ( bP > 0 , bET < 0 ) are approximately symmetric and opposite in sign, with ∣ b E T ∣ · Δ E T dominating dS under stronger forcing; monthly diagnostics indicate a negative lag from ET to TWSA. (6) The co-occurrence of low TWSA and elevated ET becomes more pronounced over 2041–2100, with a stronger signal under SSP5-8.5, followed by SSP3-7.0 and SSP1-2.6. Overall, the THB exhibits an energy–water coupling in which warming-driven ET intensification partially or fully offsets modest precipitation gains producing more rain without more storage, through vadose-zone and shallow-aquifer moisture memory, yields lagged storage deficits. Management should pivot from inputs to processes, prioritizing infiltration-oriented piedmont flood retention and managed aquifer recharge, seasonal irrigation rescheduling (night and segmented irrigation), and agronomic ET control to reduce ∣ b E T ∣ , shorten lag lengths, and mitigate end-century storage risk.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and driving mechanisms of superposition effects of rainfall-induced urban waterlogging and levee breach flooding
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 680, Part B Author(s): Ye Zhang, Xin Su, Guanghua Qin, Leizhi Wang, Jinhui Li, Lingjie Li, Yintang Wang, Xiting Li
abstract: Extreme rainfall and rapid urbanization have significantly exacerbated coupled riverine–pluvial flooding hazard interactions in urban areas, driven by the joint effects of pluvial flooding, river flooding, and levee instability. However, existing studies fall short of fully revealing the nonlinear interaction effects, hazard sources, and underlying driving mechanisms of “Pluvial flooding – Levee breach – Urban waterlogging” coupled riverine–pluvial flooding hazards.
