Positioned acoustic emission method reveals crack initiation from tensile thermal damage at the heating interface, and damage fractures morphologies (V-shaped, Y-shaped, single inclined planes). Damage evolution exhibits phased characteristics similar to biological population growth: slow accumulation, accelerated development, and stabilization. Based on this, a damage variable for granite under THM conditions is defined using biological population growth theory, and a segmented damage constitutive model is established. Theoretical curves match experimental data, showing the model effectively describes and predicts pre-peak mechanical behavior and strength characteristics under THM conditions, especially in the compaction and elastic stages.

title: Measuring the margins: A combination-based indicator for boundary ecosystem assessment
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Rei Itsukushima, Kazuaki Ohtsuki, Kota Tawa, Tatsuro Sato
abstract: Traditional richness- and abundance-based indices primarily quantify alpha diversity but do not directly represent spatial compositional distinctiveness. We developed a novel Combination Index (CI) that quantifies the rarity of species co-occurrence patterns using presence–absence data, without requiring abundance information, and is less directly dependent on species richness than conventional richness-based metrics. Using records of 46 native fish species from 818 sites across 12 Ecological Regions (ERs) in Japan, we examined relationships among the CI, Shannon–Weaver diversity, Local Contribution to Beta Diversity (LCBD), and environmental and boundary-related variables. Pearson's correlation detected no significant relationship between the CI and Shannon–Weaver diversity across all sites, whereas the Maximal Information Coefficient detected a significant association. The CI was positively correlated with LCBD across all sites, although regional relationships varied. Both the CI and LCBD were significantly higher in estuarine sections despite lower mean species richness, whereas Shannon–Weaver diversity was lower. The CI also decreased significantly with distance from riverbed gradient change points across all sites and within six ERs. Random Forest and generalized additive model analyses supported the importance of these gradient changes for the CI, while local habitat variables related to flow velocity, water depth, and substrate conditions were more frequently associated with Shannon–Weaver diversity and LCBD. These findings suggest that the CI complements alpha- and beta-diversity measures by identifying distinctive assemblages associated with certain riverine transitions, although its relationships with boundary-related factors vary geographically.

title: Arsenic spike prediction in a Hungarian drinking water distribution network using interpretable machine learning
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Jonathan G. Clayton, Victor G. Mihucz, Leigh G. Terry
abstract: Arsenic is a global contaminant of concern as chronic exposure above 10 μg/L in drinking water results in health issues including cancer, impaired cognitive development, and skin lesions. Arsenic is naturally abundant in Hungarian groundwater, posing challenges for compliance with European Union regulations. Trace amounts of arsenic accumulate in water distribution system pipes and may be mobilized downstream by fluctuations in pressure and water quality. Additionally, ambient arsenic can infiltrate from surrounding groundwater into compromised pipes during low pressure conditions. This research identifies mechanisms of interaction between water quality and pressure parameters, based on samples collected at ten public water faucets in an at-risk system on the Hungarian Great Plain, to reliably predict transient, localized arsenic spikes. Arsenic species were separated using an ion-exchange resin and measured via inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) or inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy with hydride generation (ICP-OES). Machine learning models predicted arsenic concentration using pressure data from nine hydrant-mounted sensors and water quality measurements. Random forest modeling achieved an excellent F1 score of 0.866 on unseen data. Manganese concentration and manganese interactions with iron, temperature, and mean and maximum pressure severity indices were the most important features aside from finished water arsenic concentration (SHAP = 0.229, 0.126, 0.095, 0.061, respectively). pH, redox potential, and temperature interactions with pressure events constituted the majority of the remaining features. Results were robust to exclusion of finished water arsenic concentration and missing data imputation strategy. Findings indicate that complex water quality and pressure interactions mobilize arsenic within the distribution network, yielding important implications for system management.

title: Agroecological and biological crop-protection practices for climate adaptation and food security in Nigeria: context dependence, trade-offs and evidence gaps
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Godspower Oke Omokaro
abstract: Nigeria requires crop-production strategies that address climatic stress, soil degradation, pest pressure and food insecurity. This review evaluated agroecological and biological crop-protection practices as pathways to climate resilience and food security in Nigeria. A PRISMA-guided systematic evidence review and narrative synthesis were conducted using Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, CAB Abstracts, Google Scholar and African Journals Online. Ninety substantive evidence sources were included, comprising Nigerian primary studies and contextual regional and international evidence. Nigerian primary evidence included field experiments, observational studies, household surveys and economic evaluations, while reviews, meta-analyses and mechanistic studies were used for contextual interpretation. Intercropping and crop-density management affected component-crop yields, soil moisture and resource capture; higher cassava density increased storage-root yield by 16%, whereas higher maize density increased maize yield by 11% but reduced second-cycle cassava yield by 7%. Maize–legume systems improved soil carbon, nitrogen and aggregation. Combined phosphorus and rhizobial inoculation increased soybean yield by 777 kg ha−1, although the highest-yielding combinations were not always the most profitable. Atoxigenic Aspergillus flavus reduced aflatoxin by 82%–95% at harvest and 80%–100% after storage. Botanical pesticides reduced pest survival and crop damage, but yield responses were inconsistent. Observational evidence associated conservation and climate-smart practices with higher productivity, efficiency and income, whereas household food-security outcomes were less consistent. Most evidence concerned adaptive-capacity indicators rather than performance or recovery under defined climatic shocks. Scaling requires locally tested practices, reliable biological products, extension, finance, regulatory oversight and longer-term evaluation of climatic, ecological, economic and nutritional outcomes.

title: Life cycle environmental impact assessment in palm oil industry from nursery, plantation, and mill: Case study in north Sumatera
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Muhammad Thoriq Al Fath, Maya Sarah, Seri Maulina, Amir Hamzah Sharaai, Noor Zalina Binti Mahmood, Onn Chieu Chuen, Gina Cynthia Raphita Hasibuan, Vikram Alexander, Michael Michael, Juan Akmal Nasution, Nisaul Fadilah Dalimunthe, Fadli Akbar Lubis
abstract: The palm oil industry is a cornerstone of Indonesia's agricultural economy, yet its environmental consequences across the full production chain remain insufficiently quantified in an integrated manner. This study presents a comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) of an integrated palm oil production system at PTPN III, North Sumatra, Indonesia, encompassing three interconnected operational stages: oil palm nursery, plantation, and palm oil mill. Primary input-output inventory data were collected directly from operational records over a 12-month period (April 2022–March 2023) and complemented by secondary data from the ecoinvent v.3.8 database (allocation, cut-off by classification) for upstream background processes, with Indonesian (ID) market datasets applied to electricity and Rest-of-World (RoW) or Global (GLO) datasets applied to fertilizers, fuels, pesticides, and process chemicals; environmental impact assessment was conducted using SimaPro v.9.5. Eight midpoint impact categories were evaluated: acidification, eutrophication, Global Warming Potential (GWP), photochemical oxidation, abiotic depletion (elements), abiotic depletion (fossil fuels), water scarcity, and ozone layer depletion. Stage-specific functional units (1 kg of oil palm seedling, 1 kg of fresh fruit bunches (FFB), and 1 kg of crude palm oil (CPO) were used for unit-process modelling and hotspot analysis, and were linked to a final reference flow of 1 kg CPO through the FFB-to-CPO conversion (oil extraction rate 24.70%; 4.05 kg FFB per kg CPO, or 3.41 kg after mass allocation to CPO), plantation FFB production, and seedling requirement per hectare. Cradle-to-gate GWP was 0.60 kg CO₂-eq kg−1 CPO, to which plantation, mill operations, and nursery contributed 74.2%, 23.4%, and 2.3%, respectively. Results revealed that fertilizer application was the dominant environmental hotspot across the nursery and plantation stages, accounting for up to 98.53% of abiotic depletion (elements), 96.52% of GWP, and 96.30% of acidification at the plantation stage. At the palm oil mill stage, feedstock dominated most impact categories, particularly for abiotic depletion (elements; 99.18%, 2.19 × 10−5 kg Sb-eq kg−1 CPO) and acidification (89.40%, 2.89 × 10−3 kg SO₂-eq kg−1 CPO), reflecting the upstream intensification of plantation-stage burdens transmitted through the supply chain, while FFB waste (solid residues: empty fruit bunches, fibre, and shell) was identified as the primary contributor to eutrophication (80.00%), reflecting nutrient leaching from decomposing organic residue, whereas POME, accounted for separately as the ‘Liquid Waste’ flow, contributed a comparatively minor direct share (0.70%) owing to on-site effluent treatment prior to discharge. Water scarcity was co-driven by direct water consumption and fertilizer-embedded upstream water use across all stages. These findings provide a quantitative, multi-stage environmental profile of integrated palm oil production. Model results identify fertilizer inputs (nursery and plantation) and FFB waste (mill) as priority hotspots; an indicative screening suggests that a 10% reduction in fertilizer input could lower plantation-stage GWP by approximately 9.7%, assuming constant yield, which corresponds to about 2.6% of cradle-to-gate GWP per kg CPO because the studied plantation supplies 35.9% of the mill's FFB. A first-order sensitivity screening indicates precision fertilizer management (10% input reduction) could lower plantation-stage GWP by ∼9.7% (∼2.6% cradle-to-gate); nutrient-use-efficiency improvement (15–30% field-loss reduction) by 3.1–6.2%; and POME methane recovery (60–90% capture) by ≤0.07% under the metered baseline but up to 9–41% under a literature-bounded open-pond baseline, reflecting substantial uncertainty in the site's unmetered effluent inventory. FFB waste valorization was not separately quantified and remains a literature-based recommendation.

title: Process-based life cycle assessment of bioelectricity from sugarcane bagasse: A comparison of combustion and gasification systems
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Fabiana de Oliveira Ramos, Artur Jorge de Jesus Gonçalves, Laís Fabiana Serafini, José Ramón Copa Rey, Mylena Kellyn de Paula Rosetti, Helton José Alves, Ronney Arismel Mancebo Boloy
abstract: This study presents a process-based life cycle assessment (LCA) comparing conventional sugarcane bagasse combustion with a biomass-integrated gasification combined-cycle (BIG-GT) system for bioelectricity generation in the Brazilian sugar-energy sector. A harmonized gate-to-gate framework was used to isolate the industrial energy conversion stage and ensure a consistent comparison between technological configurations. The assessment integrates thermodynamic modeling, life cycle inventory, and impact assessment, using aligned system boundaries, functional units, and inventory assumptions. The results indicate that both systems provide net environmental benefits, largely driven by electricity export and substitution effects. The gasification-based configuration consistently outperformed the conventional system across all evaluated impact categories, achieving up to ∼10% improvements in photochemical ozone formation and smaller gains in climate change, particulate matter formation, and terrestrial acidification. These benefits are primarily associated with higher electrical efficiency (23.4% versus 12.4%), lower biomass consumption, and lower internal auxiliary energy demand per unit of exported electricity, which reduces direct and indirect process burdens. However, the findings show that higher thermodynamic efficiency does not necessarily translate into proportional environmental improvements. Instead, gasification redistributes environmental burdens from core conversion processes to auxiliary operations such as biomass drying and gas cleaning, reflecting the greater complexity of advanced thermochemical systems. Furthermore, the gasification configuration exhibited lower sensitivity to operational variability, indicating greater robustness. Overall, the results demonstrate that the environmental advantages of gasification depend strongly on electricity substitution effects and system-level modeling assumptions, highlighting the importance of process-consistent methodological frameworks for unbiased comparisons of bioenergy systems.

title: Knowledge and perceptions of climate change impacts on mental health in vulnerable populations in Africa: A scoping review
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Israel Opeyemi Fawole, Monisayo Olayemi Komolafe, Ayodeji Oluwatobi Ojetunde, Ibiyosi Samuel Oluwole, Oyama Blessed Obem, Ayodeji Folorunsho Ajayi, Adesina Afeez Sulaiman, Adeyinka Ganiyat Ishola
abstract: Background Climate change is an escalating global health threat with underexplored implications for mental health. In Africa, vulnerable populations face disproportionate exposure to climate-related stressors; however, evidence regarding their knowledge and perceptions of climate-related mental health impacts remains fragmented. This scoping review mapped and synthesized evidence on how vulnerable populations in Africa understand and perceive the mental health impacts of climate change, and identified key geographical, methodological, and conceptual gaps to inform future research and policy. Methods This review followed the Arksey and O'Malley methodological framework and was reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Comprehensive searches were conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, The Lancet, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2010 and 2025. Eligible studies examined knowledge, perceptions, or awareness of climate change–related mental health outcomes among vulnerable populations in Africa. Data were extracted and synthesized using descriptive and thematic analysis. Results From 1299 records identified, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were conducted in East and West Africa, particularly Kenya and Ghana, and predominantly employed mixed-methods designs. Climate-related exposures included drought, flooding, extreme heat, storms, and water insecurity. Across studies, these exposures were repeatedly reported with adverse mental health outcomes, including anxiety, depression, stress, post-traumatic stress disorder, insomnia, and suicidal ideation. Knowledge and perceptions of climate change were experiential and culturally mediated, rather than grounded in formal scientific frameworks. Women, pastoralists, rural communities, migrants, and marginalized groups were identified as disproportionately vulnerable. Conclusion This scoping review maps a small and geographically uneven body of African literature in which climate-related stressors and adverse mental health outcomes are repeatedly reported together among vulnerable populations. Integrating mental health considerations into climate adaptation and disaster response strategies is warranted. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and underrepresented regions to strengthen the evidence base and guide appropriate policy interventions.

title: Rapid UAV-based detection of crane ( Grus grus ) mortality hotspots during an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak using deep learning
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Yotam Nagar, Assaf Chen
abstract: Rapid detection of wildlife mortality during infectious disease outbreaks is essential for ecological risk mitigation, zoonotic-risk management, and timely intervention, yet field surveys are often slow, labor-intensive, and spatially limited. This study evaluates unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery combined with deep learning as an operational surveillance tool for mapping live and deceased Common Cranes (Grus grus) during a highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) outbreak in the Hula Valley, Israel. High-resolution RGB imagery was collected over aquatic roosting and terrestrial feeding habitats and annotated to distinguish living and dead individuals. A YOLOv8-based detection framework was tested using habitat-specific training, combined multi-habitat training, and transfer learning from a large avian dataset, together with selective data augmentation, sliding-window inference, and Weighted Boxes Fusion. Living cranes were detected reliably across habitats, with AP@50 reaching 0.89 in mosaicked feeding-area imagery and 0.98 in raw feeding-area imagery. Dead cranes were detected accurately in water bodies (AP@50 ≈ 0.90), but detection in terrestrial feeding areas remained more limited (AP@50 ≈ 0.64–0.70), based on aerial annotations without in situ confirmation. Oversampling, undersampling, and focal loss provided limited improvement, suggesting that class imbalance alone does not fully explain the lower terrestrial detection performance, and that carcass scarcity, limited visual diversity, and ambiguity against heterogeneous ground backgrounds may also contribute. Joint multi-habitat training and transfer learning improved generalization for the rare dead-crane class on land. These findings demonstrate the value of UAV-based deep learning for rapid mortality assessment and hotspot identification during wildlife disease outbreaks.

title: Prediction of arsenic, cadmium, and lead bioaccessibility for regional-scale management of legacy-contaminated soils
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Aubry Vandeuren, Benoît Pereira, Hugues Titeux, Philippe Sonnet, Pierre Delmelle
abstract: Urban and peri-industrial soils contaminated by past urban and industrial activities frequently exhibit elevated contents in potentially toxic elements (PTEs) such as arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), and lead (Pb) that exceed regulatory thresholds. Accurate characterization of this contamination is essential for effective risk management of exposed populations. In this context, assessing oral bioaccessibility is a critical step for reliably evaluating exposure risks via the ingestion of soil particles and preventing the overestimation of human health hazards often caused by relying solely on total element contents. However, large-scale bioaccessibility assessments remain scarce, as most studies rely either on total contents or small, site-specific datasets, limiting the development of regionally applicable risk assessment frameworks. This study quantifies the oral bioaccessibility of As, Cd, and Pb at the regional scale, based on aqua regia contents and Unified BARGE Method (UBM) measurements for 223 topsoil samples collected across major historical industrial basins in Wallonia (Belgium). Chemical fractionation (BCR protocol) and soil properties were used to identify the main controls on PTEs bioaccessibility. The results show that while As is mainly controlled by the geogenic background, Cd and Pb are predominantly of anthropogenic origin, frequently exceeding regulatory thresholds. We further demonstrate that actual exposure risks are heavily modulated by chemical speciation: on average, only 24% of total (aqua regia content) As is bioaccessible, compared to substantially higher fractions for Cd (82%) and Pb (57%), which are primarily associated with reducible Fe/Mn oxyhydroxide phases. Bioaccessible contents can be predicted from total (aqua regia) element contents (R2 = 0.47–0.98), increasing to R2 = 0.83–0.95 for As when the cumulative BCR content after Step 3 is included. Based on a large, consolidated dataset covering seven industrial areas, this approach enables the integration of regionally derived bioaccessibility values into human health risk models, while supporting the development of site-specific tools, including predictive models based on routine soil data and spatial mapping for land managers. The proposed framework is transferable to similar contaminated environments worldwide, contributing to reduced uncertainty in regional-scale risk assessments and guiding evidence-based soil management strategies.

title: Longitudinal dynamics of nitrogen and phosphorus forms along agricultural drainage ditches: Evidence for nitrate source mixing and possible transformation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Shuiwang Duan, Fajun Sun, Gurpal S. Toor
abstract: Diffuse nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) pollution from agriculture is a leading cause of freshwater eutrophication. Agricultural drainage ditches can modify the concentrations and forms of nutrients transported from fields to receiving waters. We characterized springtime concentration patterns of N and P forms and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in four agricultural drainage ditches differing in site characteristics, vegetation, and nutrient management. Dual nitrate isotopes (δ15N–NO3 − and δ18O–NO3 −) were measured along one ditch to evaluate longitudinal nitrate isotopic patterns in relation to potential source mixing and possible transformation. DOC was strongly and positively correlated with dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) and orthophosphate–P (PO4–P), moderately and negatively correlated with NO3–N, and weakly correlated with ammonium–N (NH4–N). In the two ditches draining fields that received poultry litter during the study, DOC, DON, and PO4–P increased following litter application and subsequent rainfall, consistent with field-derived inputs. On May 17, DOC, DON, and PO4–P decreased from the field-edge to the outlet, with the largest DON and PO4–P concentration declines in two ditches occurring between the field-edge and the first in-ditch sampling location. NO3–N behaved differently, including a 6.8-fold increase from 0.46 mg L−1 at the field-edge to 3.12 mg L−1 at the outlet of the isotope-monitored ditch. In that ditch, upper-reach isotopic patterns were consistent with changing nitrate-source contributions and mixing, whereas the lower reach showed a positive relationship between δ18O–NO3 − and δ15N–NO3 − (slope = 0.907, R2 = 0.857), consistent with possible isotope-fractionating nitrate transformation. These results indicate that agricultural ditches are not uniform nutrient conduits: organic N, P, and nitrate follow distinct longitudinal patterns, and increases in nitrate concentration coincide with isotopic patterns consistent with possible fractionating transformations within the same ditch. Consequently, longitudinal nutrient patterns may reflect the combined influence of field inputs, hydrologic source mixing, and in-ditch processing.

title: Species-specific metal handling reveals the decoupling between environmental contamination and biological accumulation in Amazonian mangroves
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Jacyara Nascimento Corrêa, Daniel Richard Lemos Brito, Ricardo Luvizotto-Santos, Carlos Eduardo de Rezende, Marianna Basso Jorge
abstract: Environmental assessments of metal contamination in mangrove ecosystems are commonly based on environmental concentrations, although these measurements do not necessarily reflect biological accumulation. Here, we investigated how sediment geochemistry and species-specific metal handling, encompassing metal uptake, retention/partitioning, and translocation, are associated with biological accumulation in mangrove seedlings growing along a gradient of port influence on the Brazilian Amazon coast. Metals were quantified in water, sediments, and seedlings of three dominant mangrove species across six sites representing contrasting levels of anthropogenic disturbance, together with sediment geochemical characterization (TOC, TN, δ13C, and δ15N). Contamination indices indicated higher metal contamination at sites influenced by port activities (PLI > 1, Igeo class 2, and Cdeg up to 17.6). However, metal accumulation in seedlings did not consistently follow environmental contamination gradients. Instead, accumulation patterns varied among species and were associated with differences in sediment geochemistry and metal-handling responses. Avicennia germinans predominantly translocated metals to aerial tissues, Laguncularia racemosa exhibited context-dependent shifts between retention and translocation, whereas Rhizophora mangle maintained comparatively stable redistribution patterns. These contrasting responses indicate that biological accumulation cannot be inferred solely from environmental metal concentrations and highlight the importance of species-specific physiological responses for interpreting contamination patterns. Collectively, our findings support the Functional Triad as a conceptual framework based on correlative patterns in which sediment geochemistry, inferred metal availability, and species-specific metal handling interact to shape patterns of biological accumulation in mangrove ecosystems. This integrative perspective provides a basis for improving the interpretation of contamination gradients and may contribute to the development of biologically informed environmental assessment approaches for tropical mangroves.

title: Fingerprinting microplastics: A high-resolution framework for aquatic sediment contamination and degradation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1054 Author(s): Azza Ouni, Abdelaziz Sebei, Mohamed Maanan
abstract: This study delivers a high-resolution analysis of microplastic (MP) contamination across eight strategic sites using an integrated multi-step protocol. The optimized analytical protocol was a sequential, multi-stage process designed for maximal recovery and high-resolution characterization of microplastics. The recovered particles then underwent a rigorous, high-resolution granulometric analysis via a cascade of standardized sieves (2 mm to 63 μm), enabling precise particle size distribution profiling combined to density separation using various saline solutions, enabling the capture of particles down to 1 μm after pre-sieving through a 2-mm mesh, followed by size fractionation using a standardized sieve cascade from 630 to 63 μm; the <63 μm fraction was subsequently recovered on 1-μm membrane filters, allowing characterization down to 1 μm. Results revealed a non-uniform distribution of microplastics (MPs), with site OH14 showing the highest observed microplastic abundance among the sampled stations exhibiting the highest particle count (265 particles) and a dominance of larger fragments and microfilaments indicative of a primary discharge point. Morphological analysis showed a widespread dominance of microfilaments, particularly at OH14 and OH7, pointing to chronic contamination from domestic wastewater, while fragments and films at sites like OH1 indicated significant secondary pollution from macroplastic degradation. Chromatic profiling shows that RI16 is characterized by valuable, vibrant colors, whereas the finest fractions (63 μm–1 μm) at OH7 and OH4 consist primarily of colorless particles. This study indicates that MP pollution is a multi-source issue governed by site-specific factors such as hydrodynamics and proximity to urban zones. This study provides a high-resolution map of microplastic (MP) contamination, highlighting a highly heterogeneous and location-specific pollution profile.

title: Genetically engineered microorganisms for environmental remediation: An integrated critical review of degradation mechanisms, ecological risks, and regulatory frameworks
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Chimeme Martin Ekwueme, Daniel Hogan Itam, Michael Osang Odudu, Ibiba Taiwo Horsfall
abstract: Genetically modified microorganisms (GEMs) offer promising opportunities for enhancing microbial remediation of persistent environmental contaminants. This review critically evaluated genetic engineering technologies, remediation performance, ecological implications, mechanisms, and global research trends associated with GEM-based soil bioremediation. A systematic literature search was conducted using predefined electronic databases and database-specific search strategies, supplemented by backward and forward citation chaining. The search identified 395 database records and 123 additional records through citation searching, yielding 518 candidate records. Following duplicate removal and title/abstract screening, 505 potentially relevant records underwent full-text assessment against predefined eligibility, relevance, and methodological-quality criteria. Eligible literature was classified into primary experimental/field studies, secondary evidence sources, and contextual regulatory or policy sources, with 50 studies retained for the final evidence synthesis. The review identified progressive application of recombinant DNA technology, CRISPR-Cas9, CRISPRi/CRISPRa, base editing, emerging prime editing, synthetic biology, and multi-omics-guided engineering to enhance pollutant degradation, sequestration, detoxification, and stress tolerance. Primary studies generally reported improved remediation performance of engineered strains compared with corresponding native or control treatments, although outcomes varied with pollutant type, host organism, environmental conditions, and engineering strategy. GEMs also demonstrated potential for synergistic plant–microbe remediation. However, ecological concerns involving horizontal gene transfer, effects on indigenous microbial communities, unintended persistence, metabolic burden, and evolutionary instability remain important barriers to deployment. Regulatory uncertainty and limited field-scale validation further constrain translation.

title: Macrophyte-mediated responses of epiphytic biofilms under erythromycin stress in wetland mesocosms
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Abigail Mwin-nea Samwini, Deqiang Chen, Lydia Numafo-Brempong, Md Nashir Uddin, Chichedo I. Duru, Samendra Sherchan, Dong Hee Kang
abstract: The widespread occurrence of antibiotics in aquatic environments poses significant risks to microbial community structure and ecosystem functioning, particularly in nature-based treatment systems. This study investigates the effects of erythromycin (ERY) on epiphytic biofilm communities in wetland mesocosms containing submerged macrophytes (Potamogeton wrightii) and artificial substrates, with emphasis on substrate-dependent microbial responses and functional implications. High-throughput sequencing, diversity metrics, functional prediction (FAPROTAX), and morphological analyses were integrated to assess community restructuring in response to ERY exposure. ERY induced pronounced shifts in microbial composition and predicted functional potential. In artificial systems, Proteobacteria increased from about 63% to 70% (p 0.05). SEM revealed increased biofilm aggregation under ERY, suggesting enhanced EPS-mediated protection consistent with protective biofilm response. ERY drives substrate-dependent microbial restructuring, with macrophytes enhancing functional stability. These findings provide an integrated framework for understanding substrate-associated microbial responses in antibiotic–microbiome interactions and inform optimization of wetland treatment systems.

title: Evaluation of second-generation adenosine triphosphate measurements as a surrogate for biological oxygen demand monitoring in small-scale wastewater treatment systems
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Gábor Györki, János Kiss, Judit Knisz
abstract: In wastewater treatment, the long analysis time of key performance parameters, particularly biological oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) limits both the timely acquisition of process-relevant information and the possibility of rapid operational intervention. This limitation is amplified in domestic treatment systems, where monitoring and professional supervision are typically not available. As a result, process disturbances may remain undetected, reducing treatment efficiency and increasing environmental risk. Rapid and robust operational indicators are therefore needed to support timely assessment of process performance, especially because unlike large facilities, any intervention after off-site analyses requires returning to remote locations. This study investigates whether second-generation adenosine-triphosphate (ATP)-based biomass measurements can reliably assess biological performance in domestic systems under real operating conditions, also evaluating this rapid method for assessing activated sludge health. Influent, activated sludge and effluent wastewater samples were analyzed for BOD, COD and ATP fractions, and relationships between ATP-based parameters and conventional wastewater-quality parameters were assessed. The results indicate a statistically significant linear relationship between ATP removal and BOD removal. Positive association was also identified between activated sludge condition and overall treatment efficiency. Our findings indicate that ATP-based measurements have potential as a rapid operational indicators of biological treatment performance.

title: Hydrosalinity-mediated decoupling of inherited Zn Cu enrichment, operational bioavailability, and soil-health degradation across active and relict Caspian coastal landforms
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Ramin Samieifard, Ahmad Heidari, Patrick Joseph Drohan
abstract: Coastal salinization may alter the environmental expression of landform-associated metal pools, yet enrichment, operational bioavailability, and soil-function response are rarely evaluated together across geomorphic units. We tested whether ZnCu concentration-based screening, operational bioavailability, hydrosalinity stress, and soil-quality response co-varied across 136 surface soils (0–20 cm) from six active and relict southeastern Caspian coastal landforms. HNO₃-extractable Zn and Cu supported Zn-Cu-specific contamination and ecological-risk screening, DTPA-extractable fractions represented operational bioavailability, and EC, SAR, SAR-derived estimated ESP, and ion-sum TDS characterized hydrosalinity. Zn, rather than Cu, drove concentration-based differentiation: minimal Zn contamination was most prevalent in Lagoonal deposit (70.8%) and Modern lagoon (69.2%), whereas Cu remained in the no-contamination PI class across all landforms. All ZnCu ecological-risk values remained within the low-risk class, indicating relative screening pressure rather than direct toxicity. Strong cross-domain divergence nevertheless emerged. Lagoonal deposit had the highest integrated ZnCu risk score (0.596) but one of the lowest bioavailability-pressure scores (0.278), whereas Barrier had moderate integrated risk (0.448) but the highest bioavailability pressure (0.507). Modern lagoon combined the highest hydrosalinity stress (0.812) with the lowest soil-quality score (0.315). Scenario-based soil-health classifications also varied with weighting. These spatial mismatches show that concentration-based ZnCu enrichment is not a surrogate for operational bioavailability or soil-function degradation. The patterns are consistent with landform-associated sedimentary context structuring acid-extractable ZnCu pools and hydrosalinity acting as a modifying environmental context, while causal mechanisms and seasonal dynamics require direct validation.

title: Root uptake of carbon from soil: A systematic review comparing measured and modeled evidence
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Soroush Majlesi, Ari T.K. Ikonen, Sari Ruohonen-Petersson, Zahra Shirani, Tatiana Trubnikova, Christina Biasi
abstract: Root uptake of carbon from soil has been reported for decades, yet its quantitative importance remains uncertain. While atmospheric CO2 assimilation dominates plant carbon budgets, roots can also acquire dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from soil porewater. These pathways are ecologically relevant, particularly in radiological impact assessments, where radiocarbon (14C) from soil may enter vegetation and food chains through the same transfer processes. Here we systematically review experimental and modeling studies of root uptake of carbon from soil. Measured datasets from 15 studies indicate that root uptake averages 1.95 ± 0.51% of whole-plant carbon. Uptake was broadly consistent across functional types (2% in grasses and forbs, 1–2% in trees). By carbon form, mean contributions were 1.9% for DIC and 2.4% for DOC; these are separate subgroup means and are not additive. In contrast, modeled estimates from 10 studies largely developed for radioecological assessments predicted lower uptake of about 1% and considered only DIC. Modeled values also differed by functional type, with lower uptake in grass (0.3%) and higher in forbs (1.8%) but taxonomic scope was limited. These comparisons suggest that models tend to predict lower root uptake than in experiments, although the difference is not statistically significant with current sample sizes. We attribute this gap to omission of DOC pathways, microbial mediation, and physiological processes such as re-assimilation of transported DIC. Incorporating these mechanisms into models will improve representation of soil-to-plant carbon transfer and its roles in growth, nutrient metabolism, stress responses, and radiological assessments.

title: Integrated assessment of groundwater depletion, climatic drought and land surface dynamics in the semi-arid Barind Tract, Bangladesh
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Roni Roy
abstract: Due to intensive groundwater abstraction and climate stress, the Barind Tract in northwest Bangladesh, a semi-arid area prone to drought, is experiencing progressive aquifer depletion. The coupled interactions between subsurface storage loss, hydro-climatic drought, and land-surface dynamics remain insufficiently quantified. Integrating weekly piezometric hydrographs (1981–2022), multi-scalar drought indices (SPI/SPEI), and multi-decadal Landsat imagery (1995–2024), this study presents a comprehensive hydro-climatic assessment of the region. Non-parametric Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope analyses across 12 monitoring wells reveal widespread groundwater level (GWL) decline rates ranging from −0.01 to −0.61 m/year, with severe depletion concentrated in the elevated central sub-districts (Nachole, Tanore, and Godagari). Multi-variable Pearson correlation matrix demonstrates that subsurface drawdown is significantly more sensitive to temperature-driven potential evapotranspiration (SPEI-12; r = +0.744, p 0.05, NS). This resolves the “NDVI Paradox,” proving that dry-season canopy expansion represents an anthropogenic, deep tubewell irrigation-driven transformation rather than eco-hydrological recovery. These quantitative insights emphasize the urgent need for volumetric extraction caps, crop diversification away from Boro rice monoculture, and conjunctive water management in semi-arid environments.

title: Environmental drivers of total coliform and E. coli bioaerosol dispersal near cattle and poultry operations
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Harsimran Kaur Kapoor, Halle Greenbaum, Christina Kessler, Blanca Ruiz Llacsahuanga, Charles Bency Appolon, Rawane Raad, Mia Gale, Laurent Lagos Mendoza, Zoila Chevez Tepas, Faith Critzer, Manpreet Singh, Harshavardhan Thippareddi, Michelle Danyluk, Jason M. Scheffler, Camila Rodrigues, Elisa Tobar Sandoval, Victor Hugo Maldonado Machado da Cruz, Abhinav Mishra
abstract: Adjacent land use associated with concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) has been implicated as a potential source of microbial contamination of fresh produce; however, the role of bioaerosol-mediated transport remains poorly understood. This study aimed to quantify the relationship between meteorological conditions and concentrations of Escherichia coli and total coliform bioaerosols in environments surrounding cattle and poultry operations in the Southeastern United States. Active air sampling was conducted at multiple setback distances (0, 50, 100, 400, and 1000 m) and heights (0.5, 2, and 5 m) across cattle (N = 4 farms; n = 19 visits) and poultry farms (N = 5 farms; n = 11 visits). Meteorological variables such as temperature, relative humidity, wind, and gust speed recorded during sampling and 24 h prior were integrated into Random Forest (RF) models to identify key environmental factors. Concentrations of total coliforms and E. coli declined sharply with distance from animal operations, and Random Forest models explained up to 98% of this variance near cattle operations (R2 = 0.87–0.98, RMSE = 0.09–0.25), compared to 56–69% near poultry operations (R2 = 0.56–0.69, RMSE = 0.42–0.47). Poultry operations exhibited higher and more variable concentrations of E. coli and total coliforms compared to cattle operations. RF models identified 24-h lag temperature and relative humidity as primary predictors near cattle operations. In contrast, setback distance and real-time meteorological conditions, including temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed, were the most important predictors near poultry operations, reflecting the influence of mechanically ventilated emission sources. This study provides quantitative insights to support risk assessments and inform setback distance recommendations to reduce the risk of produce contamination associated with adjacent land use. This study provides quantitative insights into bioaerosol transport from livestock operations and supports increasing separation between agricultural fields and adjacent livestock operations, while incorporating site-specific meteorological conditions into preharvest risk assessments.

title: Strong soil functional recovery under nature-based management despite limited prokaryotic community restructuring in Mediterranean olive groves
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Gustavo Ruiz-Cátedra, Julio Calero, Evangelina Pareja-Sánchez, Pablo Domouso de Agar, José Liétor, Roberto Garcia-Ruiz
abstract: Many Mediterranean olive groves are degraded and restoring soil functioning while maintaining ecosystem resilience is a major challenge. Nature-based solutions (NBS) have been proposed to enhance soil processes, yet it remains unclear whether functional recovery is accompanied by shifts in microbial community structure or can occur within a stable taxonomic framework. We evaluated differences in soil functioning and prokaryotic community composition associated with NBS management in Mediterranean olive groves using a paired design (NBS vs. conventional management, CON) and nearby forest soils as a reference system. Soil physico-chemical properties, enzyme activities, microbial processes, carbon-use profiles, and prokaryotic communities (16S rRNA gene sequencing) were assessed. Functional recovery was quantified relative to the forest–CON gradient. NBS management markedly enhanced soil functioning compared with CON, with β-glucosidase and dehydrogenase activities increasing by 3.4- and approximately 8-fold, respectively. On average, NBS systems recovered 40.1–45.2% of the functional difference between CON soils and forest reference conditions for key soil properties and microbial processes, while CLPP-derived carbon-substrate utilization exceeded forest reference levels (144%). Despite these pronounced functional differences, broad prokaryotic community composition differed little between management systems. PERMANOVA detected a significant association with soil type (p = 0.03), whereas the association with management was not significant (p = 0.39). Variation partitioning including management, soil type, SOM and pH explained only 7.77% of total community variation; pH and soil type showed small positive unique fractions, whereas no detectable independent management-associated fraction remained after accounting for the other predictors. Thus, long-term NBS management was strongly associated with enhanced soil biological functioning despite comparatively limited changes in broad prokaryotic community composition.

title: Wastewater-based surveillance for mpox: Methodological advances and surveillance performance—A systematic review
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Ananda Tiwari, Taru Miller, Elena Sgarabotto, Melissa Kabena, Dylan Shea, Tam Tran, Paul KingPriest, Vito Baraka, Vivi Maketa, Bart Mesuere, Adriana Krolicka, Marc Christian Tahita, Rolf Lood, Tarja Pitkänen
abstract: Despite the growing use of wastewater-based surveillance (WBS) for monitoring mpox outbreaks worldwide, a comprehensive understanding of the complete methodological workflow—from sampling and laboratory analysis to data interpretation—remains limited. This systematic review aimed to evaluate (i) the geographical distribution of mpox WBS studies, (ii) concordance with clinical surveillance and the potential of early-warning detection, (iii) methodological approaches, and (iv) the influence of sample type on detection sensitivity. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, original studies on WBS of monkeypox virus (MPXV) were identified through systematic searches of Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus up to January 2026. Studies that did not report original WBS data were excluded. Where applicable, methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using predefined criteria. Due to substantial methodological heterogeneity among the included studies, findings were qualitatively synthesized using a thematic approach based on the review objectives. Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. Most were conducted in the United States, Canada, China and Switzerland, highlighting limited global coverage and a notable lack of studies from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly sub-Saharan Africa. Multiple studies detected MPXV in wastewater before or despite few, clinically confirmed cases, demonstrating the value of WBS for early outbreak detection and identifying otherwise undiagnosed community transmission. MPXV concentrations were consistently higher in wastewater solids than in liquid influent, with centrifuge pellets and primary sludge providing greater analytical sensitivity than supernatant samples. However, substantial variation in sampling strategies, concentration methods, nucleic acid extraction protocols, and molecular assays limited direct comparison across studies. Overall, current evidence supports WBS as a sensitive complementary tool for mpox surveillance. Harmonized methodologies, wider implementation in LMICs, and integration with conventional public health surveillance are needed to strengthen global outbreak preparedness and One Health surveillance.

title: Pharmaceutical removal in urban wastewater: Assessing the hydraulic retention time and climatic variability in high-rate algal pond performance
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Eliana M. Jiménez-Bambague, Ingrid V. Mendoza-Nieto, Ángela Rengifo-Vera, Fiderman Machuca-Martínez, Carlos A. Madera-Parra
abstract: The continuous discharge of pharmaceutical residues from urban wastewater into aquatic environments poses a growing environmental challenge. This study investigated the performance of two pilot-scale high-rate algal ponds (HRAPs) operated at hydraulic retention times (HRTs) of 3 and 5 days under an American tropical climate for the removal of pharmaceutical compounds. Both systems were continuously fed with real urban wastewater previously treated by chemically enhanced primary treatment (CEPT). Comparable performance was observed at both HRTs, with no significant differences in removal efficiencies. Maximum removals reached were 81.9% for chemical oxygen demand (COD), 99.6% for Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and 94.6% for lipid-lowering agents, while venlafaxine achieved up to 67.7%. Antiepileptic compounds showed the lowest and most inconsistent removal, underscoring the limitations of biological treatment and showing the necessity to couple with physicochemical processes. Overall, a 3-day HRT was enough to achieve high removal efficiencies for most target compounds while substantially reducing their associated ecological threat, showing a smaller bioreactor volume requirement and the potential of full-scale implementation of HRAP systems in American tropical regions. Similarly, the study provides evidence that climatic variability associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon might enhance micropollutant removal by promoting biodegradation and photodegradation pathways under higher temperature and solar radiation regimes.

title: Effects of pig slurry fertilization history on grassland microbiomes: Insights from field and mesocosm experiments
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Karoline Jetter, Kunal Jani, Kerstin Wilhelm, Ulrike Stehle, Rostand Chamedjeu, Christian Riedel, Simone Sommer, Lena Wilfert, Patrick Schäfer
abstract: Land use, particularly fertilization, alters species communities and ecological interactions in grassland ecosystems. While long-term pig slurry application is known to affect microbial communities across different compartments of the trophic chain, short-term effects of organic fertilization have typically been studied in isolated individual compartments. In this study, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to examine microbial communities from grassland sites with a history of pig slurry fertilization, alongside laboratory mesocosms simulating repeated short-term applications. Using Trifolium pratense as a focal plant species as well as earthworms, voles and bumblebees as animal representatives, we assessed both immediate and legacy effects across soil-plant-animal compartments of the trophic chain. Root associated microbial diversity decreased following short-term fertilization, accompanied by shifts in community composition. However, the long-term history of fertilization exerted more pronounced effects, altering microbial communities in soil, plant and animal-associated microbiomes. Although important players in pathogen-defense (e.g. Sphingomonas) decreased in flower microbial communities after fertilization, the microbial communities still hosted genera supporting beehive productivity and colony health (Lactobacillus). These legacy-driven changes in community compositions across compartments were mediated by changes in nutrient compositions, reflected in core microbiome members, and characterized by an increase in copiotrophs linked to ecosystem functioning in soil and plant-roots. Laboratory mesocosm setups, representing repeated fertilization events, successfully simulated legacy effects observed in grassland ecosystems, including key ecological interactions. Overlapping microbial genera amongst belowground compartments, along with consistent shifts in their abundances, indicate strong interconnectedness amongst microbial communities and suggest the potential propagation of compositional changes along the trophic chain. Overall, this study underscores the importance of a holistic approach to evaluate anthropogenic practices such as fertilization on ecosystems, highlighting both immediate and legacy impacts of intensive pig slurry application on grassland microbial communities, with broader implications for ecosystem functioning and health.

title: Effects of climate change and anthropogenic pressure on water resources and ecosystem services in a high-elevation Andean socio-ecosystem (Katari basin, Lake Titicaca, Bolivia): A synthesis
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Stéphane Guédron, Dario Acha, Jorge Molina-Carpio, Carlos Revilla, Alejandra I. Domic, Carlos Molina, Fabien Anthelme, Antoine Rabatel, Thomas Condom, Jhan Carlo Espinoza, Sébastien Hardy, Victor-Hugo Perales, Claude Legouill, Frédéric Satge, Eléonore Resongles, Géraldine Sarret, Dennis Archundia, Luis Roberto Hernández-Angulo, Marc Pouilly, Angela Montecino
abstract: Climate change and human activities are transforming socio-ecosystems worldwide, damaging the water cycle and biological diversity. This work analyzes the current state and vulnerabilities of the Katari watershed (Bolivia), a region representative of Andean socio-ecosystems. The high-elevation Puna is one of the biomes most affected by climate change in the South American Central Andes. Regional climate scenarios predict increasing warming, declining precipitation and enhanced evaporation, which are expected to increase the frequency and duration of droughts. Glaciers are rapidly retreating, and critical ecosystem components such as peatlands and lakes are impacted by global change. Anthropogenic pressure significantly compounds these challenges, accelerating system's degradation. The Katari watershed, which includes the large urban area of El Alto, faces persistent challenges due to insufficient sanitation infrastructure. The discharge of untreated effluents containing a mixture of organic matter, nutrients, metal(loid)s, and emerging contaminants like antibiotics damages the Katari - Lake Titicaca socio-ecosystems. This contamination poses potential public health risks associated with sustained exposure to environmental contaminants. Finally, the synergistic effects of climate and pollution can lead to abrupt degradation events, such as eutrophication and massive algal blooms in Lake Titicaca, threatening local biodiversity. Addressing these challenges urgently requires reducing contaminant discharge, preserving natural spaces and creating engineered buffer zones that leverage local ecological characteristics, like plant-based filtration systems, to naturally remove contaminants from water. Furthermore, advancing sustainable management requires the reinforcement of governance structures that incorporate local communities' needs and knowledge into decision-making processes, thereby fostering more resilient management systems.

title: Modeling Eucalyptus growth and nitrogen uptake under rainfed and irrigated conditions: A comparison of two crop simulation models
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Ramon Amaro de Sales, Júlio Cesar Lima Neves, Elvis Felipe Elli, Hélio Garcia Leite, Evandro Chaves de Oliveira, Samuel Cordeiro Vitor Martins
abstract: To support management decisions and climate adaptation, process-based growth models such as 3-PG and APSIM have become increasingly important tools for simulating forest productivity under diverse environmental conditions. Comparative evaluations of these models are essential for understanding their capacity to represent Eucalyptus growth across contrasting climates, soils, genotypes, and management regimes. This study compared the performance of APSIM Next Generation and 3-PG in simulating Eucalyptus growth and related processes following calibration and validation with field data collected under contrasting water and nutrient supply conditions. In the validation of stand volume, APSIM achieved NSE = 0.76, R2 = 0.83, and RMSD = 44.6 m3 ha−1, whereas 3-PG produced NSE = 0.66, R2 = 0.77, and RMSD = 37.3 m3 ha−1. Consistent with their structural characteristics, both models were responsive to variations in water availability and nitrogen management. Variable-specific differences were observed: both models performed well for stand volume and mean annual increment; APSIM provided a more detailed representation of biomass partitioning and nitrogen dynamics; whereas 3-PG showed advantages for structural variables requiring parsimonious parameterization, depending on site and genotype. Local deviations were reduced at harvest age. Overall, APSIM and 3-PG proved to be effective tools for simulating Eucalyptus growth across contrasting edaphoclimatic conditions, demonstrating strong predictive performance for stand volume. These results support their application as decision-support tools for site-specific genotype selection, evaluation of water and nutrient management strategies, and assessment of climate-change impacts on forest productivity.

title: Kumaraswamy distribution-based geomorphological instantaneous unit hydrograph for runoff modeling in an ephemeral stream
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Gunjan Chauhan, Himanshu Sharma, Manoj Langhi
abstract: Flood prediction in ephemeral streams is challenging due to variable rainfall patterns and limited historical data. This study develops and evaluates three Geomorphological Instantaneous Unit Hydrograph (GIUH) model variants for the ephemeral Banas River, India: Nash model-based, probability distribution function-based, and a novel Kumaraswamy distribution-based approach. Models were validated using daily and hourly discharge hydrographs at monitoring sites. Performance evaluation using R2, Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) metrics demonstrated that the Kumaraswamy distribution-based GIUH model outperforms conventional approaches in regenerating hydrographs for ephemeral streams, offering improved flood prediction capabilities in data-scarce environments.

title: Systemic translocation of micro- and nanoplastics in humans: Evidence, mechanisms and future perspectives
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Raquel Francine Liermann Garcia, José Guilherme Pickler, Christian Evangelista Garcia, Hercilio Fronza Junior, Bruna Louise Silva, Rodrigo Barbano Weingrill, Karina Munhoz de Paula Alves Coelho, Paulo Henrique Condeixa de França
abstract: Background Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are now widespread environmental contaminants, and polymeric material has been reported in a growing number of human tissues. Ingestion and inhalation are considered the main routes of exposure, yet the processes that govern particle uptake, tissue translocation, systemic distribution, retention, and clearance remain poorly understood. Objective To critically examine the available evidence on MNP translocation and organ biodistribution and to assess the analytical methods currently used to detect and characterize these particles in human tissues. Methods We conducted a critical narrative review using PubMed and Web of Science, complemented by manual screening of relevant reference lists. Particular attention was given to studies published between 2023 and 2026, while earlier landmark and methodological studies were included when necessary. Human observational studies, experimental MNP models, analytical investigations, and non-plastic nanoparticle research were evaluated according to their relevance, directness, analytical reliability, and methodological limitations. Results Polymeric material has been reported in the human placenta, lungs, liver, kidneys, brain, and other biological compartments. These findings indicate the presence and broad distribution of MNP-associated material in the human body and suggest possible systemic translocation, though the exact physiological pathways remain unconfirmed. Evidence from experimental models suggests that translocation may involve M-cell-mediated transport, endocytic uptake, vesicular trafficking, and changes in barrier integrity. These processes are strongly influenced by particle size, surface characteristics, exposure conditions, and the biological model studied. Vibrational spectroscopy, thermal analysis, and high-resolution imaging provide complementary information on polymer identity, mass burden, morphology, and tissue localization. However, contamination, matrix interference, incomplete recovery of nanoscale particles, and the absence of standardized analytical protocols continue to limit comparison across studies. Conclusion Current human studies support the occurrence of MNP-associated polymeric material in multiple tissues, whereas most mechanistic evidence for barrier crossing and cellular uptake still comes from experimental models. The routes, toxicokinetics, and clinical implications of MNP distribution in humans remain uncertain. Progress in this field will depend on standardized analytical workflows, rigorous contamination control, orthogonal particle confirmation, and larger, well-characterized human studies.

title: Integrated Model for PFAS Environmental and Public Health Risk Assessment (IMPERA): A framework for multidimensional evidence integration
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Rajendra Kothavade, Sonia Marie Frias
abstract: Background Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants of growing public health concern because of their widespread occurrence, environmental persistence, complex environmental behavior, and evolving toxicological understanding. Although advances in analytical chemistry, environmental monitoring, toxicology, and regulatory guidance have strengthened PFAS assessment, interpretation remains limited because concentration- and toxicity-based metrics alone do not capture analytical completeness, PFAS composition, environmental transport, exposure context, or scientific uncertainty. Objectives This review critically evaluates current PFAS interpretation approaches and presents the Integrated Model for PFAS Environmental and Public Health Risk Assessment (IMPERA), a multidimensional evidence-integration framework designed to complement existing PFAS risk-assessment methods. Methods IMPERA was developed through a critical synthesis of evidence from PFAS analytical chemistry, environmental fate and transport, exposure science, toxicology, regulatory guidance, and decision science. Evidence was organized into five complementary domains and integrated using structured Weight-of-Evidence (WoE) principles. Results IMPERA is founded on the premise that equivalent concentration- or toxicity-based indicators do not necessarily imply equivalent environmental or public health significance. The framework integrates Analytical Coverage, PFAS Composition, Environmental Transport, System-Level Exposure, and Toxicological Interpretation through the proposed Analytical–Chemical–Environmental Coupling (ACEC) concept to generate an Integrated Evidence Profile. Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) may be applied after evidence integration when comparison among management alternatives is required. An illustrative comparison of two hypothetical drinking-water systems demonstrates how similar toxicity metrics can produce different Integrated Evidence Profiles because of differences in evidence completeness, environmental context, and uncertainty. The framework is further contextualized within a One Health perspective linking environmental, animal, and human health. Conclusions IMPERA complements existing regulatory and health-based risk-assessment approaches by providing a transparent framework for multidimensional PFAS interpretation. Although the illustrative application demonstrates its operational logic, empirical validation through case studies and reproducibility testing is required before broader implementation.

title: Transfer of arsenic in surface waters impacted by anthropogenic activities: spatio-temporal evolution, speciation and source tracking in a former mining district (Orbiel valley, France)
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Marie Heydon, Eléonore Resongles, Corinne Casiot, Eva Schreck, Rémi Freydier, Mylène Marie, Carole Causserand, Sophie Delpoux, Martin Roddaz, Alain Pages, Philippe Behra, Jérôme Viers
abstract: Past mining in the Orbiel Valley has led to long-term arsenic (As) contamination risks for ecosystems and inhabitants. Around 12 million tons of tailings produced by As and gold (Au) mines of the last century remain on site. Despite remediation efforts, including lime treatment and waste confinement, recent studies report persistent As pollution in water and sediments. Given the area complexity, a more detailed study of As sources and fate in the watershed is essential: 1) for characterizing As contamination levels in the Orbiel River and its tributaries over various hydrological periods, 2) for identifying the main As sources, and 3) for distinguishing the natural geochemical baseline from anthropogenic inputs. From 2018 to 2023, water samples (<0.22 μm) were collected from the Orbiel River and its tributaries to analyze major element and metal(loid) concentrations, alkalinity, pH, dissolved organic carbon, Sr isotope ratio and As redox state. Rock samples from regional formations were also collected to compare natural versus anthropogenic Sr isotope signature. Upstream of the mining district, median dissolved As concentration in the Orbiel River was about 2 μg·L−1 increased to 37 μg·L−1 downstream, with over 20 to 60% of dissolved As as As(III). Arsenic concentrations peaked during summer low-flow periods, suggesting groundwater contributions. The 87Sr/86Sr ratio indicated a less radiogenic, anthropogenic signal downstream, likely linked to lime-treated mine waste. However, similar isotope ratios in certain limestone areas complicated source discrimination, highlighting the need for additional tracers. Mining-impacted tributaries were identified as significant contributors to As input in the Orbiel River.

title: Mercury dynamics in open coastal-marine system: a case study of Rosignano-Solvay (Tuscany, Italy)
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Daniela Salvagio Manta, Mattia Barsanti, Maria Bonsignore, Gaspare Buffa, Ivana Delbono, Fabio Conte, Marianna Del Core, Gabriella Di Martino, Luigi Giaramita, Elvira Oliveri, Francesco Placenti, Enza Maria Quinci, Alberto Ribotti, Nadia Sabatino, Antonio Schirone, Roberto Sorgente, Giorgio Tranchida, Vincenzo Tancredi, Renato Tonielli, Anna Traina
abstract: Chlor-alkali plants have operated along the Mediterranean coastline since the 1940s, representing major point sources of mercury (Hg) to marine sediments. This study evaluates the regional-scale impact of the chlor-alkali plant at Rosignano (central Italy), advancing the “open-system paradigm” for legacy contaminants. Our multi-proxy investigation of 51 sediment cores, coupled with hydrodynamic observations and numerical simulations, reveals that circulation-driven transport facilitates the offshore dispersal of Hg-enriched particles, creating depocenters well beyond the original point source. Reworking processes maintain elevated Hg concentrations in surface sediments, sustaining potential exposure pathways for marine biota. Historical Hg inputs dominate present-day sediment contamination, with concentrations reaching up to 23× above background levels across 100 km2 of seafloor. While nearshore areas show natural attenuation via burial process of contaminated layers, offshore depocenters act as bioactive zones. Surface methylmercury data indicate ongoing biogeochemical reactivation of legacy Hg via a “benthic pump” mechanism in suboxic offshore environments. These findings point to the need for integrated global monitoring frameworks under the Minamata Convention on Mercury and complementary instruments such as the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) that account for far-field contaminant redistribution and the spatial decoupling of ecological risk in open coastal systems.

title: Rethinking heatwave analysis under climate change: A climatic-type approach across Brazil
description: Publication date: 25 October 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1053 Author(s): Leonardo Brandão do Prado, Ana Carolina Lenz de Assis, Daniel Araújo Machado da Silva, Patrick Nascimento
abstract: This study analyzes the spatial and temporal variability of heatwaves in Brazil based on Köppen climate classification, rather than administrative boundaries, over the period 1991–2020. It focuses on key heatwave characteristics, including frequency, intensity, and duration, while also examining seasonality and long-term trends across eight climate types. This approach contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how extreme heat events manifest under different atmospheric regimes. Daily maximum temperature data from the Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (INMET) were used to calculate the Warm Spell Duration Index (WSDI), with heatwaves defined as periods of at least six consecutive days exceeding the climatological 90th percentile. Data processing involved gap-filling techniques and automated workflows implemented through HEATpulse, an R package designed for heatwave detection. The results reveal 1) A consistent intensification of heat extremes, particularly after 2010. 2) A seasonal expansion of heatwaves was identified, with events extending beyond the traditional dry season in the Amazon and becoming more persistent in Equatorial Savanna climates—specifically the As (summer dry) and Aw (winter dry) types—where monthly frequencies exceeded 15 and 21 days, respectively. 3) Heatwave occurrences have also surpassed typical seasonal boundaries in other climates, including Aw regimes. 4) Statistically significant positive trends (p < 0.05) were primarily observed in tropical and semi-arid climates, indicating that extreme heat has transitioned from episodic occurrences to a structural characteristic of these regions. The findings highlight Equatorial Monsoon (Am), Equatorial Savanna (As), and Equatorial Savanna (Aw) climates as particularly vulnerable. Applying this framework, these patterns may also be relevant to analogous regions globally, including Central Africa, southern and eastern India, mainland Southeast Asia, and northern Australia, which are susceptible to heatwaves.

title: Sedimentary and redox controls on pyrite sulfur isotopes in oxic–suboxic continental shelf sediments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Xin Chang, Tiegang Li, Zhifang Xiong, Chengguo Guan, Yu Gu, Houjie Wang, Guangchao Zhuang, Xiting Liu
abstract: Pyrite links sedimentary processes with the biogeochemical sulfur cycle and is widely used for reconstructing past redox and depositional environments. However, the controls on pyrite formation and its sulfur isotopic composition (δ34Spyr) in dynamic continental shelf settings, particularly under fluctuating oxic–suboxic conditions, remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate a late Pleistocene–Holocene sedimentary succession from the mud wedge off the Shandong Peninsula (Yellow Sea), which provides a high-resolution archive of glacial–interglacial environmental change, to resolve the relationship between δ34Spyr and shelf sedimentary evolution. We combine sulfur isotope measurements with redox-sensitive trace metals (U and Mo) and previously published sedimentological and geochemical data. Bulk δ34Spyr shows systematic variability associated with several depositional and diagenetic factors. First, δ34Spyr covaries with sedimentation rate, total organic carbon content, and water depth, indicating an important influence of depositional dynamics on pyrite formation and apparent isotopic fractionation. Second, more oxidizing conditions during the Holocene sea-level highstand coincide with generally higher δ34Spyr values, consistent with redox-related changes in sulfur burial. Third, localized sulfur cycling possibly related to anaerobic oxidation of methane may have contributed to elevated δ34Spyr in discrete intervals through isotopic mixing. These results indicate that bulk pyrite sulfur isotopes in oxic–suboxic continental shelf sediments primarily record sedimentary evolution and local diagenetic sulfur cycling, while redox-related variations in sulfur burial may further influence their stratigraphic pattern. This study provides a well-constrained example of δ34Spyr behavior in a non-euxinic shelf environment and emphasizes that depositional and early diagenetic processes must be explicitly considered when applying pyrite sulfur isotopes to paleoenvironmental reconstructions.

title: Synergistic effects of montmorillonite and microbial consortia on Cr(VI) reduction
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Yi Zhou, Guocheng Lv, Yunpu Zhao, Xiaotong Yang, Meng Liu, Xuelian Yu, Hongli Chen, Xiaoyan Li, Libing Liao
abstract: Cr(VI) contamination poses a serious threat to ecosystems and human health, making bioremediation strategies that leverage mineral–microbe interactions one of the most critical remediation approaches. Here, we systematically describe the synergistic role of montmorillonite (Mnt) and an indigenous microbial consortium in driving Cr(VI) transformation under simulated groundwater conditions. In batch experiments, abiotic systems with Mnt or sterilized biomass showed negligible or limited Cr(VI) removal, whereas the Mnt–microbe system achieved nearly complete Cr(VI) removal in Cycle 1 and maintained consistently high removal efficiencies over three consecutive redox cycles. RT-qPCR analysis revealed an adaptive strategy whereby the chromate efflux transporter gene chrA was upregulated in the late stage while the intracellular reductase gene yieF remained continuously expressed, concurrent with a strong enrichment of Gammaproteobacteria (from 11.35% to 89.90–96.35%) within Mnt-provided microhabitats. Advanced spectroscopy (XRD, XPS, EXAFS) and microscopy, together with a quantitative Cr mass balance, demonstrate that the main reduction product is Cr(III), which is retained through three pathways: (i) retention of Cr(III) compounds on solid surfaces, (ii) interlayer fixation of Cr(III) within Mnt, and (iii) coprecipitation of Cr(III) with Fe(oxyhydr)oxides. These results highlight a combined mechanism whereby Mnt acts as a chemical buffer, structural host, and ecological scaffold, providing a robust, field-relevant strategy for in situ remediation of Cr(VI)-contaminated aquifers and soils.

title: Behavior of major to trace elements, volatiles, and metals during basaltic arc magma differentiation: a slow-cooling experimental study at 1.5, 1.0, 0.7, and 0.4 GPa
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 433 Author(s): Jia Chang, Andreas Audétat
abstract: High-pressure differentiation of arc basaltic magmas in compressive arc settings is commonly invoked to generate high-Sr/Y magmas associated with porphyry Cu deposits, but why such magmas are particularly fertile remains debated. To address this question, we conducted slow-cooling crystallization experiments on a volatile- and metal-doped natural arc basalt at 1.5, 1.0, 0.7, and 0.4 GPa. The starting material contained geologically realistic volatile and metal contents, including 3.5 wt% H2O, 0.4 wt% CO2, 2200 µg/g S, and 1000 µg/g Cl. Samples were homogenized at 1250 °C, slowly cooled to target temperatures, and then quenched. Most runs used single-crystal zircon liners to minimize Fe, S, and metal loss to Pt95Rh05 capsules. In all pressure series, minerals crystallized in the sequence olivine → pyroxenes → amphibole → ±plagioclase, with early olivine and pyroxenes partly replaced by amphibole during cooling. These textures resemble those in deep-crustal arc cumulates. Comparison between experimental residual melts and global arc magma suites suggests that recurrent recharge and mixing of primitive mafic melts with variably evolved melts are common during the formation of intermediate to felsic arc magmas. At pressures ≥0.7 GPa, abundant amphibole crystallization and suppressed plagioclase crystallization generated residual melts with high Sr/Y ratios and moderately depleted HREE signatures. Despite relatively oxidizing conditions and sulfide–anhydrite coexistence in some runs [ΔFMQ = +2.4 (±0.4)], all pressure series reached sulfide saturation early, at ≤54 wt% melt SiO2. Sulfide saturation depleted the residual melts in S and likely also in Cu, Au, and Ag, whereas Mo, Pb, and Zn were less affected. Neither S nor ore-forming metals were preferentially enriched in the high-pressure residual melts. CO2 promoted early exsolution of CO2-rich fluids, which became progressively more H2O-rich during differentiation. At melt SiO2 contents ≥65 wt%, increasing fluid/melt ratios led to depletion of Cl, Mo, Pb, and Zn in the residual melts. Higher pressure delayed fluid saturation, reduced the amount of exsolved fluid, produced more CO2-rich fluids, and allowed melts at a given SiO2 content to retain more H2O and CO2. Nevertheless, high-pressure melts did not become enriched in Cl or metals relative to lower-pressure melts, probably because these elements partitioned more strongly into fluids at higher pressure. We conclude that high-Sr/Y magmas produced by high-pressure differentiation are distinguished mainly by high H2O contents, rather than by unusually high S, Cl, Cu, or other ore-metal contents.
