Simultaneously, CMB and RSB treatment significantly increased the soil pH, CEC, TOC, AN, AP, TK, microbial biomass carbon, dehydrogenase, phosphatase, catalase and urease enzyme activity, while SSB treatment slightly increased AP and TK content, only decreased urease enzyme activity. Lower bacterial alpha diversity was observed at the initial sampling of day 0, whereas treatment differences in bacterial Shannon diversity were not significant at day 225, it suggested that their effects on microbial alpha diversity were dependent on sampling stage and microbial kingdom. Partial least squares modelling (PLS-PM) speculated that CMB and RSB treatment decreased available Cd through direct effect of biochar and indirect effect of soil, whereas SSB treatment elevated available metal by indirect effect. This increase might be due to the decrease of urease activity indirectly affected by SSB, thus decelerating Cd precipitation and enhancing available Cd. These results deepen our understanding on the degree of immobilization and underlying mechanisms for Cd in soil that is critical for evaluating the application of effective biochar treatments.

title: Sustained hydrogen delivery enhances microbiome-associated cadmium and copper immobilization in co-contaminated soils
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Kuan Fang, Shaohua Chu, Zhanyuan Lu, Xianzhong Ma, Dongwei Zhang, Wenjiang Ding, Lingling Wei, Haiyan Yang, Ruiren Zhou, Dan Zhang, Pei Zhou
abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H₂) is an important energy source for soil microbes and has been implicated in biogeochemical regulation; however, whether—and how—exogenous H₂ inputs promote Cd and Cu immobilization in co-contaminated soils remains unclear. We engineered MgH₂–biochar granules capable of sustained H₂ release for up to 448 h. The granules exhibited high adsorption capacities in aqueous Cd–Cu systems (Cu: 59.76 mg g⁻¹; Cd: 35.76 mg g⁻¹). In soil, MgH₂–biochar treatment was associated with enhanced microbial hydrogenase activity, reduced oxidative stress, and enrichment of functional taxa, together with significant reductions in available Cd (10.9–22.5%) and Cu (14.2–30.1%) (P < 0.05). Notably, Mg-associated alkalization elevated soil pH and contributed to physicochemical immobilization. Microbial community analyses further revealed H₂-associated shifts in community structure and significant associations between H₂ metabolism and metal resistance (Cd: P < 0.001; Cu: P < 0.03). Genome-resolved metagenomics identified 10 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) that co-harbour [NiFe]-hydrogenases (Groups 1 and 4) and Cd/Cu resistance genes (e.g., actS, czcA, and copC). Exploratory pathway modeling further indicated associations of Cd/Cu immobilization with H₂-associated microbial processes and Mg-associated physicochemical effects. This work provides integrated material, geochemical, and microbial evidence supporting an H₂-associated contribution to heavy-metal immobilization in soils.

title: Descriptor-informed oxidant selection in pulsed electrochemical AOPs: Cathode-favored periodate activation enables selective sulfamethoxazole oxidation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Bolin Zhang, Zhao Yilin, Rongfu Huang, Igor Ying Zhang
abstract: Oxidant selection in electrochemical advanced oxidation processes remains largely empirical because molecular and interfacial factors governing activation are not quantitatively linked to degradation performance. Here, a descriptor-informed framework was developed to rationalize oxidant-dependent activation in pulsed electrochemical AOPs. Six oxidants or redox-active precursors were evaluated using sulfamethoxazole degradation, and four descriptors—the LUMO–HOMO gap, vertical electron affinity, adsorption energy, and Bader charge transfer—were correlated with apparent rate constants. The preliminary descriptor-informed analysis captured the oxidant-dependent activation trend and identified periodate (PI) as the most favorable oxidant. Under identical conditions, pulsed electrolysis/periodate (PE/PI) achieved 95.43% sulfamethoxazole (SMX) removal with a rate constant of 0.10631 min−1, outperforming pulsed electrolysis/peroxymonosulfate (PE/PMS) and PE/H2O2. Mechanistic experiments and density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that the superior PE/PI performance arose from stronger cathodic adsorption, more efficient interfacial electron transfer, and contributions from 1O2-mediated non-radical oxidation and IO3 •-associated radical oxidation, while freely diffusing •OH contributed only marginally. Matrix tests further indicated that PE/PI is better suited to relatively clean waters, whereas PE/PMS offers greater robustness in complex matrices. This work extends empirical oxidant comparison toward descriptor-informed interpretation of oxidant-dependent activation.

title: Integrated mechanisms of progestogen degradation and stress resistance in Novosphingobium sp. ES2-1
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Shunyao Li, Peng Chen, Yaohui Li, Naiyang Ye, Jingya Fang, Yiru Wang, Kai Sun
abstract: Environmental progestogens (Ps), precursors of various steroid hormones (SHs), can potentiate the endocrine-disrupting effects of SHs. Novosphingobium spp. are highly promising candidates for mitigating Ps contamination. Targeting progesterone (PGT), we found that N. sp. ES2–1 alleviated PGT-induced oxidative stress through metabolic glutathione synthesis, rerouting of electron transport entry points, and reduction of reactive oxygen species targets. PGT degradation initially proceeds via hydroxyprogesterone, following a metabolic pattern analogous to testosterone degradation. Through β-oxidation, this pathway ultimately yielded ring-cleavage products secophenol and 3aα-H-4α(3’-propanoate)-7aβ-methylhexahydro-1,5-indanedione. Cytochrome P450 and extradiol dioxygenase were identified as pivotal enzymes responsible for PGT structural modification and steroid skeleton cleavage. Proteins involved in iron acquisition, vitamin B6/B2 (VB6/VB2) biosynthesis interacted with β-oxidation-related proteins, suggesting that enzymes facilitating PGT skeleton cleavage required iron as an essential cofactor, while the necessary coenzymes and electron carriers relied on VB6/VB2. Seven putative PGT degradation genes encoding hydroxylases, dioxygenases, and dehydrogenases were proposed and harbored across four gene clusters that were significantly upregulated under PGT induction. These findings, for the first time, uncover the synergistic mechanisms in N. sp. ES2–1 where oxidative stress mitigation and optimized resources allocation supported PGT degradation, providing a theoretical framework for the rational engineering of SHs bioremediation strategies.

title: Structure-dependent cellular mechanisms of PFAS regulating antibiotic resistance genes conjugation through membrane remodeling and energy metabolism reprogramming
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Leilei Lu, Guodong Kang, Ping Wu, Mengcheng Wu, Ning Wang, Yixi Zhang, Chengmei Liao, Changwei Lü, Guanyong Su, Shenghu Zhang
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) widely coexist with antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in aquatic systems, posing ecological risks. However, how environmentally relevant concentrations and structural differences of PFAS regulate ARGs dissemination remains unclear, limiting structure-informed management of PFAS substitutes. Here, conjugation assays, transcriptomics, molecular dynamics simulations, and molecular docking were integrated to systematically investigate the structure-dependent effects of four representative PFAS (PFOA, PFBA, PFOS, and PFBS) on RP4 plasmid conjunction. At 0.01–10 μg·L−1, short-chain PFAS significantly enhanced RP4 plasmid conjunction, with PFBS showing the strongest promotion (up to 5.8-fold), followed by PFBA（3.8-fold）, whereas long-chain PFAS showed minor effects (PFOA, 1.4-fold; PFOS, 1.1-fold). Notably, PFBS exhibited relatively weak yet dynamic interactions with membrane proteins, facilitating porin accessibility and intracellular transport. Mechanistic analyses revealed that PFAS, especially PFBS, promote ARGs conjunction through coordinated modulation of membrane properties and cellular energy metabolism at environmentally relevant concentrations. Integrated molecular simulations and transcriptomic analyses suggested a structure-dependent mechanism, highlighting the overlooked risk of short-chain sulfonate PFBS. Overall, these findings demonstrated that PFAS-induced ARGs transfer was strongly structure-dependent and identify PFBS as a higher-risk short-chain substitute, with implications for targeted environmental regulation.

title: PFAS removal from drinking water and semiconductor wastewater by microbubble foam fractionation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Yu-Chi Lee, Ching-Yao Hu, Chih-Jung Yeh, Szu-Yu Wu, Kuo-En Hsu, Shang-Lien Lo
abstract: Efficient separation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from complex water matrices remains challenging because treatment performance depends on both PFAS concentration and matrix composition. This study evaluated microbubble foam fractionation (FF) in simulated waters, drinking water source waters, and real semiconductor wastewater, with and without coagulant addition. In simulated wastewater, adding 2000 mg/L NH₄Cl enhanced PFAS removal, consistent with an ionic-strength contribution. Within 20 min, FF removed 91–98% of PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxS and approximately 91% of PFBS from a natural source water with individual PFAS concentrations of 2–19 μg/L. Removal was lower in a second source water containing 0.4–1.2 μg/L PFAS but improved with coagulant addition. In semiconductor wastewater containing 0.1–0.6 μg/L PFAS, removal reached 94–99% for PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxS and approximately 90% for PFBS. These contrasting results highlight the importance of water matrix composition in enabling effective separation at low PFAS concentrations. To explore potential downstream treatment, UV/sulfite reduction was separately evaluated using a model concentrate containing 20 mg/L total PFAS. Complete parent-compound removal was achieved for PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxS within approximately 30 min, 110 min, and 7 h, respectively, whereas PFBS removal reached approximately 63% after 8 h. These findings support matrix-specific application of microbubble FF as a PFAS concentration pretreatment and provide a basis for developing multistage FF coupled with downstream UV/sulfite treatment.

title: Tracing 3D printing emissions: Micro- and nanoplastic formation and the trade-off of mass-based mitigation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Xin Zhang, Xiyuan Zhang, Guicai Liu, Lina Wang, Man Pun Wan, Bing Feng Ng
abstract: The widespread adoption of fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printing introduces undocumented inhalation risks from airborne micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in indoor microenvironments. While prior studies have focused on non-specific nanoparticles and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), the precise chemical identity, emission mechanisms, and respiratory fate of printing-emitted MNPs remain critical knowledge gaps. This study systematically quantified MNP emissions across five commercial filament types using size-resolved monitoring, morphological analysis and pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (Py-GC-MS). Substantial MNP emissions were observed for ASA and ABS filaments (2.3 ± 1.0 and 0.6 ± 0.3 mg kg–1, respectively). Crucially, morphological evidence of droplet condensation combined with chemical characterization revealed that these emitted MNPs predominantly comprised polyethylene (PE) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) not originating from the parent polymer matrices. Furthermore, respiratory dosimetry modeling unveiled a mitigation trade-off: while standard FDM enclosures removed > 90% of total nanoparticle mass, they selectively allowed ultrafine nanoparticles to escape, inadvertently driving the pulmonary deposition fraction of inhaled mass from 10.3% to 19.8% in adults, and up to 29.5% in children. These findings highlight that mass-based metrics alone do not fully capture changes in inhalation exposure and respiratory deposition patterns. We advocate for integrating particle number concentrations into indoor air quality standards and requiring disclosure and regulation of all filament constituents to reduce potential MNP exposure at the source.

title: Residual polyethylene film loading alters soil quality and maize productivity, with distinct bacterial communities in plastisphere soil
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Weijing Li, Hongyuan Wang, Zhongming Ma, Tao Wei, Danni Feng, Hude Yang, Hongbin Liu
abstract: Residual polyethylene (PE) film can alter soil resources and crop production, but its effects across loading levels and at the soil–film interface remain poorly resolved. In a maize field experiment established in 2011 in northwestern China, we assessed soil properties, bacterial communities, nitrogen cycling indicators, and crop performance across five PE loadings (0–600 kg ha−1). Soil firmly adhering to residual film was pooled across the four film treatments to characterize plastisphere soil. Soil quality and maize performance responded nonmonotonically to loading. Grain yield was 20% higher at 150 kg ha−1 and 22% lower at 600 kg ha−1 than in the control. At the highest loading, lower nutrient levels and root biomass coincided with greater soil water content after harvest and lower bacterial network connectivity. Pooled plastisphere communities showed greater diversity and contrasting assembly patterns. Their higher connectivity did not consistently correspond to greater simulated robustness. Plastisphere soil had higher nitrification potential than bulk soil, despite lower summed nitrification gene abundance than at 300 and 450 kg ha−1. Structural equation modeling linked yield positively to total nitrogen and available phosphorus. These findings identify loading and microbial differentiation at soil–film interfaces as complementary dimensions of residual-film impacts.

title: Co-expression of alnA and bphC in alfalfa enhances PCB phytoremediation by coupling bioavailability modulation and intracellular detoxification
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Wenwen Lin, Yuzhu Ding, Hejun Ren, Yan Wang
abstract: Phytoremediation of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs)-contaminated soils is hindered by low PCB bioavailability and insufficient plant detoxification. Here, we engineered transgenic alfalfa co-expressing alnA (encoding an emulsifying protein) and bphC (encoding a ring-cleavage dioxygenase) to address these barriers. Five representative congeners spanning a range of chlorination degrees were selected to evaluate the system’s efficacy. The transgenic AB lines achieved sustained rhizosecretion of AlnA, enhancing PCB solubility by 2.0- to 3.2-fold relative to wild-type (WT) plants. While enhanced bioavailability typically exacerbates phytotoxicity, endogenous BphC cleaved the biphenyl ring, preventing toxic intermediate accumulation. This extracellular solubilization-intracellular detoxification synergy enabled AB alfalfa to maintain improved growth under PCB stress, increasing root accumulation by 3.7-fold and overall removal by 2-fold compared to WT alfalfa. Metagenomic and structural equation modeling revealed that while microbial genes act as “proximate executors” directly degrading PCBs, the transgenic plant functions as the “primary driver”. The AB lines enriched specific degraders (Pseudomonas and certain genera within the order Burkholderiales) and assembled a functional network for aerobic PCB degradation. This integrated plant-microbiome system offers a low-maintenance strategy for in situ remediation of PCB-contaminated sites.

title: Retention of source microbial signals in plastispheres of fibrous plastic debris after translocation
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Jianlong Li, Ziliang Chen, Zitian Zhang, Xiaoling Shan, Ling Ding, Xinran Qiu, Bin Zhang, Xian Li, Xujun Liang, Xuetao Guo
abstract: While numerous studies have explored microbial hitchhiking on aquatic plastics, the fate and interpretability of residual source signals after translocation remain unclear. Here, disposable face masks were used as model fibrous plastic debris to examine source conditioned plastisphere formation, post transfer signal retention, and mask part specific exposure history signals. Masks were conditioned in two freshwater systems and transferred to autoclaved deionized water as a simplified receiving medium to reduce source water input. Before transfer, mask surfaces developed plastispheres that differed from surrounding water in overall composition and dominant bacterial assemblages, and the two source waters produced distinguishable original plastispheres. At transfer weeks 2, 4, and 6, whole mask plastispheres remained distinguishable by their source origin; PERMANOVA explained 20.9%, 18.9%, and 19.5% of variation across Bray Curtis, Jaccard, and Aitchison CLR distances. Similarity contrast based affinity indices were further used to distinguish water-source carryover from affinity to the original plastisphere state. Whole mask water source affinity was weak and non-significant (mean = −0.0015, p = 0.728), whereas plastisphere source affinity was marginal at the whole mask scale (mean = 0.0033, p = 0.074) and significant under part matched comparisons (mean = 0.0015, p = 0.014), and source separation was clearer in inner and outer layers than ear loops. Overall, these findings indicate that source-history-associated compositional information remained detectable during post-transfer reassembly, supporting further exploration of plastisphere profiles for source tracing.

title: Spatiotemporal distribution and rainfall-runoff transport characteristics of microplastics in a typical agricultural watershed
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Yajun Zhao, Haoxin Hao, Rumeng Wei, Peiqi Zhang, Jian Wang, Zhonglu Guo
abstract: Rainfall runoff is one of the key drivers of microplastic transport from sources to sinks, but the dynamic changes of microplastics remain insufficiently quantified. This study systematically investigated the spatiotemporal distribution of microplastics in a typical agricultural watershed from April to December 2025 through soil sampling and monthly water monitoring, combined with high-frequency monitoring of 13 rainfall events to quantify the impact of rainfall on microplastic transport. Results showed that soil microplastic abundance was higher near residential areas. The water microplastic abundance in the downstream was higher than that in the upstream, and elevated concentrations in ponds may serve as both sinks and export sources of microplastics. The mean of event mean concentrations (EMCMP) during rainfall events was significantly higher than that of baseflow, representing a 1.9-fold increase (p < 0.05). The predominance of counter-clockwise hysteresis (62% of events) supported the hypothesis that microplastic transport may be influenced by proximal supply limitation and distal-source delayed delivery as hydrological connectivity increases. Microplastic load was significantly correlated with most of the hydrological variables examined. Load-discharge model estimated that the 23.2% of rainfall time contributed 54.1% of the annual load, highlighting the necessity of incorporating high-frequency rainfall event monitoring into watershed microplastic load assessment frameworks.

title: Systematic insights into 6PPD-quinone biotransformation by acclimated aerobic sludge: Kinetics, pathways, toxicity, and enzymatic mechanisms
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Hao Han, Lele Zhou, Mingxuan Yu, Shuailing Wang, He Sha, Xingxing Peng
abstract: This study acclimated aerobic (AeS), nitrifying (NS), and denitrifying (DS) sludge systems to N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone (6PPD-Q) at 1–20 mg·L⁻¹ . Within an environmental to high concentration range (1 μg·L⁻¹ to 5 mg·L⁻¹), acclimated AeS removed 88.9%–95.2% of 6PPD‑Q within 14 days, significantly outperforming the NS and DS systems. The first-order degradation rate constant of the aerobic sludge ranged from 0.175 to 1.006 d⁻¹ . Based on the Haldane kinetic model, its substrate inhibition constant was 29.3 mg·L⁻¹ , demonstrating the broadest substrate tolerance range. This study proposed 13 biotransformation products (7 of which were reported for the first time), and constructed a complete degradation pathway accordingly. Ecological Structure-Activity Relationship modeling and in vitro bioassays jointly confirmed that AeS treatment significantly reduced the acute toxicity of 6PPD-Q. Metagenomic binning identified Sphingopyxis, Achromobacter, and Pseudomonas as the dominant genera, while molecular docking further implicated cytochrome P450 and peroxidase may serve as key enzymes in the catabolism of the parent compound. A 40‑day experiment showed that combining acclimated aerobic sludge with activated sludge significantly reduced 6PPD‑Q concentrations in real wastewater effluents. This study systematically elucidated the degradation pathway, toxicity evolution, and enzymatic mechanisms of 6PPD-Q in activated sludge, providing new insights for its bioremediation.

title: Resuscitation-promoting factor enhances PFOA biodegradation and modulates cellular stress responses in two PFOA-degrading bacterial strains
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Mengting Yang, Keyi Zhang, Faqian Sun, Xiao Xiao, Xiaomei Su
abstract: Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), a highly persistent and toxic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS), poses significant environmental and health risks. Microbial degradation offers a promising remediation strategy but is limited by the scarcity and low efficiency of known degraders. Here, two PFOA-degrading strains, Alcaligenes sp. MT1 and Pseudomonas sp. MT3, were isolated and characterized. Whole-genome analysis identified multiple genes potentially involved in fluorinated compound transformation. Supplementation with resuscitation-promoting factor (Rpf) significantly enhanced PFOA degradation, with an optimal dosage of 1.5% (v/v), increasing removal efficiencies by 16.8% (MT1) and 18.7% (MT3) relative to controls. Rpf improved cellular performance by elevating antioxidant enzyme activities (peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, catalase) and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity while reducing malondialdehyde levels, indicating enhanced oxidative stress tolerance and energy metabolism. Consistently, key genes associated with decarboxylation and dehalogenation pathways were markedly upregulated. LC-MS/MS analysis revealed that PFOA degradation involved sequential decarboxylation and defluorination, with Rpf affecting metabolite abundance but not the core degradation pathways. These findings demonstrate that Rpf-mediated activation effectively enhances microbial PFOA degradation and provides a promising strategy for PFAS bioremediation.

title: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and metabolic transformation of Flonicamid in rats: Insights from radiotracing, metabolite profiling and multi-scale analysis
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Xinying Chen, Yongli Liu, Chen Meng, Xialu Wang
abstract: Understanding flonicamid (FLO) disposition is important for interpreting its potential health implications. We investigated FLO metabolism in male Sprague-Dawley rats using 14C-radiotracing, high-resolution mass spectrometry, hepatic transcriptomics, density-functional-theory calculations, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. FLO was rapidly absorbed, widely distributed, and detected in the brain and testes. Parent FLO predominated in the radiochromatographic profiles, accounting for 70.3% of the total integrated radioactive peak area. TFNA-AM was the predominant metabolite, representing 72.3% of the total metabolite peak area. Its formation was consistent with cyanomethyl oxidative cleavage and computational predictions of molecular reactivity. Within 192 h, urinary recovery accounted for 84.1% of administered radioactivity, indicating predominantly urinary elimination. Integrated transcriptomic and molecular-simulation analyses further prioritized CYP2B2 as a candidate enzyme for subsequent biochemical evaluation of its potential role in the oxidative metabolism of FLO. FLO exposure was also associated with transcriptional changes in several hormone-related pathways in male rat liver. Collectively, these findings complement existing FLO studies by quantifying the recovery of FLO-derived material across excretion routes and the contributions of parent FLO and major metabolites to the recovered components. This information supports the interpretation of FLO disposition and the selection of analyses for subsequent exposure and toxicological studies.

title: Flyway-scale lead and multielement exposure in globally threatened Cinereous vultures ( Aegypius monachus ) wintering on the Korean Peninsula: Insights from tissue burdens and stable lead isotopes
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Sub Hur, Jung-Hoon Kang, Ju-Young Moon, Minjoo Jang, Dam-Chae Lee, Kyung-Soon Jin, Jong-Gil Park, Dong-Ha Nam
abstract: Lead (Pb) is a major toxicant in avian scavengers, but its ecological role and exposure pathways along the East Asian flyway remain unclear. Immature Cinereous vultures (Aegypius monachus) migrate from Mongolia through China to winter on the Korean Peninsula, where they mostly congregate near the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), creating a potential flyway-scale bottleneck where local hazards may affect much of the population. This study investigates Pb and multielement exposure in 74 immature vultures recovered near the DMZ by quantifying Pb concentrations in liver and muscle, measuring hepatic Cd, Cu, Zn, Ni, As, V, and Fe, and analyzing stable Pb isotope ratios (206Pb/207Pb, 208Pb/206Pb, 208Pb/207Pb) in tissues to assess potential exposure sources. Hepatic Pb concentrations ranged from 1.17 to 33.4 μg/g dw, and 16.2% of individuals reached levels consistent with Pb-induced mortality. Hepatic Pb burdens did not differ among probable causes of death (gunshot, trauma, emaciation, electrocution, suspected poisoning, and unknown), indicating pervasive Pb exposure across the wintering cohort. Muscle Pb concentrations were generally low, except in one gunshot-injured bird, which had an extreme level of 120.9 μg/g dw. In contrast, other hepatic elements showed comparatively moderate concentrations, identifying Pb as the primary toxicological concern. Tissue Pb isotope signatures overlapped with ammunition-related and other anthropogenic Pb sources, supporting a mixed-source exposure scenario in which Pb-based ammunition likely contributes. These findings indicate that immature Cinereous vultures wintering on the Korean Peninsula are widely and persistently exposed to Pb, highlighting the need for flyway-scale monitoring and targeted mitigation across the Mongolia–China–Korea flyway.

title: Compound-specific porewater-surface water relationships of taste and odor compounds under contrasting water-level conditions in a reservoir drawdown zone
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Zilong Wang, Zhicong Wang, Yifan Tang, Si Wu, Dunhai Li
abstract: Elevated odorant concentrations in sediment porewater may not correspond to surface-water occurrence. This study examined four taste-and-odor compounds (odorants), β-cyclocitral (CYC), β-ionone (ION), 2-methylisoborneol (2-MIB), and geosmin (GSM), in paired sediment porewater and surface-water samples from 11 sites in Xiangxi Bay, Three Gorges Reservoir, China. Sampling on 2 July 2025 and 6 January 2026 captured contrasting low- and high-water conditions. CYC and ION showed positive site-level porewater–surface water associations during the July campaign. In January, 2-MIB and GSM generally exhibited higher concentrations in porewater than in surface water, without corresponding site-level associations between compartments. These contrasts show that porewater enrichment and cross-compartment covariation provide different evidence about odorant distribution. Because each condition was sampled once, the differences are interpreted as campaign-specific rather than replicated seasonal or water-level effects. Joint analysis of porewater and surface water may therefore improve the assessment of odorant occurrence in regulated reservoir bays.

title: Chronic heavy metal exposure drives mitochondrial remodeling and metabolic reprogramming to enhance sperm velocity in wild tree sparrows
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Ming Zhang, Yuquan Miao, Rui Su, Yue Shen, Wenya Zhang, Yingmei Zhang
abstract: Environmental pollution is widely assumed to impair reproductive performance, yet whether organisms can sustain reproductive function under chronic stress remains poorly understood. Here, using natural populations of tree sparrows from a heavy metal-contaminated site and a reference site, we reveal a paradoxical increase in sperm velocity despite clear physiological costs. Males from the polluted population exhibited reduced body condition and elevated cadmium and lead accumulation in reproductive tissues, but their sperm velocity parameters were significantly enhanced. Mechanistically, sperm from exposed birds showed coordinated mitochondrial optimization, including elevated mitochondrial membrane potential, enhanced complex I activity, and higher ATP content. In the testis, genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis (TFAM) and mitophagy (BNIP3) were upregulated, indicating enhanced mitochondrial quality control during spermatogenesis. Functional inhibition using the oxidative phosphorylation uncoupler carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone (FCCP) confirmed that elevated sperm velocity depends on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Integrated proteomic and metabolomic analyses further revealed a systemic metabolic reprogramming from glycolysis toward OXPHOS, characterized by upregulation of OXPHOS-related proteins and suppression of glycolytic pathways. Together, our findings demonstrate that chronic heavy metal stress can enhance sperm performance through mitochondrial and metabolic remodeling, revealing a key mechanism by which avian reproductive behavior responds to long-term environmental stress.

title: Comparative assessment of the behaviour and potential ecological risks of pretilachlor and its metabolites in contrasting soil environments
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Vidhi Dhanda, Ravi Kumar, Jayant Sindhu, Ajay Pal, Sachin Dhanda, Ankit Goyat, Anil Duhan
abstract: A comparative evaluation of degradation behaviour and possible ecological risks associated with pretilachlor and its metabolites was conducted. Five metabolites (M1–M5) were synthesized and characterized. Pretilachlor and the metabolites were applied at 0.25 and 0.50 µg/g in different soils. Despite having shorter half-lives (t1/2 = 1.18.1 days) than pretilachlor (t1/2 = 5.313.7 days), metabolites residues persisted in soil from 3 to 45 days. Based on the conservative and first-tier screening of measured soil residues, some compounds showed risk quotients, RQ > 1 for earthworms, fish and honeybees; whereas the RQ for algae, birds and rats ranged from moderate to negligible. M2 and M3 reduced soil dehydrogenase activity by 1.11.5 times, while pretilachlor and remaining metabolites enhanced it. M2 and M3 bound strongly to the catalytic site of the dehydrogenase near Zn2 + ion with docking scores of −5.45 and −5.22 kcal/mol, respectively. The overall stability of the docked complexes was also established through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. The root mean square deviation (RMSD) and root mean fluctuations (RMSF) remained within the acceptable limits (less than 2.5 Å), indicating stable protein-ligand interactions. In summary, pretilachlor metabolites may persist in the environment with potential risk implications to different non-target species.

title: Component-specific effects shape shifts between synergism and antagonism in organophosphate ester mixtures
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): Na Luo, Guiying Li, Yanpeng Gao, Taicheng An
abstract: Organophosphate esters (OPEs) frequently co-occur in human exposure, yet their combined hazards cannot be reliably inferred from single-compound toxicity. How individual OPEs reshape non-additive effects across compositions and effect levels remains unclear. Here, we investigated interaction patterns and associated biological responses of representative OPE mixtures, including tributyl phosphate (TNBP), triphenyl phosphate (TPHP), and tris(1,3-dichloro-2-propyl) phosphate (TDCIPP), using human keratinocytes as a dermal exposure model. Combination index (CI) analysis revealed composition- and effect-level-dependent interactions. Ternary mixtures exhibited distinct composition-dependent CI–Fa trajectories, with some compositions trending toward additivity at higher effect levels, whereas TPHP-rich mixtures showed progressively stronger synergism. Binary mixtures showed pair-dependent interactions, with TPHP–TDCIPP and TNBP–TDCIPP exhibiting contrasting interaction modes. At total nominal molar concentrations of 0.1, 1, and 10μM for the 1:1:1 ternary mixture, co-exposure modestly increased HaCaT monolayer permeability, reaching statistical significance at 10μM, and altered differentiation-related gene expression, revealing barrier-associated effects. Untargeted metabolomics of individual and mixture exposures further revealed distinct lipid remodeling patterns, including interaction-associated differences in glycerophospholipid responses. Collectively, OPE mixture hazards depend not only on individual toxicity but also on the capacity of specific components to modify combined effects, supporting improved mixture hazard characterization and prioritization of interaction-modifying contaminants.

title: Dynamic changes of chicken gut microbiota and resistome during enrofloxacin treatment against multidrug-resistant Salmonella based on metagenomics
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): Yang Chen, Jinhua Chu, Yali Guo, Muhammad Haris Raza Farhan, Xinru Lu, Hanqi Wei, Changqing Xie, Xu Wang, Lingli Huang, Guyue Cheng
abstract: Antibiotics are widely used to treat and prevent bacterial infections in human and animals. However, the impact of antibiotic dose on bacterial burden and diachronic changes and transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in gut bacterial infections remains unclear. Here, we used enrofloxacin (ENR) at sub-inhibitory (1mg/kg b.w.), prophylactic (3.03mg/kg body b.w.), and therapeutic (10mg/kg b.w.) doses to treat infections with Salmonella harboring plasmid pJX-4, with infected but untreated groups as controls. We found that subtherapeutic ENR may pose potential risks to the gut ecosystem. Specifically, sub-inhibitory ENR led to persistently high Salmonella and its carried resistance gene qnrS1 levels; under this dose condition, preliminary evidence suggested that intestinal Escherichia coli was a potential host for in vivo transfer of plasmid pJX-4. The prophylactic dose group showed significantly higher relative abundances of human bacterial pathogens and ARGs, especially during treatment. Furthermore, this group was enriched in genes related to oxidative stress, cellular signaling, and secretion systems, and these functional genes were primarily associated with ARGs. Overall, different ENR doses shaped distinct evolutionary trajectories of the gut microbiome and resistome. This study provides a theoretical basis for the rational use of antibiotics in treating bacterial infections.

title: Investigation of bubble dynamic evolution and evaporation micro-explosion characteristics of tire pyrolysis oil-diesel blended fuel droplets
description: Publication date: Available online 21 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): Dongyuan Guo, Yasong Sun, Donghui Qi, Di Nian
abstract: Tire pyrolysis oil (TPO) has physicochemical properties similar to diesel and can be regarded as a promising alternative fuel for diesel engines. This study employed a suspended-droplet evaporation apparatus to capture the evaporation process of TPO-diesel-blended fuel droplets and investigated the effects of TPO blending ratio and initial droplet volume on the bubble nucleation mechanism and the micro-explosion mode transition. The results show that the evaporation process of the blended fuel droplets can be divided into three stages: fluctuation evaporation, intense micro-explosion, and stable evaporation. Surface pit nucleation is the primary bubble nucleation mode, while raft-interface nucleation serves as a secondary mechanism, together facilitating the initial formation of bubbles within the droplet. As the TPO blending ratio increases, the bubble nucleation mode changes from multi-point nucleation to single-point nucleation, the nucleation location shifts from the droplet surface toward the center, and the maximum micro-explosion intensity increases. The blended fuel with a 20% TPO exhibits the shortest droplet lifetime. Variations in the initial droplet size can not alter the bubble nucleation mode or micro-explosion mode, but can increase the degree of droplet expansion. Increasing the initial droplet size effectively enhanced the micro-explosion intensity, but had no significant effect on droplet lifetime.

title: Influence of ultraviolet/chlor(am)ine processes on the formation of toxicity and aromatic byproduct from the dipeptide tyrosyl- L -phenylalanine
description: Publication date: Available online 21 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): Changhui Zhou, Yiyi Hu, Yao Lu, Xingxing An, Ye Du, Bo Lai
abstract: Amino acids and peptides in wastewater are key precursors of highly toxic nitrogenous disinfection byproducts (N-DBPs) during chlor(am)ination. The UV/chlor(am)ine processes have been increasingly employed for toxicity control, yet their efficacy against peptide precursors remains poorly understood. This study evaluated the toxicity control of UV/chlor(am)ine on tyrosyl-L-phenylalanine (Tyr-Phe), its monomers (Phe, Tyr), and real secondary effluents. At a UV dose of 1200 mJ·cm-2, 5 mg-Cl2·L-1 disinfectant and 4 mg-C·L-1 precursor, UV/chlorine reduced the cytotoxicity and genotoxicity of Tyr-Phe by 75.7% and 82.8%, respectively (UV/chloramine: 55.5% and 64.4%). Total organic chlorine (TOCl) and Tyr-Phe-derived byproduct counts decreased by > 70% and > 30%, accompanied by a shift toward higher oxidation states and lower aromaticity. Four low molecular weight DBPs (trichloromethane, dichloroacetonitrile, trichloroacetaldehyde, and chloroacetone) and seven identified emerging aromatic DBPs were also significantly reduced. Similar trends were observed for Phe, Tyr, and real secondary effluents. Radical quenching coupled with TOCl measurements indicated that ·OH and ·Cl, individually or together, contribute to the suppression of DBP formation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that UV/chlor(am)ine effectively controls DBP formation and associated toxicity from aromatic peptides and their monomers in wastewater disinfection.

title: Systematic review on the toxicity of wildfire emitted particulate matter: State of science, knowledge gaps and way forward
description: Publication date: Available online 21 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): Luis Augusto Visani de Luna, Yohannes Tesfaigzi, Shuo Xiao, Audrey Gaskins, Joseph A. Jude, Reynold A. Panettieri, Jose Guillermo Cedeno Laurent, Philip Demokritou
abstract: The intensity and frequency of wildfires have increased worldwide. The health impact of wildfire emitted particulate matter (WFPM) has been considered an emerging field in air pollution research. This review presents the state of toxicological science related to WFPM for the 2005-2025 period. We found 46 peer-reviewed in vitro and in vivo studies, excluding clinical, epidemiological, and ecotoxicological studies. Environmental WFPM collected during active wildfires was used to model exposure in only 42% of in vitro and 27% of in vivo studies. Most in vitro studies investigate effects on the pulmonary system (50%) and on macrophages (17%), with all other biological systems corresponding to 33%. Mechanisms of toxicity focused mostly on inflammatory and stress response, and DNA damage/mutation. Inhalation studies evaluated lung (46%), cardiovascular (15%) and brain (15%) effects, with the remaining 24% addressing reproductive, genetic or immune effects. WFPM induced significant toxicity with distinct mechanisms as a function of concentration, particle-size, biomass type and burning conditions. Knowledge gaps included: lack of a comprehensive physicochemical characterization of WFPM to achieve robust structure-activity conclusions, use of realistic concentrations representing human exposure scenarios, chronic exposure studies, evaluation of systemic effects and toxicokinetic studies, potential synergistic effects with other anthropogenic air pollution sources.

title: Widespread antibiotic resistance and multidrug resistance in Escherichia coli from surface waters near dairies and a calf ranch in Wisconsin: implications for hotspot screening and multi-method monitoring
description: Publication date: Available online 21 October 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials Author(s): K.P. Osborn, Y. Zhang, S. Ray, Y. Kong, S. Levy, S. Jun, M. Chang, J. Lin, J. Vuong, C. Ives, A. Jones, L. Henning, C. Dickerson, S. Mahendra, W. Bodeau, A. Casillas, R. Chowdhry, J. Chung, N. Curristan, A. Espinoza
abstract: Although concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are known sources of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), gaps remain regarding AMR dissemination to environments and monitoring methods. Impacts of large dairies and a calf ranch in Wisconsin on the environmental resistome were assessed at nine surface water sites near CAFOs and two nearby unimpaired sites. 1297 Escherichia coli (EC) isolates were tested against a suite of antibiotics by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion. Up to 68% of EC isolates at dairy-impacted sites and 70% downstream of the calf ranch exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR), versus up to 8% at the unimpaired sites. Fecal indicator bacteria kits modified with antibiotics detected elevated extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) EC at the site exhibiting highest MDR, suggesting use as a screening tool. Metagenomic analysis showed elevated antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), abundance, diversity, and human health risk scores at the calf ranch-impacted site. Follow-up sampling just upstream and downstream of the calf ranch showed dramatic increases in multiple measures, indicating calf ranches may warrant additional monitoring and elucidate more complex processes such horizontal gene transfer. Culture-based results revealed pronounced AMR hotspots and differences among sampling events only partially reflected by metagenomic analysis and a limited quantitative PCR (qPCR) panel, underscoring the importance of monitoring through complementary methods.

title: Environmental fate of ciprofloxacin in agricultural soils under realistic irrigation water matrices: kinetic, column transport, thermodynamic, mechanistic and machine learning insights
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Saurabh Kumar, Lucas Joseph Makuni, Renu Meena, Nitin Khandelwal
abstract: The combined influence of soil properties, irrigation water chemistry, and transport processes on antibiotic fate remains poorly understood. Here, ciprofloxacin (CIP) retention, transport, and remobilization were investigated in three agricultural soil types under four different irrigation water matrices using batch, column, thermodynamic, mechanistic, and machine-learning approaches. At elevated concentrations (10 mg/L), all soils exhibited comparable retention capacities, whereas substantial differences emerged at extremely elevated concentrations (150 mg/L), with maximum adsorption capacities following the order black soil (≈17.6 mg/g) > alluvial soil (≈15.6 mg/g) > red soil (≈10.4 mg/g). Transport behaviour differed markedly among soils, with retardation factors following the order black soil (7.9) > alluvial soil (2.24) > red soil (1.4). After 180 pore volumes, relative breakthrough remained below 0.03 in black soil but reached 0.25 and 0.45 in alluvial and red soils, respectively. Rainfall flushing further revealed contrasting environmental outcomes, with black soil strongly immobilizing CIP, red soil promoting rapid transport, and alluvial soil acting as a persistent contaminant leaching reservoir. Thermodynamic analyses indicated predominantly endothermic adsorption with enhanced spontaneity at elevated temperatures. FTIR and zeta potential analyses identified surface complexation, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and cation bridging as the primary retention mechanisms. Random Forest modelling identified soil type as the dominant control on CIP retention, accounting for ~92% of total feature importance (R2 = 0.96–0.97). These findings demonstrate that soil properties govern CIP fate and determine contrasting pathways of sequestration, persistence, and groundwater contamination risk.

title: Substrate-explicit coupled modeling of organic matter degradation and sulfide production using a generalized kinetic approach
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): P. Trinchero, A. Nordström, M. Calpe, G. Román-Ross, A. Costa-Solé, O. Silva, G. Deissmann
abstract: In natural subsurface systems, Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) is a potent reducing agent, as it sustains and catalyzes a number of microbially-mediated reactions. One of such reactions, namely the reduction of sulfate to sulfide mediated by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) is particularly relevant for the evaluation of the long-term stability of deep geological repositories (DGRs) for spent nuclear fuel. Some of these proposed DGRs will be hosted at great depth in fractured crystalline rocks where sulfide, potentially produced by SRB, is practically the only oxidant of relevance for the copper canisters used to safely store and keep isolated the radionuclides from the natural environment. One important limitation to this reaction is substrate availability, as the DOM that typically infiltrates, e.g. from overlying surficial sediments, is typically bound in complex polymeric organic compounds (cellulose, starch, proteins, fats, etc.) that cannot be directly used by SRB. A further intermediate step is therefore needed which consists in the degradation of ’complex’ organic matter into ‘simpler’ organic substrates. This intermediate step is performed by a different microbial group (typically acetogens and/or fermenters) that acts on a substrate characterized by significant heterogeneity. Previous studies have documented that the organic carbon substrate typically comprises thousands of species depending on the type of subsurface environment. In this study we argue that the evaluation of microbially mediated sulfate reduction by means of reactive transport modeling should explicitly account for the substrate heterogeneity. However, explicitly accounting for thousands of chemical species of complex organic matter presents two significant challenges. The first is how to parameterize each individual reaction. The second is how to include this large number of species in the mass balance calculations. The first challenge was addressed through the development of a Generalized Kinetic Model (GKM) that formulates all rates as a function of a universally accepted rate of electron transfer along with the underlying stoichiometry of each individual metabolic reaction. The computational challenge was overcome by using weight-based reaction rates. In practice, we solve transport and mass balance for the equivalent total concentration of complex organic carbon while retaining information on the underlying substrate and associated microbial population through the use of two weighting functions, which are updated on lagged time based on mass balance. The numerical framework is first verified and then applied to simulate sulfide production in a single fracture–matrix system. Important modeling outcomes, such as the dependence of SRB activity on the degradation of a complex organic substrate and the role of the matrix as a temporary storage term for substrates, are derived.

title: Seasonal changes in petroleum NSZD biodegradation rates associated with water table fluctuations within the zone of soil contamination
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Michael J. Donn, John L. Rayner, Kaveh Sookhak Lari, Andrew King, Greg B. Davis
abstract: Natural Source Zone Depletion (NSZD) is widely used to manage petroleum-contaminated sites, but estimating NSZD rates is challenging because most methods rely on short period, averaged or point-in-time measurements. These can be misleading due to seasonal variability in biological activity, moisture and water table fluctuations influencing NSZD rates. Here we utilise continuous inground sensor measurements and light non-aqueous phase liquid (LNAPL) distributions from cores to understand seasonal processes affecting NSZD rates. Linked to multiphase modelling these data are used to test the hypothesis that seasonal NSZD variations result from LNAPL distributions and water table fluctuations. Using ~3.5 years of continuous oxygen and temperature data across four fuel types, NSZD rates were shown to vary by up to an order of magnitude seasonally. Rates ranged from 0.1 to 0.8 kg/m2/y for diesel to ~5 to 13 kg/m2/y for aviation gasoline, with broadly comparable trends between oxygen- and temperature-based methods. Rising water tables generally reduced NSZD rates at the diesel, gasoline, and crude oil sites by inundating the LNAPL depth distribution and disconnecting it from oxygen in the vadose zone. In contrast, at the aviation gasoline site, where LNAPL persisted above the maximum water table, NSZD rates remained high or increased. Modelling reproduced observed trends at the diesel site and showed that NSZD rates are influenced by the exposure of LNAPL to the vadose zone air phase (i.e., oxygen), with inundation suppressing rates, while exposure enhanced it. This is further supported by soil core TPH measurements that show loss of shorter chain TPH ranges at shallower depths above and within the zone of water table fluctuation relative to deeper in the formation. Continuous monitoring and modelling have provided insights into the dynamic NSZD rate estimates, indicating that care is needed to align field measurements with conceptualisation of LNAPL distributions and water table dynamics.

title: Reactive solute transport driven by coupled stress fields affected by injection pressure and permeability during in-situ chemical oxidation remediation of contaminated groundwater
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Guiyao Xiong, Zhiyu Jiao, Xiaobin Zhu, Qi Zhang, Yun Zhang, Yun Yang, Shujun Ye, Jinguo Wang, Jichun Wu, Brent Sleep
abstract: Groundwater contamination at the site is worsening, and in-situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) has been widely adopted for contaminated groundwater remediation due to its low environmental risk and low cost. Through laboratory experiments and field simulations, we optimized the system for TCE degradation using activated sodium persulfate and explored how injection pressure and formation permeability affect TCE remediation. The results show that both sodium citrate (TCD) and citrate (CA) chelating agents can increase TCE oxidation by persulfate, with optimal molar ratios of Na2S2O8:TCD:Fe2+:TCE of 20:10:10:1, and Na2S2O8:CA:Fe2+:TCE of 20:5:10:1, achieving high TCE removal rates of 97% and 98%, respectively. Pressurized injection increases the hydraulic gradient and flow velocity, thereby enhancing advection and mechanical dispersion, especially in high-permeability media. In low-permeability media, pressurization also modifies porosity and tortuosity and increases the effective diffusion coefficient, which is relatively more important for solute transport. Pressure-induced permeability changes were limited under the tested 0.1–1 MPa range and were secondary to advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. In layered subsurface systems, placing horizontal wells at the interface between high- and low-permeability layers was more effective in delivering oxidants to contaminated regions than vertical wells. In summary, higher-pressure oxidant injection improved remediation in the simulated low-permeability formations by increasing advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. The relative contributions were site-specific, and diffusion enhancement was not the sole controlling mechanism. The numerical model can effectively simulate ISCO of TCE by accounting for the multi-field-coupled stress field. It can provide valuable insights for designing groundwater remediation projects.

title: Diffusion of inert and reactive tracers: Overview of the DIR field experiment in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay rock (France)
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): V. Blin, M. Descostes, J. Radwan, E. Tevissen, T. Grangeon, T. Fierz, C. Frechou, P. Brisset, M. Filippi, C. Landesman, S. Ribet, P. Meier, M. Saint-Jalmes, R.V.H. Dagnelie, S. Dewonck, J.-C. Robinet
abstract: The geological disposal of radioactive waste is under investigation in several countries, especially in Europe. In this field, clay-rich sedimentary rocks are promising natural barriers to limit and delay the release of radionuclides toward the biosphere, due to their diffusion-driven transport and retention properties. In addition to laboratory studies, field studies in Underground Research Laboratories (URL) represent a significant value to strengthen safety demonstrations. In this context, the DIR experiment (Diffusion of Inert and Reactive tracers) was developed and implanted in the Meuse/Haute-Marne URL located in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay-rich formation. Over 6 years, several diffusion experiments were performed with radioactive tracers: HTO (tritiated water), 36Cl−, 125I−, 22Na+, 134Cs+, assessing the behaviour of neutral, anionic and cationic species. The evolution of each radiotracer activity was monitored in the injection borehole, from at least 100 days up to 3 years. Overcoring of the rock at the end of the experiments allowed the accurate characterization of radiotracer profiles. An overview of the DIR experiment is provided here, illustrating the large amount of data gathered in 4 specific boreholes at two different depths: −445 and − 495 m, within the Callovo-Oxfordian geological layer. The modelling of experimental results allowed the quantification of diffusion properties parallel to the bedding of the rock for the studied radionuclides. Diffusion parameters for HTO are in agreement with those determined on samples using the conventional through diffusion method. Anions are partially excluded from porosity with quantified values 0.3 < ε a(anion)/ε(H2O) < 0.6. On contrary, the diffusion of cations is limited by their adsorption on clay surfaces with the evidence of surface diffusion processes. The sensitivity analysis on adjusted parameters provided additional insights on the local properties, such as homogeneity of the diffusion plume and the limited extension of the damaged zone surrounding boreholes: L EDZ ~ 1–3 cm. Still, further field experiments are necessary to measure diffusion in such EDZ and to improve accuracy on the diffusion anisotropy ratio.

title: Oxidative sulfide weathering and weak mineral attenuation controlling arsenic mobility in a crystalline aquifer
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Swati Ganveer, Kamal Lochan Pruseth, David Anand Aind
abstract: This study investigates the source–sink dynamics and hydrogeochemical controls governing arsenic fate and transport within a fractured crystalline aquifer system. The hydrogeologic framework is characterized by spatial heterogeneity in redox conditions and persistent undersaturation with respect to key Fe-, sulfate-, and Ca-bearing mineral phases. Mineralogical characterization identifies arsenopyrite and cobaltite as the primary geogenic sources; oxidative weathering of these sulfide phases drives the continuous release of arsenic. Aqueous speciation modeling reveals a predominance of A s ( V ) and F e ( I I I ) species, with minor A s ( I I I ) occurring within reducing microenvironments. Persistent undersaturation of Fe- and As-bearing minerals, together with other attenuation-controlling phases, suggests limited potential for secondary mineral precipitation, while allowing arsenic to remain predominantly in the dissolved phase. Weak correlations between arsenic and hydrochemical gradients indicate that contaminant distribution is highly heterogeneous and controlled by the occurrence of mineralized zones. The results demonstrate that persistent arsenic mobility in fractured crystalline aquifers can occur under predominantly oxidizing conditions through sustained sulfide weathering combined with limited attenuation capacity within the aquifer system.

title: Hidden contaminants in a coral paradise: fate, transport, source apportionment, and toxicity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the coral reef ecosystems of the Lakshadweep archipelago
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): E.R. Vignesh, T.R. Gireeshkumar, A. Ramzi, A.R. Jithu, Midhun M. Nair, P.S. Rakesh, K.S. Arya, Anjana Jayaprakash, K. Sudheesh, K.R. Muraleedharan, Narayan Panda, K.U. Abdul Jaleel
abstract: This study examined the environmental fate, source apportionment, and associated ecological and human health risks of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the coral reef ecosystems of four inhabited islands in the Lakshadweep Archipelago (Kadmat, Kiltan, Kalpeni, and Minicoy). Water, suspended particulate matter (SPM), and sediments were collected from reef lagoons during April 2025 and analysed for 16 PAHs congeners designated as priority by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA). PAHs were in the range of 20.9–240 ng/L in the dissolved phase, 146–356 ng/L in the SPM, and 2.05–22.2 ng/g in sediments. PAH transport and sedimentary accumulation differ markedly from those in siliciclastic coastal environments due to the dominance of carbonate-rich, organic-matter-deficient, highly permeable sediments and strong hydrodynamics that promote rapid particle export to adjacent offshore waters. As a result, reef lagoons act as dynamic conduits that promote contaminant exchange with the Arabian Sea, thereby limiting long-term contaminant accumulation in the lagoon sediments. Source apportionment studies indicated mixed petrogenic and pyrogenic PAHs sources, primarily associated with navigational activities, fuel handling, diesel-powered energy generation, and combustion-related activities. Ecological risk assessment indicated negligible risks from sedimentary PAHs, while dissolved and SPM-bound PAHs posed low to moderate ecological risks. Incremental lifetime cancer risk (ILCR) values for all age groups were within the potential low-risk category, with dermal contact identified as the dominant exposure pathway. This study provides critical baseline information on transport behaviour and ecological implications of PAHs in the coral reef ecosystems of Lakshadweep and recommends sustained environmental monitoring and targeted management strategies to protect the ecological integrity of these coral reef systems under mounting anthropogenic perturbations.

title: Experimental investigations into the evolution of reactive fronts under radial injection conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zhipeng Du, Xingrun Wang, Jiajun Chen, Kaiyu Shi, Haixu Duan, Xianghua Yan
abstract: Reactive fronts form at interfaces where remediation agents encounter contaminant plumes in subsurface environments. The contaminant degradation is largely confined to this narrow mixing zone, but the transient reaction dynamics within it remain poorly understood. Existing models often assume uniform flow or constant dispersion, failing to capture how the spatial deceleration of radial velocities alters interfacial mixing. To address this, two-dimensional sandbox experiments were conducted by radially injecting potassium permanganate into a Naphthol Green B-dyed perchloroethylene (PCE) plume. Image analysis, advection-dispersion modeling, and breakthrough-curve measurements were combined to characterize reactive mixing zone evolution and product generation dynamics. The results indicate that (i) the 1/r decay of radial velocity drove a spatial transition from a proximal reaction-limited regime (Damköhler number, Da = 0.14–0.99) to a distal mixing-limited regime (Da = 3.98–27.38), producing a bimodal chloride breakthrough pattern; (ii) the sampling-based effective mixing-zone width exhibited a pronounced non-monotonic evolution, increasing rapidly during the early stage, reaching a maximum at approximately τ ≈ 0.10, and subsequently decreasing, with a more pronounced decline at higher injection rates; and (iii) the apparent reaction rate similarly increased during the early stage and then declined, while cumulative product mass continued to increase but its growth slowed markedly after τ ≈ 0.07. These results suggest that while higher injection rates enhance mechanical dispersion and initial migration, they can reduce local contact time, highlighting the need to balance physical mixing and reaction residence time in radial injection strategies.

title: Driving factors for the distribution of i/eARGs in livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater across China
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Yuru Zhao, Wenjie Zhang, Siyu Chen, Ting Ma, Xiaoqin Li, Shunluo Liu, Yue He, Ting Xu, Xiangkai Li, Bin Liang, Hui Yun
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), as emerging pollutants, have become a growing environmental concern owing to their wide distribution, durability, and potential adverse effects on humans, animals and the surrounding environments. Livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater (LPMW), the major reservoir of antibiotics, has higher abundance of extracellular ARGs (eARGs) compared with other environments. This review summarizes the abundance of intracellular ARGs (iARGs) and eARGs in LPMW in China. The absolute abundance of iARGs and eARGs in LPMW were 103–1012 and 102–1010 copies/mL or copies/g, respectively, with sul1, sul2, tetQ, tetW, tetG, ermB, ermF, bla TEM and bla ampc as the main detected i/eARGs types. Subsequently, the study summarized the intrinsic molecular and biological properties, extrinsic drivers, and methodological influences that may influence the abundance of i/eARGs. Discrepancies in the absolute abundance of i/eARGs could be due to factors such as genetic location, sample sources, antibiotic residues and manure treatment methods. Besides, the efficiencies of extracellular DNA(eDNA) extraction methods commonly used for LPMW samples were compared and quantitative methods of i/eARGs were evaluated, which could also introduce subjective bias into i/eARGs abundance. Limitations related to the current eDNA extraction methods and quantitative methods, the establishment of the safety thresholds for eARGs, in situ monitoring methods, and the role of phages in the spread of ARGs were discussed as future prospects. This review highlights the importance of environmental risk assessment for i/eARGs, lay theoretical basis for the effective removal of i/eARGs for further researches and provides advice for future governance and regulatory measurement.

title: Spatial evolution and geochemical controls of U- and Th-series radionuclides in acid mine drainage affected waters of the Odiel Basin, SW Spain
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): V.H. Le, J.L. Guerrero, J.P. Bolívar
abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) affects the mobility of naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM), but its influence on the distribution of U- and Th-series radionuclides in polymetallic mining districts and downstream estuaries remains poorly understood. Here, we characterize the spatial evolution and isotopic signatures of U- and Th-series radionuclides in the dissolved fraction along the Oraque–Meca–Odiel river–estuary system (SW Spain). This system shows a strong geochemical gradient, from highly acidic AMD headwaters (locally pH 1, indicating isotopic disequilibrium and preferential 234U mobilization. The 230Th/232Th activity ratios remained close to unity, indicating limited isotopic fractionation within the dissolved Th pool. These results show that the spatial variations of dissolved U and Th across the investigated river-estuary system coincided with hydrochemical gradients and changing source contributions, while the selected confluences showed nominal element-specific departures from the adopted sulfate-based mixing predictions.

title: Concurrent interactions between PFAS and bacteria during 6:2 fluorotelomer sulfonate transport in saturated and unsaturated porous media
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Xinyue Zhang, Ni Yan, Fawang Zhang, Tianhui Ji, Haiying Hu, Yujing Ma, Jiani Fu, Mark L. Brusseau
abstract: The role of microbial communities in regulating the transport and retention of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in the subsurface environment, particularly under water-unsaturated conditions, remains poorly understood. Here, miscible-displacement experiments were conducted with saturated and unsaturated sand-packed columns to investigate the influence of biofilms on the transport of 6:2 fluorotelomer sulfonate (6:2 FTS), considering biofilm age, bacterial species, and flow rate. The underlying mechanisms were further elucidated through characterization of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), zeta potential, and cell surface hydrophobicity, while microbial community responses to 6:2 FTS exposure were also evaluated. Compared with clean sand, biofilm-coated sand enhanced 6:2 FTS retention under both saturated and unsaturated conditions. Under saturated conditions, retention differences among bacterial species were primarily governed by EPS content and protein-to-polysaccharide ratios. In contrast, species-level effects became less pronounced under unsaturated conditions, indicating a shift from species dependent controls to coupled biofilm interface processes. Quantitative analysis of these specific experiments showed that biofilms-associated processes contributed 42% of the additional apparent retention observed upon transition from saturated to unsaturated conditions, compared with 58% attributed to air-water-interfacial adsorption. These results demonstrate that biofilm-associated processes constitute an important and previously overlooked retention domain contributing substantially to the enhanced retention of 6:2 FTS under unsaturated conditions. Biofilm maturation further increased retention through EPS accumulation and associated changes in surface physicochemical properties, including surface potential, roughness, and hydrophobicity. Moreover, 6:2 FTS exposure altered bacterial community composition, suggesting reciprocal interactions between PFAS transport and microbial ecology. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into PFAS fate in the subsurface and improve the basis for predicting PFAS transport and designing remediation strategies for PFAS-impacted sites.

title: Using concentration–discharge hysteresis to infer recharge processes in karst springs: A case study of the Malenščica and Unica springs, SW Slovenia
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Blaž Kogovšek, Igor Jemcov, Nataša Ravbar, Cyril Mayaud, Matej Blatnik, Sara Skok, Janez Mulec, Metka Petrič
abstract: Karst aquifers are recharged both by diffuse infiltration through soil and rock (autogenic recharge) and by concentrated inflow through swallow holes and sinking streams (allogenic recharge). Differences in the origin of water are reflected in rapid changes in its physicochemical and microbiological characteristics. Various approaches are used to monitor these changes and analyse the data obtained. In this paper, concentration–discharge hysteresis analysis is used to define and compare the recharge characteristics of two karst springs. The study was conducted in a binary karst aquifer in the catchment of the Malenščica and Unica springs in south-western Slovenia, an area known for complex hydrodynamics with both autogenic and allogenic recharge. The area offers extensive prior hydrogeological knowledge and is equipped with a dense monitoring network that has been operating since 2016. High-frequency monitoring of temperature, specific conductance, and discharge in springs, water-active caves, and sinking streams was supplemented by event-based sampling for chemical and microbiological analyses. The data obtained were first analysed using descriptive statistics to compare the characteristics of individual monitoring sites and to infer connections between them. In the next step, individual storm events under various hydrological conditions were analysed in more detail. Hysteresis plots between discharge and specific conductance of the springs were compared with those of the sinking streams and underground channels in their catchments to characterise the mixing of groundwater originating from different recharge sources. Additionally, for a selected storm event, hysteresis plots between discharge and water quality parameters (specific conductance, temperature, turbidity, [Ca2+/Mg2+] ratio, Cl−, and bacteria) were analysed. Significant differences in recharge characteristics, water transfer through the system, and the chemical and microbiological composition between the two springs were detected. These findings provided information about the differences in the spatial and temporal distribution of autogenic and allogenic recharge of the two springs, which is very important for planning the protection of these karst water sources.

title: Study on the mechanism of enhanced remediation of nitrobenzene contamination in groundwater by hydraulically driven synergistic in-situ microelectrolysis system
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Bowen Li, Lamei Duan, Yuxin Liu, Han Jiang, Xinhui Wang, Shijie Wu, Meng Yao
abstract: Groundwater circulation well (GCW) can effectively control the migration and diffusion of organic contaminants in aquifer through hydraulic driving force. However, its poor direct removal capacity for contaminants restricts the engineering application of GCW. To address this issue, this study coupled GCW with FeC microelectrolysis to enhance the removal of nitrobenzene. Experimental results demonstrated that the FeC microelectrolysis system simultaneously generates hydroxyl radical (•OH) and hydrogen radical (H•), leading to two degradation pathways for nitrobenzene: oxidative pathway and reductive-oxidative pathway. Accordingly, kinetic fitting revealed that the degradation of nitrobenzene can be divided into two stages: rapid degradation stage dominated by reduction in the early phase and slow degradation stage dominated by oxidation in the later phase. Investigations on influencing factors indicated that a low aeration rate and low pH value favor the degradation of nitrobenzene, while the initial concentration of nitrobenzene has an insignificant effect on the degradation efficiency. Two dimensional sandbox simulation results showed that the coupling of FeC microelectrolysis with the hydraulic driven of GCW continuously reduced the concentration of nitrobenzene in aquifer and gradually formed a high-efficiency remediation zone centered on the GCW. The degradation efficiency of nitrobenzene reached 83.85% within 48 h, which was 19.93% higher than that of the single GCW system. These findings confirm that FeC microelectrolysis and GCW exhibit favorable synergistic effects, presenting significant application potential in the in-situ remediation of organically contaminated groundwater.

title: Effects of vegetation type and seasonal hydrology on soil carbon and nitrogen stocks in the Dianchi Lake ecological buffer zone
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Qiaochu Zhang, Rui Liu, Bin Gao, Kun Wang, Hua Zhang, Dasong Lin, Yanan Chen
abstract: Ecological buffer zones play an important role in nutrient retention and carbon sequestration, but variation in soil carbon and nitrogen stocks among different plot types and between dry and rainy season remains insufficiently understood. Soil samples were collected from three plot types in the Dianchi Lake ecological buffer zone: Populus canadensis plots, Taxodium ‘Zhongshanshan’ plots, and flooded Taxodium ‘Zhongshanshan’ plots. Samples were taken at five depths, namely 0–15, 15–30, 30–50, 50–70, and 70–100 cm, during dry and rainy season. Soil organic carbon (SOC), total nitrogen (TN), bulk density (BD), soil water content (SWC), pH, and electrical conductivity (EC) were measured, and soil organic carbon density (SOCD) and total nitrogen density (TND) were calculated. SOC and TN generally decreased with increasing soil depth, with the highest values occurring in the 0–15 cm layer. Significant differences in carbon and nitrogen concentrations and stocks were observed among plot types, and seasonal changes were evident between the dry and rainy periods. BD was consistently negatively associated with SOC, SOCD, TN, and TND. Redundancy analysis indicated that SWC and BD were the main explanatory variables in the dry season, whereas pH and BD were more important in the rainy season. The vertical distributions of soil carbon and nitrogen differed among plot types and between season. These findings indicate that plot characteristics and seasonal conditions should both be considered in the management of lake ecological buffer zones for carbon storage and nutrient retention.

title: Beyond advection: A Lagrangian framework for microplastic transport in depth-averaged shallow water flows
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): P. Vallés, M. Morales-Hernández, V. Roeber, D. Caviedes-Voullième, P. García-Navarro
abstract: Microplastics are an emerging contaminant in aquatic environments, posing risks to ecosystems and human health. Reliable computational tools capable of predicting microplastic transport are therefore essential for environmental assessment and mitigation strategies. This work presents a Lagrangian Particle Tracking (LPT-MP) model for microplastic transport under depth-averaged shallow flow conditions, coupled online with a two-dimensional Eulerian shallow water solver. The LPT-MP model incorporates the main processes governing microplastic dynamics, including horizontal advection and turbulent dispersion, settling velocity, degradation and biofouling, as well as a vertical flow velocity approximation. The model is implemented within the open-source SERGHEI framework using a Kokkos-based architecture, ensuring performance portability across CPU and GPU platforms and enabling large-scale simulations. Model performance and computational efficiency are evaluated through two synthetic benchmarks and one experimental validation case. Results demonstrate that settling and biofouling significantly influence the particle trajectories, while degradation produces negligible effects within the simulated time scales. The additional MP physical processes increase the total computational cost by approximately 6% with respect to the baseline advection–dispersion implementation, demonstrating the computational efficiency of the proposed extensions. The predictive capability of the model is assessed against an experimental benchmark, showing reasonable agreement in global deposition metrics while revealing limitations in the representation of turbulent lateral mixing. In summary, the presented framework provides an extensible and performance-portable tool for microplastic transport simulations in shallow water environments.

title: Mechanistic insights into Mn(II) retention and release at soil-water interfaces: Contrasting natural soils and hydrochemical controls
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zhenhao Fan, Yunchao Qi, Shengqiang Meng, Zijun Ye, Meiyang Jiang, Benyi Cao, Fei Wang
abstract: The retention and release of manganese (Mn) at soil-water interfaces control its subsurface mobility and secondary-remobilization potential, yet their dependence on the combined physicochemical and mineralogical properties of natural soils remains poorly resolved. Here, three compositionally contrasting natural soils, designated as sandy (S), clayey (N), and loamy (R) soils, were evaluated under a common batch framework using adsorption-desorption experiments, hydrochemical perturbations, and complementary interfacial characterization. The clayey soil exhibited the highest Mn(II) retention, with a Langmuir-estimated apparent maximum adsorption capacity of 2.0214 mg g−1, followed by the loamy (1.2825 mg g−1) and sandy (0.8231 mg g−1) soils. This retention hierarchy coincided with differences in specific surface area, cation-exchange capacity, organic matter content, and crystalline mineral assemblage.
