The results show how event magnitude, particle density, and channel morphology interact to control redistribution and retention, offering a quantitative framework for interpreting monitoring data and for assessing the sensitivity of sedimentary microplastic inventories to hydrological extremes.

title: Removable alginate gel barriers for contaminant source zone isolation in aquifer remediation: A bench-scale study
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Geon Namgung, Heonki Kim
abstract: Non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPLs) in aquifers act as persistent sources of groundwater contamination, while conventional flushing and sparging methods often suffer from inefficient sweep and excessive reagent consumption. This study proposes a novel strategy to hydraulically isolate the contaminant source zone using a temporally constructed alginate gel barrier (AGB) to enhance remediation efficiency. A two-dimensional flow chamber model packed with a sand was used for this bench-scale study. The AGB was formed in the flow chamber by sequential injection of sodium alginate and thickener solutions, followed by Ca2+-induced crosslinking, and subsequently removed using a sodium-rich solution. A series of experiments were conducted to evaluate ozone sparging, surfactant flushing (SDS + n-butanol), and cosolvent flushing (ethanol) within the confined source zone containing either a dissolved contaminant (fluorescein) or NAPL (mixture; PCE/hexane/oil-soluble fluorescence agent). The AGB effectively confined gas and liquid flow to the target region, significantly improving contact between remedial agents and contaminants. Ozone sparging removed >96% of the fluorescence from the oil-soluble fluorescence agent dissolved in the NAPL, surfactant flushing eliminated >90% within 12 h, and ethanol flushing achieved >97% removal within 5 h, with 78% PCE recovery in the effluent. Notably, required reagent volumes were substantially lower than those estimated for full-domain treatment. These results demonstrate that temporary source-zone encapsulation using AGB can markedly reduce chemical usage while enhancing remediation performance in NAPL-contaminated aquifers.

title: Laboratory spectral induced polarization monitoring of phosphogypsum leachate-carbonate interactions in karst aquifer materials
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Rujun Chen, Xunzhe Li, Na Hao, Shaoxiu Xue, Wen Zhang, Jian Yin
abstract: Reactive groundwater systems often involve strongly coupled hydrological, geochemical, and electrochemical processes, complicating the interpretation of hydrogeophysical observations. Karst carbonate aquifers are particularly vulnerable to contamination by acidic, sulfate-and phosphate-rich leachates derived from phosphogypsum landfills. In this study, laboratory column experiments were conducted to investigate spectral induced polarization (SIP) responses during phosphogypsum leachate‑carbonate interactions under static, dissolution-dominated, and dynamic breakthrough conditions representative of karst environments. SIP measurements were performed synchronously with geochemical monitoring of pH, fluid electrical conductivity, and major ion concentrations. Multivariate statistical analyses were applied to explore relationships between SIP parameters and evolving geochemical conditions and to aid interpretation of overlapping electrochemical behavior. Results indicate that the conductivity reflects pore-fluid ionic strength but exhibits weak linear correlations with individual ions due to the superposition of electrolytic conduction and reaction-induced pore structure modifications. In contrast, polarization signals and their frequency dependence are primarily sensitive to interface associated with carbonate dissolution and the formation or removal of secondary sulfate and phosphate-bearing mineral phases. Dual-frequency polarization features suggest the coexistence and temporal evolution of matrix-scale interfacial polarization and smaller-scale polarization associated with secondary mineral particles or surface coatings. Principal component analysis separates the dominant variability associated with bulk geochemical conditions from variations in SIP parameters related to interfacial polarization, while independent component analysis identifies statistically independent patterns that are consistent with dissolution- and precipitation-influenced electrochemical responses under heterogeneous experimental conditions. These results indicate that SIP, when interpreted in a multivariate manner and constrained by geochemical and mineralogical evidence, can provide process-sensitive information beyond bulk conductivity and help distinguish hydrologically and geochemically different reaction regimes in laboratory carbonate systems.

title: From boundary delineation to causal interpretation in wetland mapping: HRU-scale wetland identification and evolution mechanisms from a hydrological connectivity perspective
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Zeyu Wei, Hongfei Hou, Xiaocong Qiu, Nan Gou, Hexiang Zheng, Changfu Tong, Cheng Xu, Zengfeng Zhao
abstract: Wetland degradation and areal loss driven by global change and intensified human activities pose increasing challenges to wetland conservation and restoration. Reliable decision-making requires accurate identification of wetland extent and type, which is currently dominated by remote sensing-based mapping. However, gradual wetland boundaries, high intra-class heterogeneity, and spectral similarity among land-cover types often lead to classification uncertainty. Concealed wetlands are particularly prone to omission because of canopy obstruction, temporary absence of open water, and weak spectral separability. More importantly, remote sensing products alone have limited capacity to explain the hydrological mechanisms governing wetland expansion, contraction, and persistence under varying flow regimes. Hydrological connectivity provides a process-based perspective for linking wetland occurrence and function to runoff generation, lateral flow redistribution, and groundwater–surface water interactions within watersheds. To address these limitations, this study developed a SWAT+-based hydrological connectivity wetland classification system, termed SWAT+ HWC. Driven by physically based simulations at the hydrological response unit (HRU) scale, SWAT+ HWC provides a transferable framework for candidate wetland screening and functional wetland classification. Daily HRU-scale fluxes and state variables were used to derive ten process indicators characterizing dominant hydrological connectivity mechanisms, and candidate wetlands were further classified into three functional units: riparian wetlands, shallow depressional wetlands, and deeply connected wetlands. Classification thresholds were adaptively calibrated in quantile space using a particle swarm optimization–classification and regression tree algorithm combined with a K-out-of-N voting rule, thereby constraining the candidate wetland proportion while improving the spatial transferability of classification rules across watersheds with contrasting hydrogeomorphic settings. Model performance was evaluated through process-consistency analysis, quantitative comparison with the WetlandConnectivity v1.0 dataset, and spatiotemporal validation in the Altamaha River Basin. The identified wetland types showed stable correspondence with their expected dominant hydrological indicators. Quantitative evaluation demonstrated strong discriminatory performance across representative geomorphic units, with most ROC-AUC values ranging from 0.89 to 0.95, and seasonal wetland-area dynamics were highly synchronized with the reference dataset, with correlation coefficients exceeding 0.84. By linking wetland identification to testable hydrological process chains, SWAT+ HWC provides a physically traceable basis for wetland mapping, functional interpretation, and cross-period comparison. The resulting hydrological connectivity-based classification enables wetland mapping to move beyond identifying where wetlands are located toward explaining why wetlands occur and persist in specific landscape positions, thereby improving the interpretability and targeting of wetland conservation, ecological restoration, and watershed water resources management.

title: Integrating macroscopic geometry and fluid-fracture feedback in dissolution analysis beyond isolated factors
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Menghan Chu, Haichun Ma, Chunchao Zhang, Jiazhong Qian, Xian Li, Qiankun Luo, Lei Ma
abstract: The acidic dissolution behavior of calcite is an important process associated with geological environments such as karst-related systems and carbonate weathering. The study investigates the fundamental coupling mechanisms among geometric characteristics, fluid transport, and dissolution kinetics through controlled numerical simulations. The core innovation lies in the systematic quantification of the independent impact of the macroscopic curvature (represented by the aspect ratio Rm) on dissolution kinetics by introducing the parameter “Curvature-Dissolution Rate Coupling Response Coefficient (RC)” for the first time, and in revealing the interplay between two-dimensional fracture structure and fluid dynamics. Two-dimensional geometric models of isolated calcite particles and fractured matrices were established coupled with a dynamic mesh approach. For elliptical particles, the dissolution rate initially decreases and then increases with increasing Rm, a trend consistent with the variation of the specific surface area analogy value (B v ). The variation of RC indicates that the reaction rate is highly sensitive to curvature changes when Rm < 1. Multiple nonlinear regression analysis (Sd = 0.037 V a 0.763 ac 1.822 Rm −0.283 (R2 = 0.972)) further reveals that among the acid injection rate (V a ), acid concentration (ac), and aspect ratio (Rm), ac exerts the most dominant control on the shrinkage degree (Sd). At the fracture scale, acid etching drives the morphology toward channelization and significantly attenuates the nonlinear behavior of fluid flow, clarifying the dynamic feedback mechanism inherent in fluid-fracture interaction.

title: Comparative metabolomics reveals stage-specific hypoxia tolerance during early development of the rare minnow ( Gobiocypris rarus )
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Weihui Huang, Nanyan Weng, Hanxiao Zhang, Jingtian Zhang, Shouliang Huo
abstract: Hypoxia is a common environmental stressor in aquatic organisms. It is well known that juvenile and adult fish possess developed gills and livers to adapt to hypoxia. However, the mechanisms by which early undeveloped fish tolerate hypoxia remain unclear. Here, we selected rare minnow (Gobiocypris rarus) to investigate the hypoxia tolerance thresholds of three early life stages: embryo, larvae, and juvenile. We found that embryos could survive for 24 h under hypoxia at 0.5 mg/L, while juveniles were the most sensitive to hypoxia, with a 24-h LC₅₀ of 1.58 mg/L. To explore the differences in hypoxia tolerance across developmental stages, we investigated the oxygen demand and metabolic changes following exposure to hypoxic conditions (2 mg/L). The oxygen consumption rate increased from the embryo to the juvenile stage, generating more aerobic respiration to support the development of additional organs. Growth was inhibited by hypoxia, particularly in the embryo and larvae, which produced energy to maintain survival by consuming fats and amino acids, respectively. Juveniles showed minimal changes in metabolites before and after hypoxia, with sex hormone and lysophosphatidylcholine synthesis affected. Juveniles responded to hypoxic stress by increasing corticosterone via neuroendocrine control. The limited hypoxia adaptation and metabolic suppression methods explain the low tolerance of juvenile fish to acute hypoxia during a critical growth period with high routine metabolic rates. Our results reveal metabolic differences and hypoxia adaptation strategies across different early life stages, providing basic thresholds and guidance for biodiversity conservation.

title: Physics-informed spatiotemporal graph neural network models for groundwater contaminant prediction
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Dai Wan, Ge Ying, Hu Danxin, Xu Ruibing, DengYi, Yi Shuping
abstract: Groundwater contamination prediction is challenging because of the strong concealment, complex spatiotemporal coupling, and high parameter dependence of physical mechanism models. However, traditional data-driven models lack spatial representations. To address these limitations, this study developed and compared three physics-driven spatiotemporal graph neural network (STGNN) architectures for groundwater contamination prediction: a recurrent model (RGNN-ST), a convolutional model (ConvGNN-ST), and an attention-based model (AttentionGNN-ST). A dynamic graph construction strategy was designed to embed hydraulic head and hydraulic conductivity into edge weights, thereby linking data-driven learning to Darcy-flow constraints. Training and testing datasets were generated using coupled MODFLOW-MT3DMS simulations of homogeneous and heterogeneous aquifers. The model performance was evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness, and interpretability of the results. The results indicate that RGNN-ST provided the most reliable overall performance: under homogeneous conditions, R2 reached 99.95% and NRMSE was 1.68%; under heterogeneous conditions,the average R2 was 99.60%. RGNN-ST also exhibited the strongest stability and the best accuracy-efficiency balance across monitoring configurations. All models exhibited good robustness to monitoring node density, time window length, and aquifer heterogeneity, and accurately captured the spatiotemporal migration patterns of contaminants. Interpretability analysis revealed that RGNN-ST balances multi-source physical features (concentration, hydraulic head, hydraulic conductivity), automatically identifies key monitoring nodes and critical time steps, and its prediction behavior conforms to the physical mechanism of groundwater movement. The proposed physics-informed STGNN framework provides a transferable modeling strategy for groundwater contamination forecasting, risk management, and monitoring-network optimization.

title: Synergistic amplification and threshold vulnerability of coastal aquifer barriers under sea-level rise and freshwater decline
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Rajagopal Sadhasivam, Venkatraman Srinivasan
abstract: Coastal aquifers are increasingly threatened by saltwater intrusion (SWI) driven by climate change-induced sea-level rise (SLR) and anthropogenic freshwater decline (FWD). Although physical barriers such as cutoff walls (COWs) and subsurface dams (SSDs) are widely used to mitigate SWI, their performance under hydrological stresses such as SLR and FWD remains underexplored. In this study, four widely investigated field-scale conceptual aquifers are used to systematically evaluate the resilience and vulnerability of COWs and SSDs to these hydrological stresses under contrasting inland boundary conditions. Numerical simulations with the variable-density SEAWAT model show that inland boundary conditions strongly control barrier performance. Barriers remain largely resilient under flux-controlled (FC) conditions but become vulnerable under head-controlled (HC) conditions. Under HC conditions across a range of stress levels, COWs provide consistent mitigation benefits. However, SSDs exhibit distinct threshold behavior: they remain effective up to a critical stress level, beyond which their performance rapidly deteriorates. Model simulations reveal synergistic amplification under the combined effects of SLR and FWD, wherein SWI magnitudes far exceed the sum of their individual impacts. Furthermore, vulnerability maps are developed to delineate resilient and vulnerable regimes of barrier performance across a range of hydrological stress scenarios. These findings highlight the boundary-condition-dependent, threshold-driven, and synergistic amplification of barrier vulnerability, underscoring the need to explicitly account for combined climatic and anthropogenic stresses in the design of coastal groundwater protection strategies.

title: Migration and retention of polystyrene nanoplastics in porous media regulated by walnut shell biochar
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Yuheng Wu, Hui Li, Ming Wu, Qusheng Li, Yanru Hao, Jianfeng Wu, Jichun Wu, Bill X. Hu
abstract: The extensive accumulation of plastic waste in soil-groundwater poses a significant threat to subsurface environments. This study systematically elucidates the regulatory mechanisms governing the transport of polystyrene nanoplastics (PSNPs) in porous media amended with walnut shell biochar (WBC) through a combination of column experiments, Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) analysis, and two-site kinetic modeling. The results indicate that the incorporation of WBC markedly retards the migration of PSNPs. Owing to the pronounced microscopic surface roughness and well-developed lamellar pore structures of the biochar, the repulsive potential barrier between PSNPs and WBC is consistently lower than that between PSNPs and quartz sand, thereby providing abundant irreversible deposition sites. The modeling confirms that the synergistic effects of roughness-induced physical entrapment and short-range hydrophobic interactions drive the enhanced immobilization of the contaminants. Furthermore, the transport process of PSNPs is highly sensitive to hydrodynamic and hydrochemical variations. Increasing the WBC mass fraction, ionic strength, or acidity significantly compresses or neutralizes the electrical double layer, minimizing electrostatic repulsion and intensifying retention; here, divalent calcium ions exhibit a superior charge-neutralization and bridging capability compared to monovalent sodium ions. Conversely, elevated flow velocities, alkaline conditions, and the presence of humic acid enhance PSNPs mobility due to enhanced hydrodynamic shear, strengthened electrostatic repulsion, or competitive site occupation. These findings clarify the environmental behavior and interfacial mechanisms of nanoplastics under soil amendment practices, providing a scientific baseline for risk mitigation within soil-groundwater regimes.

title: Freshwater inflow, riverine nutrient load and salinity: Unraveling dominant drivers of dissolved inorganic nutrients in a bay-estuary system using Generalized and Neural Additive Models
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Sumon Hossain Rabby, Ebrahim Ahmadisharaf, Megan Lamb, Mark Rains, Jason Garwood
abstract: Nutrient dynamics in bay-estuary systems are shaped by the complex interplay between hydrology, biogeochemistry and hydrodynamics. Riverine nutrient loads are widely recognized as primary drivers of nutrients, yet how these loads translate into internal nutrient dynamics across varying hydrologic and salinity regimes remains poorly resolved. We addressed this gap by investigating long-term (19 years) dynamics of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) and dissolved inorganic phosphorus (DIP) loads and their role in governing nutrient variability under varying freshwater inflow and salinity regimes in Apalachicola Bay, Florida. We applied a series of generalized additive models (GAMs) that incrementally accounted for freshwater inflow, nutrient load and estuarine salinity alongside Neural Additive Models (NAMs) with concurvity regularization to account for the correlation among these drivers. Our results showed that riverine nutrient load is the dominant driver of estuarine nutrient dynamics. Although freshwater inflow and riverine nutrient loads are often used interchangeably in past studies, we show that “inflow as a proxy for nutrient load” is an oversimplification, particularly under low-flow conditions. We further showed that estuarine DIN exhibits more predictable, seasonally coupled variability with freshwater inflow and salinity. In contrast, episodic and localized biogeochemical processes make DIP dynamics less predictable and obscure the influence of salinity on DIP at monthly timescales. However, we showed that the dependence of estuarine DIN concentrations on the riverine load is strongly structured by salinity regimes, with fresher conditions favoring this dependence. Increasing variability in sea level and freshwater supply under climate change can make these dynamics less predictable.

title: An explainable machine learning surrogate framework for colloid-facilitated contaminant transport in porous media
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Mayur Mundada, Akhilesh Paswan
abstract: Colloids act as important transport carriers in subsurface environments, facilitating the migration of strongly sorbing contaminants and significantly influencing breakthrough curve (BTC) in porous media. This study develops a machine-learning surrogate model capable of accurately reproducing BTCs generated by an equilibrium colloid-facilitated contaminant transport model over a wide range of transport conditions. The mechanistic model was first validated against the experimental phenanthrene transport data, demonstrating excellent agreement under both colloid-free and colloid-present conditions. The presence of colloids significantly accelerated contaminant transport, reducing the retardation factor from 339.69 to 64.76. Three machine-learning algorithms, namely Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were evaluated for BTC prediction. Among them, RF exhibited the highest predictive accuracy with an R 2 of 0.9982, RMSE of 1.23 × 10 − 2 , and MAE of 5.89 × 10 − 3 . Explainable artificial intelligence analyses based on feature importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed that flow velocity was the dominant controlling parameter, followed by contaminant partitioning coefficients associated with mobile and immobile colloids. Furthermore, the RF surrogate accurately reproduced BTCs across diverse transport scenarios while maintaining excellent generalization capability. The novelty of this study lies in the integration of a physics-based colloid-facilitated contaminant transport model with interpretable machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence to develop a computationally efficient surrogate framework that not only accurately predicts BTCs but also reveals the relative importance of governing transport parameters.

title: Fulvic acid-iron colloid promotes the migration of As(III) in porous media
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Yanhao Li, Youru Yao, Xinyi Wang, Huimin Zhang, Fengman Fang, Yuesheng Lin, Zhiming Zhang, Qing Ji, Jia Yu
abstract: Fulvic acid (FA), a highly reactive and soluble fraction of dissolved organic matter in cultivated soils, facilitates the formation of stable colloids through complexation with iron (Fe), thereby significantly modulating the environmental mobility of arsenic (As). However, the migration behavior of As associated with FA-Fe colloids in porous media remains insufficiently characterized, particularly regarding the integration of coupled migration processes with quantitative modeling. This study investigated colloid-mediated As(III) migration in saturated porous media using column experiments and a time-fractional advection–dispersion equation (fADE). Increasing FA concentration enhanced As mobility, as evidenced by elevated breakthrough ratios and an increase in the fractional order α from 0.475 to 0.881, signifying the attenuation of memory effects and a transition toward Fickian migration. Conversely, elevated Fe concentrations promoted colloidal aggregation and suppressed As migration, with α decreasing to 0.437, capturing non-Fickian behavior associated with particle retention and deposition. Mechanistically, FA stabilizes FA-Fe colloids through electrostatic repulsion and steric hinderance while competing for adsorption sites, whereas Fe induces aggregation and enhances pore-scale interception, leading to As sequestration via inner-sphere complexation with Fe-OH groups. Under alkaline conditions, surface charge effects strengthened electrostatic repulsion and promoted migration, while elevated ionic strength compressed the electrical double layer, facilitated deposition. These results demonstrate that As migration is governed by the coupling between colloidal stability and interfacial interactions, which is effectively quantified by fADE. These findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding As mobility in subsurface environments and offer critical insights for groundwater remediation strategies involving colloid-facilitated migration.

title: Hydrological conditions regulate dissolved organic matter transport in the Yangtze River
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Xinyue Hu, Feng Liu, Chenxue Zhang, Nuoxiao Yan, Yao Yan, Zhiqiang Qiu, Mengmeng Yang, Dong Liu
abstract: The third longest Yangtze River plays an important role in transporting organic matter from the land to the global oceans, but the impacts of hydrological conditions remain unclear. Based on weekly measurements during 2020–2023, this study demonstrated the regulating effects of hydrological conditions on the transport of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in the Yangtze River. The results showed that DOM concentration and composition seasonally fluctuated along with the hydrological addition-dilution effects. Weekly DOC concentration at the Datong station had a variation range of 0.45–6.58 mg/L. In the rainy summer, high water discharge flushed humic substance output from the land and phytoplankton also produced protein-like DOM; water discharge was positively correlated with DOC concentration (p < 0.01). However, extremely high water discharge diluted DOC concentration when water volume increase exceeded DOM supply. By constructing a piecewise concentration-discharge quantitative model, we identified a water discharge threshold of 25,000 m3/s for the transition of addition (b = 0.23) and dilution (b = −0.45) effects. Additionally, potential hydrological regulation and watershed-scale human activities may further modify downstream DOM transport, although their individual contributions require further research. In sum, this study reveals the synergistic regulation effects of hydrological conditions on DOM transport in the Yangtze River, which are of great significance for managing river water quality and optimizing carbon cycle models.

title: Influence of iron mass on Cr isotope fractionation associated with Cr(VI) reduction by zero-valent iron
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Filip Budimir, Richard T. Amos, Carol J. Ptacek, David W. Blowes
abstract: Chromium contamination in groundwater remains a significant environmental concern, primarily due to the toxicity and mobility of its hexavalent form (Cr(VI)). The effect of ZVI mass on Cr(VI) reduction and isotope fractionation was investigated under dynamic flow conditions. Flow-through cell (FTC) experiments were conducted to simulate permeable reactive barriers, with stable Cr isotope fractionation (δ53Cr) used to differentiate direct ZVI-mediated and indirect Fe(II)-mediated Cr(VI) reduction pathways. Results showed a dual-phase removal mechanism: an initial rapid surface-mediated reduction followed by a slower aqueous-phase reduction. Isotope fractionation increased as Cr(VI) concentrations declined. Cr(VI) removal efficiencies of 1.6 mg g−1 were observed in FTCs containing 2 g or 4 g of ZVI. A transition from a rapid surface-mediated mechanism to a slower aqueous-phase reduction occurred at 85% and 75% breakthrough in the 2 g and 4 g FTCs, respectively. Isotopic enrichment was greater with increased ZVI mass, with maximum δ53Cr values reaching 0.23‰ (2 g ZVI) and 0.30‰ (4 g ZVI), compared to 0.47‰ for 6 g systems observed in previous studies. An updated MIN3P reactive transport model, incorporating mineral passivation and refined kinetic parameters, captures these trends. The optimized model assigns an isotope fractionation factor (ε) of –0.07‰ for the rapid, surface-mediated reduction reaction and –3.5‰ for the slower Fe(II)-mediated reduction. These values align with fractionation factors reported for analogous geochemical processes. This study isolates the influence of reactive surface area on Cr(VI) removal efficiency and isotopic behavior, enhancing mechanistic understanding and model reliability.

title: Physiological and metabolic responses of a freshwater gastropod to fenpyroximate: Insights from respiratory and behavioural alterations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Auroshree Sadhu, Surajit Ghosh, Nimai Chandra Saha, Caterina Faggio, Federica Impellitteri, Shubhajit Saha
abstract: Fenpyroximate, a pyrazole acaricide widely used in agriculture, may unintentionally reach aquatic environments and affect non-target organisms. The present study evaluated the physiological responses of the freshwater gastropod Filopaludina bengalensis following 96-h exposure to fenpyroximate, focusing on respiratory, metabolic, and behavioural endpoints across juvenile and adult life stages. A concentration-dependent decline in oxygen consumption and metabolic rate was observed, indicating impaired energy metabolism. Behavioural alterations, including reduced crawling and tentacular activity, increased mucus secretion, and impaired retractability, further supported the occurrence of physiological stress. Juveniles exhibited greater sensitivity than adults, as reflected by lower LC50, LOEC, and MATC values. Additionally, molecular docking analysis suggested potential inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, supporting the observed metabolic disturbances. Overall, these findings highlight fenpyroximate-induced physiological alterations in freshwater gastropods and underline the importance of evaluating sublethal responses in non-target aquatic organisms. Environmental implication Fenpyroximate is widely used in agriculture and may reach freshwater ecosystems through runoff and drift, posing risks to non-target organisms. This study demonstrates that fenpyroximate induces physiological, metabolic, and behavioural disturbances in a freshwater gastropod, with juveniles showing greater sensitivity than adults. Reduced respiration and metabolic impairment suggest disruption of energy metabolism, potentially affecting survival and ecological functioning. These findings highlight the physiological and ecological risks associated with fenpyroximate exposure and support the use of freshwater snails as sensitive bioindicators. Multi-level physiological assessment improves environmental risk evaluation of emerging pesticides in freshwater ecosystems.

title: Evolution of Micro-pore structure in saline agricultural soil driven by sand addition of specific particle sizes and its regulation mechanism on water and salt transport
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Yi Meng, Shuanhu Li, Chi Li, Bing Zhang, De Yao, Xiaorong Wang
abstract: Due to the dense structure and low permeability of saline-alkali soils with high clay content, the vertical migration of water and salt within the soil profile is severely restricted, posing considerable difficulties for saline-alkali land amelioration. To address the aforementioned deficiencies of shallow saline-alkali soils, this study proposes directly incorporating river sand with a specific particle size gradation into the shallow layer of saline soil to reconstruct the soil skeleton and improve pore connectivity. Through laboratory soil column leaching tests and direct shear tests, the incorporation ratio of river sand was systematically optimized, and the evolution of the microstructure before and after amelioration was characterized by scanning electron microscopy. The results indicate that incorporating river sand with a particle size of 0.075–1.0 mm at an incorporation rate of 20%–30% can significantly shorten the leaching duration and effectively promote the vertical transport of water and salt. Furthermore, compared with unamended saline soil, sand-amended saline soil exhibits improved pore structure and permeability, with the pore network becoming coarser and progressively more open, thereby forming continuous and efficient drainage and salt-discharge channels. Notably, an incorporation rate of approximately 30% represents a critical threshold for the evolution of cohesion; once this threshold is exceeded, the system response mechanism undergoes a transition, and cohesion enters a recovery phase. The technical approach proposed in this study is economical, practical, and broadly applicable, demonstrating promising application prospects not only in the fields of saline-alkali land remediation and ecological restoration, but also providing a reliable scientific basis and an efficient solution for relevant engineering practice.

title: Water quality assessment in multi-salinity groundwater of muddy coastal zones using a function-adaptive weight water quality index
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Qiming Sun, Xinyue Chang, Rui Xu, Xin Ji, Jianhe Yang, Hongwei Liu, Maosheng Gao, Guohua Hou, Zhenlin Liu, Xianmin Ke, Jie Dong
abstract: Muddy coastal aquifer subject to seawater (saltwater) intrusion suffer from severe freshwater scarcity and fragile groundwater environments. Traditional groundwater water quality evaluation frameworks relying merely on drinking water standards often categorize high-salinity groundwater (total dissolved solids, TDS > 3 g/L) as low-quality resources, while neglecting their exploitable value for diversified functional applications. To fill this research gap, this study proposes a salinity-based Function-Adaptive Weight Water Quality Index (FAWQI) for targeted, multi-functional groundwater quality assessment. Based on salinity thresholds, groundwater bodies are categorized into three functional types: low-salinity water (3–10 g/L) applicable to livestock breeding, medium-salinity water (10–35 g/L) fit for aquaculture, and high-salinity water (>35 g/L) that can serve as liquid mineral raw materials. Hydrochemical evaluation results indicate that freshwater zones are generally of fair quality, with 27% of samples rated “good” and 43% rated “fair.” Brackish groundwater quality is largely restricted by saltwater intrusion and elevated nitrate, which severely restricts its applicability for farmland irrigation. Approximately 52% of low-salinity groundwater samples is acceptable for livestock use, and medium-salinity water consistently meets the standard thresholds for marine aquaculture. Though hypersaline brines are unsuitable for conventional purposes, more than 76% of brine samples are enriched in K+, Na+, Mg2+ Br− and I−, demonstrating great exploitation potential as industrial mineral resources. The proposed FAWQI framework transforms conventional groundwater assessment dominated by single drinking-water-oriented standards into a function-driven classification framework. This novel evaluation method provides robust scientific support for zoned groundwater management and sustainable exploitation of water and mineral resources in saline coastal areas with severe water scarcity.

title: Parameterization and prediction of environment-dependent colloid transport in saturated porous media: A physics-informed machine learning approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Lin Han, Zhihong Zhang
abstract: Colloid transport in porous media exhibits pronounced variability under varying solution chemistry, hydrodynamic conditions, and pore structural characteristics. Conventional advection-dispersion models typically treat transport parameters as constants, which limits their predictive capability across variable environmental conditions. This study develops a physics-informed machine learning (ML) framework to parameterize and predict colloid transport under varying environmental conditions by deriving explicit expressions for key transport parameters. Built on 98 column-scale experimental records, the method first identified the dominant environmental controls on each transport parameter through an integrated importance analysis. It then applied nonlinear fitting constrained by colloid filtration theory (CFT) to the reversible retention-release parameters and a hybrid eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-Python Symbolic Regression (PySR) framework to the irreversible retention parameters. The explicit expressions relate transport parameters to flow rate, ionic strength, pH, porosity, and particle-to-grain size ratio. Predictive performance was evaluated by cross-validation, comparison with literature parameters, and breakthrough curve simulation. Results show that the proposed parameterizations accurately captured environment-dependent transport parameters and reproduced breakthrough curves. Flow rate mainly controlled colloid transport through advection, whereas its indirect effect through parameter regulation was limited. Porosity influenced both transport pathways and retention related parameters, with parameter regulation playing the dominant role. pH, ionic strength, and particle-to-grain size ratio primarily controlled deposition, release, and retention capacity by modifying interfacial interactions, electrostatic repulsion, and physical straining. The proposed framework provides a physically interpretable and transferable strategy for modeling colloid transport in saturated porous media under varying environmental conditions.

title: Global sensitivity of laboratory-scale groundwater reactive transport simulations for sorption and degradation: Breakthrough dynamics across Péclet–Damköhler regimes
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): W. Taylor, J.D. Herman, V.L. Morales
abstract: Groundwater contaminant transport models rely on parameters that are often difficult or time-consuming to measure, generating uncertainty that complicates interpretation and decision-making. We apply global sensitivity analysis (GSA) to identify the parameters and interactions that most strongly control laboratory-scale reactive transport. Numerical simulations of one-dimensional, fully water-saturated systems governed by advection–dispersion–reaction transport of a single solute with sorption and decay are performed that systematically vary porosity, bulk density, dispersivity, decay rate, sorption distribution coefficient, and desorption rate. We employ GSA in three complementary ways to interrogate reactive transport behavior. First, we evaluate parameter influence across key breakthrough times (early arrival, peak concentration, and late-time tailing), offering a temporally resolved view of transport dynamics; as well as value of peak concentration to capture the worst case exposure. Second, we quantify both individual and interactive parameter effects, revealing how coupled processes control breakthrough behavior and how interaction-driven variance increases as the contaminant plume evolves in time. Third, we interpret sensitivity patterns within dimensionless transport regimes defined by Péclet and Damköhler numbers, allowing parameter importance to be evaluated across distinct advective–reactive conditions and facilitating comparison across systems and scales. Results show that, for typical laboratory-scale systems with constant pore velocity, sorption emerges as a consistently dominant driver across all scenarios. As the contaminant plume ages, additional processes and increasingly complex parameter interactions contribute to output variance. Decay dominates in reaction-dominant regimes and when evaluating parameter influence on the magnitude of peak concentration, whereas dispersion can unexpectedly dominate in advection-dominant regimes. By combining temporal resolution, interaction analysis, and regime-based classification, this work expands on how uncertainty propagates through contaminant transport models and provides practical guidance for prioritizing parameter measurements that most effectively improve predictive reliability.

title: Modeling PFAS sorption characteristic patterns across the conterminous United States and utilizing these data for groundwater vulnerability assessment
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Mahlet M. Kebede, Mesfin M. Mekonnen, Leigh G. Terry, T. Prabhakar Clement
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants that pose significant risks to groundwater due to their widespread presence and resistance to degradation. The soil-water partitioning coefficient (Kd) is one of the key parameters used for predicting PFAS transport processes, yet the availability of Kd data is currently limited. This study developed a data-driven framework to map PFAS sorption characteristics (Kd values) at a large scale and employed the dataset to assess groundwater vulnerability across the conterminous United States (CONUS). We trained a stacked ensemble machine learning model, which combined Random Forest, XGBoost, GBM, and LightGBM with a ridge regression meta learner, on a literature derived Kd dataset. Soil properties, such as organic carbon content, CEC, silt, sand and clay percentages, molecular weight, chain length, and pH served as predictors and measured Kd values as target. Organic carbon content emerged as the dominant control for predicting PFAS sorption. Overall, the stacked ensemble model achieved strong predictive performance with R2 and RMSE values of 0.87 and 0.32, respectively. We applied this model to the Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO) dataset to generate spatially explicit Kd maps for multiple PFAS species across CONUS. The predicted Kd values were subsequently integrated with groundwater recharge, depth to water table, and proximity to known PFAS sources data within a Random Forest classification model to map groundwater vulnerability to PFAS contamination. The vulnerability map identified approximately 33,400 km2 as high-risk (probability >0.67) areas. These areas are primarily concentrated in the Northeast, upper Midwest, and portions of the Southeast regions. This study provides useful CONUS-scale Kd data and utilizes these data to develop a modeling framework that can help prioritize monitoring and remediation strategies to minimize PFAS risks.

title: Effect of surface water-groundwater exchange on heavy metal transport in the vegetated rivers
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 283 Author(s): Linlin Li, Jiahao Zou, Hang Li, Jiadong He, Hao Zhang, Canyong Li
abstract: In river ecological restoration, the mechanical and morphological properties of vegetation are critical modulators of hyporheic exchange, thereby influencing the broader fate of nutrients and contaminants. However, few studies have considered the effect of the dynamic interplay of vegetation flexibility on surface water-groundwater exchange, limiting our ability to predict the coupled dynamics of “flow-vegetation-hyporheic exchange”. To address this concern, a coupled model integrating surface water-groundwater exchange and heavy metal transport was developed to investigate the synergistic regulatory mechanisms of river vegetation characteristics on hyporheic exchange at the sediment-water interface, and also the transport of copper ions. The results indicate that: (i) vegetation height significantly influences the surface flow field structure; higher vegetation creates a high-velocity zone above the canopy (approximately 0.35 m/s) and a low-velocity zone within the vegetation, forming a distinct velocity stratification that is considerably more pronounced than that observed with shorter vegetation; (ii) vegetation height is the dominant factor regulating hyporheic exchange, the hyporheic exchange flux under higher vegetation conditions are approximately 123% greater than that of the shorter vegetation, and rigid vegetation enhances flux by about 17% compared to flexible vegetation of the same height; (iii) vegetation height significantly promotes the transport of copper ions within the hyporheic zone; under higher vegetation conditions, the vertical transport depth of copper ions increases by up to 100% within 24 h, whereas the effect of vegetation flexibility on this process is fewer than that of the vegetation height. This study reveals the multi-scale regulatory mechanisms of vegetation mechanics and morphological parameters on hyporheic exchange processes, providing a theoretical basis for the rational configuration of vegetation and the integrated hydrological-ecological design in river ecological restoration.

title: Coupled sediment and microplastic fluxes revealed by check-dam sediment records
description: Publication date: Available online 21 October 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology Author(s): Kazem Nosrati, Fatemeh Lak, Zahra Etminan, Adrian L. Collins
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, yet their redistribution through erosion and accumulation within sediment-retention structures remains poorly quantified. This study quantified MPs in sediments retained behind check dams and examined their relationships with sediment storage and erosion-related sediment yield at the catchment scale. Twenty check dams in a semi-arid mountainous catchment in northeastern Iran were investigated. Sediment storage ranged from 531 to 9828 Mg (mean: 2683 Mg), while specific sediment yield ranged from 16.2 to 855.4 Mg km−2 yr−1 (mean: 247.1 Mg km−2 yr−1). MPs were detected in all sediment samples, with concentrations ranging from 800 to 5240 particles kg−1 dry sediment (mean: 2702 particles kg−1). Estimated MP inventories ranged from 9.0 × 108 to 2.4 × 1010 particles per check dam. Strong positive relationships were observed between specific sediment yield and estimated MP yield (r = 0.99, p < 0.01) and between accumulated sediment mass and estimated MP inventory (r = 0.80, p < 0.01), indicating a close association between sediment dynamics and MP redistribution. Fibrous MPs dominated the assemblage (86.6%), and the 500–1000 μm size class accounted for the largest proportion of detected particles (44.7%). Raman spectroscopy confirmed several polymer types within the analyzed subset. Overall, the findings show substantial accumulation of sediment-associated MPs behind check dams and indicate that erosion-driven sediment mobilization may represent an important pathway for MP redistribution in erosion-prone catchments. However, the persistence of this retention may depend on the stability of accumulated sediments, which can potentially be remobilized during high-energy hydrological events.

title: How do stabilized river meanders affect microbial communities and water quality in urban rivers?
description: Publication date: Available online 20 October 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology Author(s): Dantong Zhu, Jiaxing Zeng, Jiajie Su, Shoushu Liu, Zhuoyin Lu, Saiyu Yuan, Xianglong Wei, Hongwu Tang, Xiangju Cheng
abstract: Urban river meanders are frequently stabilized and hardened for flood control, thereby substantially altering their natural hydrodynamics and ecological functions. However, the influence of such engineered bends on sediment microbial communities, key players in nutrient cycling and thus water quality, remains poorly understood. Here, we integrate 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, co-occurrence network analysis, and community assembly modeling to investigate seven stabilized meanders along Guangzhou's Yangmei River during a single summer sampling campaign. We found that bend-position-related habitat differences were associated with the spatial organization of microbial diversity and putative co-occurrence patterns. Mid-bend sections showed ecological patterns consistent with stronger local hydraulic disturbance, while post-bend sections were more consistent with relatively depositional habitat conditions. Mid-bend sediments, associated with relatively high hydraulic energy, exhibited the lowest α-diversity and distinct co-occurrence patterns, consistent with greater local hydraulic disturbance than at pre- and post-bend sites. Within the sampling campaign, spatial differences in water chemistry were more closely associated with external nitrogen and phosphorus inputs, whereas the spatial heterogeneity of benthic microbiota was more strongly linked to localized hydrodynamic conditions. Co-occurrence patterns also varied among bend positions along the meander transition. Neutral-community modeling suggested that stochastic processes played an important role in bacterial community assembly during the sampling period. Complementary βNTI–RCbray null-model analyses identified dispersal limitation as the predominant inferred process, whereas heterogeneous selection contributed relatively more in post-bend depositional sediments. Our findings highlight local heterogeneity in benthic habitats and water–sediment exchange conditions within stabilized meanders, which may influence local nutrient dynamics. These results suggest that bend-scale hydraulic conditions and microbial habitats warrant consideration in urban river restoration.

title: Effect of entrapped water on NAPL migration in unsaturated fractures
description: Publication date: Available online 20 October 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology Author(s): Song Xue, Qingteng Fan, Zexiong Zhou, Zhibing Yang, Gang Liu, Biao Li
abstract: The migration of non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPL) in unsaturated fractures involves NAPL-water-air three-phase displacement. Understanding the impact of entrapped water on this migration process is crucial for predicting NAPL flow and solute transport in the fractured vadose zone. This study presents visualized flow experiments to systematically investigate NAPL (n-octane) invasion behaviors in initially dry and water-entrapped unsaturated single fractures by varying fracture inclination angle and injection flow rate. The experimental results reveal that entrapped water fundamentally shifts NAPL flow patterns from fingering flow in dry fractures to film flow propagating along entrapped water droplets in water-entrapped fractures. Compared to fingering flow in dry fractures, film flow in water-entrapped fractures exhibits enhanced lateral expansion, longer fracture penetration time, higher breakthrough saturation, larger perimeter-area ratio, and stronger ability to invade large-aperture channels. The morphology of the film flow is jointly regulated by injection flow rate and fracture inclination angle. Lower flow rates and larger inclination angles result in thinner films, while sufficiently high flow rates at small inclination angles can trigger a transition from film flow to fingering flow in the main flow channels. We also find that the distribution of NAPL-occupied apertures consistently follows a normal distribution, independent of flow rate and fracture inclination angle, and aligns with the statistical properties of the fracture aperture field. These findings elucidate the regulatory role of entrapped water on NAPL migration and advance the mechanistic understanding of NAPL invasion in unsaturated single fractures, thereby informing groundwater contamination risk assessment and remediation design.

title: Non-reactive solute transport in coupled macro-meso-micro porous system: experiments and HYDRUS-2D modeling with GSA-PEST integration
description: Publication date: Available online 20 October 2026 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology Author(s): Aman Chandel, Deepak Swami, Nitin Joshi, Jiri Simunek
abstract: This study investigates the processes governing tracer transport in a stratified porous medium, which produces asymmetric breakthrough curves (BTCs) with multiple inflection points. Such complex BTCs are often analyzed using multi-porosity or multi-permeability flow and transport models. However, these models introduce increased parameter complexity and associated sensitivity, necessitating thorough evaluation. In this context, we coupled the Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) and Parameter Estimation (PEST) with the DualPerm (DP) HYDRUS module to quantify parameter sensitivity and enhance BTC representation. A micro-aquifer experiment was conducted on a stratified porous medium using a non-reactive tracer for testing the capabilities of the developed framework. The sensitivity analysis aimed to examine how different model parameters contribute to different segments of the asymmetric BTC. This analysis revealed that the fracture and immobile domain parameters dominate early tracer breakthrough (64% of the total sensitivity). In comparison, the matrix parameters and the porosity of the immobile region contributed 48% of the total sensitivity during the rising limb period. The prolonged tailing limb was primarily influenced by the matrix parameters (porosity and permeability, 91% sensitivity), with the porosity of the immobile region adding only 4%. It was also established that BTC-based parameter estimation emphasizes peak concentration, but often overlooks critical features like mass recovery, solute residence time, and spatial variance. An alternate approach, which is based on cumulative solute mass recovery, showed efficiency in capturing complex features of experimental BTCs such as inflection points, peak timing, and long-tailing behavior. The proposed framework enhances the capability of the HYDRUS (DualPerm) module to investigate various flow and transport processes, improving mass recovery estimation compared to conventional BTC-based methods.

title: Guidelines to writing a review paper for the journal of environmental radioactivity
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Sheldon Landsberger
abstract: The art of writing a good, meaningful and well-appreciated review paper for respective audiences is not an easy task to undertake. Often review papers have no hypothesis and are just a rehash of references, data, figures and tables with little inference to what future scientific directions need to be undertaken. On the other hand, some review manuscripts lack figures and tables and make reading cumbersome. There is a plethora of review styles in science, engineering technology, social sciences, business, etc. which can differ depending on the subject matter and journal expectations. This paper is a modest effort to outline guidelines to enhance the review contributions to the Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, (JENVR) while achieving a high standard of submission.

title: Experimental study on the radon barrier performance of cover materials under frozen and unfrozen isothermal conditions
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yongjun Ye, Ao Huang, Ting Yu, Shiyu Mou
abstract: Seasonal temperature variations, particularly frozen and unfrozen conditions, exert a considerable influence on radon exhalation from the surfaces of uranium tailings impoundments. To evaluate the radon barrier performance of cover materials under frozen and unfrozen isothermal conditions, three indoor-cured materials—pure laterite, a laterite-bentonite mixture (1:1 mass ratio), and a laterite-zeolite powder mixture (1:1 mass ratio)—were tested across five temperature setpoints (−20 °C, −10 °C, 0 °C, 10 °C, and 20 °C) in a temperature-controlled test chamber, using bare uranium tailings as a control. The results indicate that: (1) At a cover thickness of 15 cm, the radon barrier efficiencies of pure laterite, the laterite-zeolite powder mixture, and the laterite-bentonite mixture ranged from 89.07% to ∼100%, 81.99% to ∼100%, and 98.59% to ∼100%, respectively, with barrier efficiency gradually increasing as temperature decreased. (2) For all materials, the rate of change in radon barrier efficiency with temperature was lower above 0 °C than below 0 °C. The temperature sensitivity followed the order: laterite-zeolite powder mixture > pure laterite > laterite-bentonite mixture, demonstrating that the laterite-bentonite mixture maintained the most stable performance across thermal fluctuations. Additionally, preliminary empirical piecewise equations were established to describe the relationship between barrier efficiency and temperature across frozen and unfrozen regimes. Overall, this study demonstrates that radon exhalation barrier by cover materials depends not only on their intrinsic physical properties and ambient temperature, but also exhibits distinct behavioral shifts between frozen and unfrozen states.

title: Machine learning for atmospheric radioxenon source discrimination based on isotopic activity concentrations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Xiangrui Jiang, Ruiqin Zhang, Yungang Zhao, Qilong Guo, Shaohang An, Yazhou Niu, Yuhao Qin, Qi Li, Yuanqing Fan, Xinjun Zhang, Huaimao Jia, Shujiang Liu, Shilian Wang
abstract: Monitoring the activities of radioxenon isotopes (131mXe, 133Xe, 133mXe, 135Xe) in the atmosphere is a key task of the International Monitoring System (IMS) under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Discriminating the source of radioxenon detected at monitoring stations is crucial and highly challenging. This paper investigates the performance of machine learning for radioxenon source discrimination. Based on simulated and measured data, a synthetic dataset of radioxenon isotopic activity concentrations was generated, comprising samples from nuclear explosion, reactor, and hybrid sources. This dataset was then used as training data for machine learning models. The performance of the trained models was evaluated on a series of randomly generated test datasets. Under an idealized low-MDC scenario, the radioxenon source discrimination accuracy reaches 88.6%, and the probability of correctly identifying nuclear explosion signals is as high as 94.2%, corresponding to a false negative rate of 5.8% and a false positive rate of 14.9%. A sensitivity analysis using more realistic MDC settings shows that the discrimination performance decreases substantially as the MDC increases.

title: Enrichment of uranium-resistant microbial flora for U(VI) removal and mechanism analysis
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Taotao Zeng, Zhiyu Xiong, Yi Xiao, Jiayao Liu, Guohua Wang, Mingjuan Zhang, Shiyou Li
abstract: A community of uranium-tolerant microorganisms was isolated from a soil sample collected from the vicinity of a uranium tailing mine in South China to investigate the efficiency and mechanism of uranium removal. The maximum uranium (U(VI)) removal efficiency for microbes reached up to 90.9% at pH 6 and 35°C. Uranium can cause membrane lipid peroxidation to produce malondialdehyde, and activity levels of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase and catalase, changed accordingly. Fourier transform infrared spectrometry (FT-IR) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) showed that oxygen-containing functional groups and amide groups were the main functional groups involved, and that H2(UO2)2(PO4)2·8H2O and HPUO6·4H2O were formed. The isolated uranium-resistant bacterial flora included Aeromonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, Unclassified f-Enterobacteriaceae, Shewanella and Pseudomonas. Microbial functional gene prediction revealed an increased abundance of genes associated with intracellular transport, lipid transport and metabolism, inorganic ion transport and metabolism. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis showed that mainly genes related to the tricarboxylic acid cycle and quorum-sensing-related enzymes in resistance to uranium toxicity. This comprehensive analysis of the mechanisms of uranium resistant by microbial communities offers novel perspectives on the defensive responses of microorganisms under such stress.

title: A spatiotemporally corrected radiological contamination mapping platform for multi-scenario nuclear and radiological emergencies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Hyunsung Kim, Myeongsik Shin, Ku Kang
abstract: Rapid, quantitative assessment of the environmental consequences of radioactive contamination (and protection of responders operating within it) requires reconstructing continuous contamination fields from heterogeneous reconnaissance measurements. We present an automated platform that converts geo-referenced dose-rate data from ground and airborne assets into hazard-consequence maps. This study presents the platform architecture and quantitatively validates its spatial-reconstruction and decision-support modules; the altitude-correction and temporal-normalization modules are formalized as architecture components whose empirical validation is identified as future work. Airborne measurements are first converted to ground-equivalent dose rates through an altitude-dependent air-to-ground correction factor (AGCF) modeled as a segmented broken power-law (SBPL), then normalized to a common reference time using radionuclide half-life decay for radiological accidents or the Kaufmann power law for nuclear detonations. Normalized data are reconstructed into continuous 2-D fields by interpolation. Five methods, namely inverse distance weighting (IDW), ordinary kriging (OK), universal kriging (UK), anisotropic OK, and thin-plate spline (TPS), were evaluated in two scenarios: a 2000 kT nuclear surface burst (HotSpot 3.1.2) and the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant accident (JAEA airborne surveys, 2011–2025). Performance was strongly scenario-dependent: for the detonation, TPS and anisotropic OK far outperformed isotropic OK ( R 2 = 0.866 and 0.849 vs. 0.256), a gap robust across resampling (95% CIs non-overlapping), whereas all methods converged in the Fukushima field (mean R 2 = 0.938 –0.957) under random hold-out; under spatially-independent block cross-validation this convergence is weaker and accuracy is lower ( R 2 ≈ 0.70 –0.75), yet the anisotropy-aware advantage in the detonation field is reinforced. No single method is universally optimal; scenario-adaptive selection is essential for consequence estimation, exclusion-zone delineation, and minimum-dose routing in operational platforms.

title: Nonlinear dynamics and predictability limits of indoor radon under temperature and humidity variability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Dragutin T. Mihailović, Mounir Aït-Ziane
abstract: Indoor radon variability is shaped by coupled physical processes that limit short-term predictability and challenge conventional statistical modeling. We analyzed high-resolution 10-min indoor radon measurements (4842 samples, October–November 2023) at the Centre de Recherche Nucléaire d’Alger, alongside simultaneous indoor temperature and relative humidity records. Nonlinear time-series metrics, including Kolmogorov complexity (KC), the Kolmogorov complexity spectrum (KCS), and the largest Lyapunov exponent (LLE), were applied to characterize dynamical structure. The KC spectrum indicates that radon exhibits non-zero algorithmic complexity over a broader range of normalized amplitude thresholds than temperature or humidity, reflecting enhanced multiscale structural heterogeneity. Radon also shows a larger LLE (λ = 0.0826 per 10-min interval; 95% CI: 0.0728–0.0924), corresponding to a characteristic Lyapunov divergence timescale ∼ 2 h. Because the observations were obtained from a single indoor location over approximately one month, this estimated predictability timescale should not be generalized to indoor radon dynamics beyond the analyzed conditions. By comparison, temperature and humidity display lower dynamical instability and longer predictability horizons. These findings demonstrate that indoor radon has stronger short-term instability and reduced deterministic predictability relative to microclimatic variables. The results provide a quantitative framework for assessing structural complexity and intrinsic forecast limits in radon time series, offering practical insights for predictive modeling and ventilation-based mitigation strategies.

title: Fukushima-derived radiocesium in the subarctic and transition areas of the North Pacific in 2017
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yuichiro Kumamoto, Yasunori Hamajima, Mutsuo Inoue
abstract: The East-Japan Earthquake and the subsequent tsunami on 11 March 2011 damaged the Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant (FNPP1). As a result, radioactive cesium isotopes (134Cs and 137Cs) and other radionuclides were released into the North Pacific Ocean. Over the past decade, previous studies have examined the transport processes and total inventory of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in the North Pacific. In this study, we measured vertical profiles of dissolved radiocesium at stations along nominal 47°N zonal and 145°W meridional lines during the summer of 2017. With these data, we delineated the three-dimensional distribution of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in the subarctic and transition areas of the North Pacific and discussed its transport process by 2017. Additionally, we estimated the total inventory of the FNPP1-derived radiocesium in this area in 2017 to be approximately 6 PBq. This inventory in 2017 was approximately half of that estimated in 2014 (12 PBq). The missing inventory of approximately 6 PBq had been partially transported northward into the Bering Sea (0.3−1.3 PBq). In contrast, the expected southward transport from the subarctic/transition to the subtropical areas has not yet been observed. We proposed that one of the possible export paths is subduction in the eastern subarctic/transition area, followed by southward transport through the subsurface layer to the eastern subtropical and then the tropical areas.

title: Particle-tracking assessment of potential groundwater pathways for radionuclide transport across the Futaba Fault, coastal Fukushima, Japan
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Fengrui Zhang, Shinji Takeuchi
abstract: Radiocesium deposited after the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant accident remains a long-term environmental concern, but its groundwater pathways toward inhabited coastal lowlands are poorly constrained. This study evaluates conservative groundwater pathways potentially relevant to radionuclide transport near the Futaba Fault in coastal Fukushima by coupling a steady-state MODFLOW-2005 model with MODPATH 7. One thousand realizations varied hydraulic conductivity and the porosity components used to derive effective porosity for the fault zone, granitic basement, mudstone, and three sandstone units using bounded PERT and log-PERT distributions. Fixed particles were released separately on each side of the fault. Of 2,000,000 western endpoint records, 93.24% terminated west of the fault, 6.33% reached eastern non-ocean cells, and 0.43% reached the ocean boundary. Western paths were concentrated in local circulation cells and valley-directed discharge zones. Eastern non-ocean outcomes originated from 465 of 2000 western release locations and were spatially clustered rather than controlled by fault distance alone. Of 6,000,000 eastern endpoint records, 89.02% remained within the eastern sedimentary domain and 10.98% reached the ocean boundary; none returned to the western block. Within the adopted barrier-dominated conceptual model and specified hydraulic-property distributions, endpoint maps, travel-time-distance densities, ensemble cross sections, and representative-realization visualizations show that the limited west-to-east pathways remain spatially restricted. Because sorption and decay were omitted, the results represent a conservative, retardation-free pathway assessment rather than a concentration forecast. Even under this formulation, west-derived pathways into the eastern lowland were spatially restricted, indicating limited potential for widespread groundwater-mediated radionuclide transport under the modeled conditions.

title: National intercomparison of environmental gamma radiation dose rate in China based on ice surface cosmic ray response measurements
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Meiqun Xiao, Tao Wang, Xun Ding, Jun Xiao, Jianfeng Lu, Zhonggang Cao, Liang Wang
abstract: This study reports the first national intercomparison of environmental gamma radiation dose rate in China where each device’s response to the ubiquitous cosmic rays was measured on top of a frozen lake ice surface. A total of 78 ambient gamma dose rate instruments from 38 institutions were tested at four typical sites, including a low-terrestrial-background site on the ice surface of the Bosten Lake to measure the detector-specific cosmic ray responses, and wilderness, road, indoor sites nearby. The measured dose rates on the ice surface show significant variations for different detector types but exhibit good consistency within the same model. The cosmic ray responses were then subtracted from the measured dose rates at the other three environmental sites, and the corrected terrestrial gamma radiation dose rates are generally very similar for all instruments. A robust Z-score analysis was applied to evaluate proficiency and identify outliers. This work demonstrates the feasibility of ice-based measurement of the detector-specific apparent cosmic-ray response, and offers a practical technical reference for future intercomparison activities and quality assurance in environmental gamma radiation measurements.

title: Evaluation of gamma-irradiated Barbula indica moss bags for monitoring geogenic dust and norm deposition in bauxite mining areas
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Sang Nguyen Thi Minh, Khiem Le Hong, Son Nguyen An
abstract: This study investigates a biomonitoring approach using gamma-irradiated Barbula indica moss bags to evaluate atmospheric elemental deposition at the Tan Rai bauxite mining complex in Lam Dong, Vietnam. Moss samples were pre-treated with a 14 Gy dose to modify the matrix before a three-month dry-season deployment across four industrial nodes (P1–P4). Elemental quantification was performed using Total Reflection X-ray Fluorescence (TXRF). The results demonstrate a systematic increase in elemental concentrations for the irradiated matrix, with values rising by 12.4% to 28.1% compared to non-irradiated controls. Specifically, the relative difference in sequestration for Thorium (25.9%) and Uranium (28.1%) reached a peak at the industrial hotspot (P3), suggesting that radiation-induced surface modification may enhance the affinity for these elements. Comparative analysis indicates that while geogenic markers (Fe, Al, Ti) align with reported data from global bauxite-impacted regions, the elevated Thorium levels (mean 1.31 mg/kg) signify a distinct geochemical signature in the study area. These findings suggest that 14 Gy irradiated moss can serve as a stable passive sampler, providing a potential framework for environmental forensic monitoring in mining regions.

title: Effects of initial water content and Na 2 SO 4 on pore structure and radon exhalation of dried remolded loess
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Yuxin Zhang, Qiang Sun, Yuzhen Han, Zetang Wang, Hui Liu, Liangfu Xie, Houen Li
abstract: The pore structure of loess directly governs the storage and migration of radon. In this study, remolded loess specimens were prepared at four initial water contents (8%, 10%, 12%, and 14%) and five Na2SO4 contents (0%, 0.4%, 0.8%, 1.2%, and 1.6%). Low-temperature nitrogen adsorption, Frenkel–Halsey–Hill (FHH) fractal analysis, and radon exhalation tests were conducted to investigate the pore-structure evolution and radon-release characteristics of loess under coupled water–salt effects. The results showed that the pore system was dominated by micropores and mesopores, and all specimens exhibited typical type IV adsorption isotherms with H3 hysteresis loops. With increasing initial water content, the pore structure evolved nonlinearly with increasing water content, with enhanced micropore–mesopore development at intermediate water contents, while the fractal dimension D2 first increased and then decreased, reaching its maximum at approximately 12% water content. The radon exhalation rate followed a similar trend, increasing initially and subsequently decreasing, with relatively high values observed near 12% water content. By comparison, Na2SO4 had only a limited influence on the fundamental pore type but likely modified pore connectivity through salt migration and crystallization. These findings indicate that initial water content is the dominant factor controlling pore-structure evolution and radon release in loess, whereas salt primarily modifies the connectivity of the pore network. Radon release from loess is jointly governed by pore-size composition, pore connectivity, and pore-structure complexity. This study elucidates the intrinsic relationship between pore-structure evolution and radon release under coupled water–salt conditions and provides a theoretical basis for evaluating radon migration and environmental radiation risk in saline loess regions.

title: Bioaccumulation, food web transfer, and tissue distribution of polonium-210 and lead-210 in Canadian freshwater ecosystems
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Stephanie Walsh, Hailly Degagne, Jamie Carr, D.J. Rowan, J.M. Blais, M.J. Bond
abstract: Understanding the bioaccumulation and trophic transfer of naturally occurring radionuclides is essential for assessing ecological risk in freshwater systems. This study provides a large-scale assessment of polonium-210 (210Po) and lead-210 (210Pb) bioaccumulation, trophic transfer and tissue-specific biodistribution in freshwater food webs across Canada. Activity concentrations were measured in water and biota samples collected from multiple ecozones and land-use settings. Bioaccumulation factors were calculated to evaluate water-to-food web transfer, while trophic position patterns and 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratios were used to assess trophic transfer and preferential radionuclide uptake and retention. Results showed the bioaccumulation of 210Po in freshwater biota relative to surface water, while 210Pb was generally less enriched in biota and showed lower relative retention across organisms. Relationships with trophic position indicated that 210Po transfer was not well described by a linear trophic magnification factor, showing enrichment from primary producers to primary consumers, followed by substantial variability among higher trophic positions. The 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratio was generally elevated in consumer organisms, indicating preferential biological uptake and retention of 210Po relative to 210Pb. Tissue-specific analyses indicated that 210Po was concentrated primarily in viscera and internal organs, whereas muscle contributed a smaller proportion of whole-fish 210Po burden. Together, these findings demonstrate that 210Po bioaccumulates, but its biological uptake and retention vary nonlinearly with trophic position, and that 210Po:210Pb activity concentration ratios provide a consistent and integrative metric of trophic enrichment.

title: Selecting a spectrometric detector for drinking water monitoring in the case of nuclear and radiological emergencies
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Jonathan Sundström, Charlotta Nilsson, Mats Isaksson, Christopher Rääf
abstract: Rapid and reliable radionuclide-specific monitoring of drinking water may be required following a radiological or nuclear (RN) emergency. In this study, ten gamma-detector configurations were evaluated for continuous drinking-water monitoring using Monte Carlo simulations combined with measured detector backgrounds. Two source terms were investigated, representing fallout from a nuclear weapon detonation and a nuclear power plant accident, each at 48 h and 7 d after release. Two measurement geometries were simulated: a 4 L Marinelli beaker and a shielded detector positioned directly against a water pipe. A conservative scenario was assumed in which the complete source-term radionuclide composition was transferred to the drinking water. Minimum Detectable Activity (MDA) and Minimum Quantifiable Activity (MQA) were calculated for 131I and 137Cs, including contributions from other radionuclides within the respective regions of interest. Larger detectors generally provided lower MDA and MQA values, with the lowest values mainly obtained for HPGe. Despite substantially lower volume-normalised full-energy peak efficiency for the Pipe geometry, its concentration-based MDA and MQA values were relatively similar to those of the Marinelli geometry because of the much larger sampled water volume. Energy resolution strongly affected radionuclide-specific quantification. For 131I, 7 d after a nuclear weapon detonation in a Marinelli geometry, non-target radionuclides contributed approximately 79% of the NaI(Tl) ROI counts, compared with approximately 29% for HPGe. The results show that both detection efficiency and energy resolution must be considered when selecting detector systems for radionuclide-specific drinking-water monitoring following an RN emergency.

title: Metabolic and oxidative stress biomarker responses to enhanced levels of natural radioactivity in three edible bivalve species
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): D. Hunt, M.G.L. Assunção, T. Davis, C. Martin, L. Pearson, N. Willey, F.L.G. Dal Molin
