Study focus: Flood early warning in these catchments requires resolving flood peaks that evolve within hours, yet conceptual models and calibration metrics are still evaluated overwhelmingly at the daily scale. We assess three lumped conceptual models (GR4H, TUW, and SAC-SMA) calibrated at hourly resolution, using seven objective functions under a traditional full-record approach (T) and a flood-hydrograph-centred approach (FHC), with continuous and categorical (event-detection) metrics. New hydrological insights: Among the tested models, model structure, rather than the choice of objective function, governs temporal transferability. SAC-SMA is the most stable across regimes and approaches (NRMSE increases below 33 percentage points under FHC) and GR4H the most sensitive (below 53). High-flow skill deteriorates systematically from rainfall- to snowmelt-dominated basins, with median correlation falling from 0.65 to 0.10 under T. This pluvial-to-nival degradation quantifies a real limitation of Andean snowmelt regimes, whose prolonged, energy-driven flood response is not resolved at sub-daily resolution by conceptual snow routines, although uncertainty in high-elevation reanalysis forcing plausibly contributes. For rainfall- and mixed-dominated basins, a promising operational strategy combines LCE (T) for detection with KGE-K HiLo (FHC) for peak refinement.

title: A hybrid SWAT-LSTM-transformer model for transferable runoff simulation in ungauged basins
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zhengbo Peng, Dedi Liu, Jiayu Zhang, Yicheng Li
abstract: Runoff simulation in ungauged basins remains a fundamental and challenging issue in hydrological science, with far-reaching implications for water resources management, flood control, and agricultural planning. While previous studies have extensively developed physically-based and data-driven models for runoff simulation in ungauged basins, both models are still constrained by limited cross-basin transferability and inadequate physical interpretability. To address these constrains, we propose a hybrid model for runoff simulations in a target ungauged basin through integrating the physically-based Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model with the data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Transformer models as a hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model. SWAT model with default parameters simulate runoff generation processes to quantify the relationship between meteorological forcing variables and observed runoff variables. And the bias of the relationship is simulated by the LSTM-Transformer model. Three metrics of R 2, NSE, PBIAS are employed to evaluate the performances of the models. After the proposed SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model has been calibrated in a gauged basin, it is transferred to a target ungauged basin. There are three basins referring to Tao River water diversion project that are taken as case study area. One is the Upper Wei that is taken as the gauged basin for calibrating models while the other two are Tao, and Zuli River basins that are assumed to be target ungauged basins. The means of R 2, NSE, and absolute PBIAS values are 0.897, 0.841, and 13.37% from transferring the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model while they are 0.206, −4.405, and 106.65% from the transferring calibrated SWAT model and 0.257, −1.244, and 81.74% from the transferring LSTM-Transformer model in Tao, and Zuli River two target ungauged basins. The results demonstrate that the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model outperforms both the calibrated SWAT model and the trained LSTM-Transformer model when they are transferred to the target ungauged basins. The relationships between the runoff and the runoff generation processes simulated by a physically-based model even with its default parameters can be captured by the data-driven model, which help to transfer the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model. And the Transformer model was integrated with the LSTM model to improve the stability of model transfer and alleviate the limitation in high runoff simulations in the target ungauged basins. The sensitive parameters of the SWAT model and the contributions of inputs to the LSTM-Transformer are similar in both gauged and ungauged basins. Therefore, the proposed hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model is not only an effective approach in the case study area but also can be applied in a ungauged basin.

title: Investigation into the transforming mechanism from flash-to-conventional drought in different soil moisture layers in a highly climate-diverse basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tahira Khurshid, Qiongfang Li, Chuanhao Wu, Muhammad Shafeeque
abstract: Study region The Indus Basin, a highly diverse climate basin in South Asia. Study focus The transformation from flash drought to conventional drought (FD-CD) poses significant challenges to drought risk and management systems, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of the dynamics involved. Previous studies focused on the FD-CD process solely through the perspective of the recovery phase, overlooking the persistent phase between drought onset and recovery. This study aims to determine which phase of drought contributes the most to FD-CD and explore the impact of various climate characteristics on this phase. New hydrological insights We found that FD-CD is more likely to occur in deeper soil moisture layers, particularly in semi-arid and arid regions of the Indus Basin, with its peak period from July to October. The persistent phase of drought is most significant contributor to FD-CD development, with an average duration of 13 octads, significantly longer than the recovery phase (~ 5 octads), while the average rate of soil moisture change is relatively low during the persistent phase (0.025%) compared to the recovery phase (0.08%). XGBoost SHAP analysis reveals significant differences in the contribution of meteorological variables to the persistent phase in various climate zones. The contribution of high temperature to the persistent phase is most significant in the arid zone, while precipitation deficit is a dominant associated factor in other climate zones of the study domain. These findings contribute to understanding the FD-CD dynamics, providing new insights into the importance of the persistent phase in the life expectancy of the FD.

title: Assessing groundwater favourability using multi-scale spatial regression techniques within a GIS framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Imran Ahmad, Mithas Ahmad Dar, Mariya Belete, Mezid Kassa Abebe, Martina Zelenakova, Amare Adane, Milashu Sisay, Zinabie Mekonnen Taye, Shewaye Amakelew, Getanew Sewnet Zewdu
abstract: Study region Raya Azebo Woreda in northern Ethiopia faces increasing groundwater stress due to variable rainfall, heterogeneous lithology, and growing agricultural and domestic water demand, making reliable groundwater-potential assessment essential for sustainable water management. Study focus This study integrates Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) with GIS to map groundwater potential using lithology, rainfall, land cover, distance to lineaments, and distance to rivers. The model achieved an adjusted R² of 0.8796, with RMSE = 0.3412, MAE = 0.2736, and AUC = 0.964. MGWR identified broad-scale effects for lithology, rainfall, lineaments, and rivers (bandwidth = 101,990.79 m), while land cover exhibited a localized influence (bandwidth = 48,037.78 m). New hydrological insights The MGWR–GIS integration advances conventional groundwater mapping by capturing the scale-dependent spatial influence of individual hydrological controls rather than assuming uniform relationships across the landscape. The resulting classification into poor, moderate, high, and very high groundwater-potential zones provides spatially targeted information for groundwater exploration, recharge planning, and sustainable resource management.

title: Basin-scale organization of groundwater and surface water during the monsoon season: Hydrochemical and isotopic insights from the Brahmaputra River Basin, Northeast India
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sourav Kumar, Madhusmita Nanda, Abhishek Dixit, Archana M. Nair, Michael Manga
abstract: Study region The Indian sector of the Brahmaputra River Basin (BRB). Study focus We co-evaluated groundwater (GW) and river water (RW) across the Indian BRB using a synoptic monsoon-season survey (July 2022; n = 83; 36 GW, 47 RW). Hydrochemistry, stable isotopes (δ²H, δ¹⁸O), water-quality indices, and principal component analysis (PCA) were interpreted within a geomorphic–hydrogeological framework to resolve solute-acquisition processes, water-quality controls, and setting-dependent GW–RW relationships. New hydrological insights for the region GW–RW organization varied systematically with geomorphic setting and subsurface storage. Monsoon-season RW was comparatively dilute and carbonate-weighted, consistent with rapid routing and preferential expression of carbonate-derived solutes during high flow, whereas GW recorded greater solute accumulation, stronger silicate-weathering signatures, and widespread cation exchange. Stable isotopes showed pronounced GW–RW separation in low-gradient alluvial settings, where GW integrated recharge across broader spatial and temporal scales, but greater correspondence in mountainous settings characterized by shorter flow paths and limited storage. PCA independently reproduced this setting-dependent hydrochemical structure. Glacier- and snow-fed rivers preserved depleted high-elevation signatures that were progressively modified by downstream mixing. Drinking-water suitability was constrained principally by Fe, Mn, and Al, with As and NO₃⁻ contributing locally, whereas irrigation suitability was broadly favorable. Exceptional antecedent rainfall coincided with multi-constituent enrichment in two Himalayan tributaries, demonstrating that event-scale perturbations can locally disrupt basin-scale river-water patterns.

title: Evapotranspiration in tropical basins of Madagascar: A water-balance consistency assessment of different products
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Rojin Alimohammad Nejad, Ludovic Oudin, Fara Pascale Rakotomandrindra, Camille Ollivier, Albert Olioso, Zonirina Ramahaimandimby, Simon D. Carrière
abstract: Study region This study focuses on humid and semi-humid basins in the tropical regions of Madagascar. The study area is characterized by a limited number of hydrometeorological monitoring systems. Madagascar is particularly prone to extreme weather events (droughts and floods), which significantly affect water resource management. Study focus Ten evapotranspiration (ET) products derived from remote sensing (RS), land surface modeling (LSM), and reanalysis datasets were evaluated for the period 2009–2021. These ET products were assessed interannually and seasonally across nine basins in humid and semi-humid climate zones. ET product estimates were compared with ET determined using a water-balance approach, since no direct ET measurements were available across the region for the period 2003–2019. New hydrological insights for the region This study presents a typical case aiming to determine ET spatially in an area lacking ET measurements a common situation worldwide. However, accurate ET knowledge is essential for sustainable water resource management policies. The results indicate high variability and strong contrasts with substantial uncertainty in ET across Madagascar’s humid and semi-humid regions. Temporal analysis reveals clear seasonal patterns in ET for all products, but their ability to reproduce interannual dynamics varies widely. ERA5 and ETMONITOR show relatively comparatively better agreement with water balance, capturing interannual ET patterns with low bias and acceptable correlation. This study provides the first basin-scale evaluation of diverse ET products in Madagascar.

title: A computational framework for high-resolution drought assessment using conditional GAN downscaling of GPM IMERG precipitation over Jeju Island
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): YeonJi Chung, Ju-Young Shin, Myoung-Jin Um
abstract: Study Region Jeju Island, South Korea, is a groundwater-dependent volcanic island with steep orography, coastal exposure, and sparse high-elevation gauges, where precipitation variability strongly influences drought diagnostics. Study Focus This study develops a supervised conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) framework to downscale GPM IMERG precipitation from 0.1° to 0.01° and evaluate the resulting fine-grid (0.01° gridded) precipitation reconstruction for Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI)-based drought assessment. A co-kriging (CK) precipitation field derived from ground observations and DEM elevation served as both training target and primary reference; therefore, the evaluation quantifies CK-referenced reproducibility rather than independent precipitation accuracy. The cGAN used upsampled IMERG, elevation, elevation-gradient, and precipitation-intensity channels and was applied to the 2004–2023 IMERG archive. SPI-3, SPI-6, SPI-9, and SPI-12 were evaluated against CK-SPI at grid, watershed, and elevation-band scales, with bilinear interpolation as a baseline. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The cGAN reproduced CK-SPI temporal variability, with mean CC decreasing from 0.858 at SPI-3–0.685 at SPI-12. Errors were largest in the high-elevation interior and western coastal watershed, where CK LOOCV indicated greater reference uncertainty. Relative to bilinear interpolation during 2022–2023, the cGAN reduced RMSE, MAE, and absolute bias across all SPI windows and improved CSI for SPI-6 to SPI-12, while bilinear retained higher correlation. Thus, the cGAN added value mainly through CK-oriented error reduction, not stronger temporal co-variability.

title: Integrating habitat configuration and biotic integrity into an ecological flow framework for the heavily regulated Huai River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qimeng Wang, Yicheng Fu, Haishen Lü, Zhidong Liu
abstract: Study region The Huai River Basin (HRB), China, is a heavily regulated floodplain river system characterized by intensive flow regulation, longitudinal fragmentation, and chronic nutrient loading. Its aquatic ecosystems face compounded stressors from altered hydrological regimes and progressive habitat degradation, making it a representative case for ecological flow (e-flow) optimization in human-altered basins. Study focus This study develops a multidimensional, indicator-based e-flow framework that transitions from conventional hydrological indices to integrated hydro-biological metrics. Synthesizing data from five field campaigns across 27 monitoring sites, we coupled two-dimensional hydrodynamic-habitat simulations for the indicator species Parabramis pekinensis with multi-metric biotic integrity assessments. The framework explicitly quantifies life-stage-specific habitat requirements by prioritizing the spatiotemporal sensitivity of hydro-morphological indicators—including Weighted Usable Area (WUA), spatial connectivity, and fragmentation metrics—while decoupling flow-driven habitat optimization from load-based water quality management. New hydrological insights for the region The HRB’s aquatic communities are hydrologically co-constrained by physical habitat fragmentation and disrupted longitudinal connectivity, with chronic nutrient loading and low-flow regimes acting as primary ecological bottlenecks. The proposed framework significantly outperformed the conventional Tennant method, increasing spawning Habitat Suitability Index (HSI) values to 9.31~13.62 and improving connectivity metrics by 19~26% (p < 0.05), while reducing spawning habitat fragmentation to 6.51~8.77 hm². We identified a critical spawning discharge threshold of ~1500 m³ /s and a minimum overwintering depth of 2.5~3.0 m. The optimized e-flow, representing approximately 33% of the mean monthly reference flow, provides a mechanistic, biologically grounded benchmark for balancing ecological restoration with regional water security. This phased, indicator-driven approach offers a transferable hydrological template for adaptive e-flow management in regulated floodplain rivers globally.

title: Quantitative attribution of the drivers of Poyang Lake water level changes based on similarity analysis and the DA-GRU model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xingbo Wang, Lvze Duan, Shuanghu Zhang, Yiman Tian, Hangyu Guo
abstract: Study region The Poyang Lake basin, China. Study focus Poyang Lake (PYL) has experienced a pronounced decline in autumn water levels, yet the relative contributions of different drivers remain controversial. This study integrates similarity analysis with a Dragonfly Algorithm (DA) optimized Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model, forming a control variable framework that explicitly separates timing and magnitude effects of different drivers, enabling quantitative attribution of the effects of the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) regulation and channel morphological changes on PYL water level decline. New hydrological insights for the region The similarity analysis indicates a structural shift in the hydrological linkage between the Yangtze River and PYL after 2003, marked by a decoupling of mainstream discharge and lake water levels. Scenario simulations indicate that TGR regulation primarily alters the seasonal discharge regime, leading to earlier post-flood water level recession. In contrast, channel morphological changes, including riverbed incision and cross-sectional enlargement, emerge as the dominant and more persistent control on water level decline. Quantitative attribution shows that about 77% of PYL’s water level decline since 2003 is attributed to channel morphological changes, while about 23% is associated with TGR regulation. Overall, TGR regulation primarily influences the timing of water level decline, whereas channel morphological changes play a dominant role in determining its magnitude.

title: Unraveling scale effects in naturalized runoff processes: Insights from interpretable machine learning across the Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fenghua You, Shanshui Yuan, Liliang Ren, Chenglong Cao, Xiuqin Fang, Shanhu Jiang, Yi Liu, Xiaoli Yang
abstract: Study region The Yellow River basin (YRB), China. Study focus Effective water resource management requires a comprehensive understanding of runoff processes across spatial scales and their interconnections. However, scale effects pose major challenges to deriving a universal spatial scaling law when extrapolating runoff research from fine to broad scales. Previous studies have mainly focused on relatively small study areas ( 100 km²). Our results indicate that the runoff coefficient (RC) of most sub-basins did not follow a single scaling rule. Instead, RC-area relationships varied among scale domains, and RC did not consistently increase or decrease with basin area. In smaller sub-basins, the spatial distribution of precipitation dominates runoff scale effects, whereas in larger sub-basins, the spatial distribution of land use governs these effects.

title: A novel framework for reservoir outflow simulation combining satellite observation and hydrologic modeling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tianyao Liu, Jianzhong Lu, Xinbo Liu, Yonglin Lv, Ting Ye, Dunxian She
abstract: Study region The Minjiang River Basin is located in Sichuan Province, China, within the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, characterized by complex mountainous terrain and reservoir systems. Study focus Many reservoirs in ungauged regions lack sufficient data, making satellite remote sensing a viable solution for long-term monitoring. Previous satellite-based approaches are mainly limited to monthly or semi-monthly scales, especially in complex terrain, limiting the timely estimation of reservoir outflow. This study presents a method coupling hydrologic modeling with satellite imagery for subweekly estimation of reservoir inflow, storage, and outflow, achieving high accuracy across the target reservoirs. New hydrological insights for the region The reconstructed area and storage series reveal consistent seasonal regulation across the target reservoirs in the mountainous Minjiang River Basin. However, the reservoirs storage showed an anomalous increase in anticipation of the drought in 2022, which likely reflects anticipatory water storage in response to expected water shortages. Besides, the subweekly series captured short-term reservoir responses following individual rainfall events that were not clear from monthly or coarser records, revealing short-term changes in reservoir inflow, storage, and outflow. The dynamics inform water allocation and demand planning in mountainous areas around the reservoirs. The estimated outflow series provide inflow information for downstream cascade reservoirs, supporting reservoir operation and water-resource management across the Yangtze River Basin, including the Three Gorges Reservoir.

title: Contrasting contributions of vertical water transport processes to WUE variability across vegetation types in the karst critical zone of Southwest China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Junlan Nie, Feng Hu, Xu Zhou, Guangyan Ran, Xuyang Cai, Longyu Hou
abstract: Study region Southwest China. Study focus Although WUE is widely used to characterize ecosystem water–carbon coupling, the mechanisms by which water transport across different interfaces of the Earth's Critical Zone constrains WUE remain unclear in karst ecosystems. The study developed a vertical water transport processes (VWTPs) framework that decomposes water transport into four sequential components and integrated variance decomposition, random forest analysis, and structural equation modeling to quantify their contributions to WUE variability across major vegetation types during 2002–2022. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Results revealed that WUE in karst ecosystems is governed by vegetation-specific vertical water transport processes rather than by a single ecohydrological pathway. Variance decomposition of the complete VWTPs chain (GPP/TWI) showed that RWSE had the largest main-effect contribution across vegetation types, while TWCE contributed relatively more in grasslands. Pairwise covariance effects accounted for 39.30% of the total contribution, indicating that joint variability among VWTPs components represented an important component of the overall variability. Vegetation structure consistently played a prominent role in regulating VWTPs, whereas climatic regulation shifted from precipitation-dominated water-supply pathways in croplands and grasslands to atmospheric demand-driven physiological pathways in forests and shrublands. These findings provide a process-based understanding of vegetation-specific carbon–water coupling in karst critical zones.

title: Advancing flood forecasting: physics-informed cascade non-stationary transformers tailored for reservoir-regulated rivers
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tianyu Xia, Yanlai Zhou, Yuxuan Luo, Hanbing Xu, Hua Chen, Chong-Yu Xu, Fi-John Chang
abstract: Study Region The Minjiang River Basin, a cascade reservoir-regulated watershed in southeastern China. Study Focus Timely flood forecasting is critical for disaster mitigation, yet conventional deep learning models struggle in reservoir-regulated basins due to their inability to capture hydrological non-stationarity. To address this, we introduce the Physics-Informed Cascade Non-Stationary Transformer (PIC-NONST). By coupling a series stationarization module with a physical-state-aware de-stationary attention mechanism and a rule-driven decoder, PIC-NONST explicitly captures both stationary natural flows and abrupt, regulation-induced non-stationarity. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Enforcing strict physical mass-balance constraints, this architecture substantially outperforms benchmark models, improving Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) by 3.5–26.9% and reducing Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by 6.0–46.9%. Its stability is particularly evident during extreme events and extended horizons: during a major flood (peak flow > 20,000 m³/s), the model achieved an NSE of 0.97 at a 1-hour lead time and maintained an NSE of 0.89 at 12 h, exceeding standard Transformer accuracy by 18.7%. SHAP analysis reveals that reservoir storage and upstream flow dominate short-term predictions, whereas precipitation drives longer-term forecasts. By resolving data non-stationarity and forecast lag, PIC-NONST offers a highly adaptable, interpretable framework for real-world flood management in complex, regulated watersheds.

title: Disentangling climate, soil and land-cover controls on hydrological response under extreme rainfall in Northern Italy
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Binyam Alemu Yosef, Angelo Basile, Antonio Coppola, Fabrizio Ungaro, Marialaura Bancheri
abstract: Study Region: The study was conducted across a hydro-climatic gradient spanning the Bologna Apennines and adjacent lowlands in Northern Italy, a region severely affected by the catastrophic floods of 2023 and 2024. Study Focus: Extreme rainfall events are increasingly driving hydrological hazards, yet disentangling the roles of climate, soil, and land cover remains challenging. We used the 1D hydrological model FLOWS, based on the Richards equation, to quantify their relative contributions to rainfall partitioning. Simulations were performed for 268 soil profiles representing six climatic zones and agricultural and forest land covers over 2020–2024. Across three complementary experimental designs, we distinguished between runoff-generation magnitude and runoff efficiency. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: ANOVA showed that climate accounted for the largest variance in runoff-generation magnitude, explaining 54%–76%, with higher values occurring in wetter years and under extreme conditions. Soil properties primarily influenced the spatial variability of hydrological partitioning. In contrast, land cover mainly regulated runoff efficiency: under identical soil and climatic conditions, forest cover reduced event-scale flux-to-runoff coefficients by 9%–25% relative to agricultural land, while increasing evapotranspiration. These results indicate that climate primarily governs runoff-generation magnitude, soil contributes to its spatial differentiation, and land cover regulates partitioning efficiency. By providing soil-explicit, process-based information, the framework can support the identification of areas where vegetation-based interventions and other NBS may enhance hydrological regulation.

title: Salinity intrusion dynamics in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta: Combined effects of upstream development, climate change, and coastal engineering
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Dung Duc Tran, Edward Park, Nguyen Duc Thien, Sonu Kumar, Tran Quang Tho, Tran Manh Thu, Long Phi Hoang, Jingyu Wang, Paolo Tarolli
abstract: Study region Vietnamese Mekong Delta (VMD) in Southern Vietnam Study focus This study assesses and predicts spatial and temporal salinity intrusion dynamics under changing inflows, climate scenarios, and sea-level rise. Using the MIKE 11 hydrodynamic model, calibrated with 2016–2020 salinity data, dry-season (February–May) intrusion was simulated across nine scenarios: a historical 1998 baseline (SCE1), 2020 present conditions (SCE2), projected sea-level rise (SCE3) under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 (SCE4–5), and a future combined upstream-development package that integrates full hydropower operations with moderate or high irrigation expansion (SCE6–9). Three additional scenarios (SCE7-G1–G3) tested the effects of salinity-regulating sluice gates. New hydrological insights for the region Compared to the historical baseline SCE1 and the present-day scenario SCE2, projected scenarios exhibit higher salinity, stronger penetration, and earlier arrival times due to upstream alterations. The most severe regional degradation occurs when climate-driven sea-level rise directly coincides with intensive upstream water diversions, with the combined drivers under RCP4.5 paradoxically generating a larger area enclosed by the 2 PSU interpolated river-salinity surface than the higher-emission RCP8.5 due to lower projected dry-season inflows. Furthermore, the simulations expose an important hydrodynamic trade-off in coastal engineering, while localized sluice gates successfully mitigate salinity on a local scale, restricting these natural channels alters tidal distribution and can inadvertently intensify saltwater encroachment in adjacent, unfiltered river branches.

title: Evaluation of CMIP6 models for projecting climate trends and variability in the Didessa sub-basin, Ethiopia: Implications for the Blue Nile basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Selamawit Bekele Degefu, Tena Alamirew, Sintayehu Fetene Demessie
abstract: Global warming intensifies extreme events, requiring bias-corrected climate models for effective adaptation and mitigation. This study utilizes data from nine climate models in the sixth phase of Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) to evaluate projected changes in temperature and precipitation over Didessa sub-basin. Projections are made for two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5, for the periods of 2030–2059 and 2070–2099. CMIP6 outputs are bias-corrected using a distribution-mapping method based on daily observations from 14 meteorological stations for the baseline period of 1985–2014. Model performance is assessed using the Comprehensive Rating Metric (CRM), while climate trends are analyzed using the Modified Mann–Kendall test. Among individual models, EC-Earth3 most accurately simulates observed precipitation, while GFDL-CM4 and MRI-ESM2–0 best capture maximum and minimum temperatures, respectively. The multi-model mean ensemble (MMME) outperforms all individual models across all variables. Conversely, INM-CM5–0 and BCC-CSM2-MR perform poorly in replicating observed precipitation and temperature. Spatial projections indicate increasing precipitation and temperature across both scenarios. The greatest changes occur under SSP5–8.5 in the 2080 s, with precipitation changes of 16.4–32.9% and temperature changes of 2.5 ℃ to 3.7 ℃ and 3 ℃ to 7.3 ℃ for maximum and minimum, respectively. These findings highlight substantial spatial variability in climate variables, providing policymakers with essential insights to develop site-specific mitigation strategies.

title: Load- versus concentration-based water quality metrics: Field assessment of permeable pavement and filter drain under Mediterranean rainfall in Valencia, Spain
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): A. Martínez-Biosca, C. Hernández-Crespo, E. Asensi, I. Andrés-Doménech, M. Martín
abstract: Study Region Valencia, Spain. Study Focus Two full-scale Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems (SUDS), a permeable pavement (PP) and a filter drain (FD), were monitored over one year at a residential street in Valencia under Mediterranean rainfall conditions. Hydraulic and water-quality performance were evaluated using concentration-based (Event Mean Concentration, EMC) and mass-based (Pollutant Mass Loading, PML) indicators. Rainfall, flow, and water quality were monitored at a conventional gully (CG) as a reference point and at both SUDS outlets across 14 rainfall events. Parameters included conventional pollutants (TSS, COD, BOD, TN, TP), 12 trace metals and metalloids, hydrocarbon fractions, and 16 PAHs. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Both systems attenuated runoff consistently, with volumetric efficiencies of 24–100% (mean: PP 57%, FD 65%) and no measured overflow for events below 10 mm, extending to 30 mm for FD. Concentration-based efficiencies were moderate and event-dependent, with occasional negative values for TSS, Cr and Ag at PP. Mass-based indicators revealed consistently higher reductions for most pollutants (SOL: 65–95%), even when outlet EMCs exceeded those at CG, indicating that volume reduction drives pollutant export reduction in highly retentive systems. A general first-flush tendency was observed across the 20 analysed pollutants. These findings indicate that, in highly retentive systems, EMC-based assessments alone can understate SUDS performance in terms of pollutant export, and that both metrics provide complementary information.

title: A two-stage cascaded prediction framework for urban inundation depth using a dual-branch CNN-ConvLSTM network
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tongxin Ren, Zhenghui Lu, Jiangjiang Xia, Qingfeng Zeng, Peiyuan Zang
abstract: Study region Shenzhen, China, is a densely urbanized subtropical megacity characterized by extensive impervious surfaces, rapid runoff responses, and frequent rainfall-induced inundation. Study focus To address the underestimation of urban inundation depth driven by severe zero-inflation, this study proposes a two-stage Cascaded Multi-scale CNN-ConvLSTM Network (CMC-Net). A Random Forest classifier first identifies hazardous inundation samples using a 0.15-m threshold. A dual-branch CNN-ConvLSTM then estimates water depth by integrating the local spatial context represented by static geographical features with the spatiotemporal evolution of multiscale cumulative rainfall. Structural ablations evaluate the contributions of multiscale convolution, channel attention, and recurrent spatial interactions. New hydrological insights for the region Evaluation on chronologically held-out positive samples shows that the conditional CNN-ConvLSTM is better than other benchmark regression models, achieving an NSE of 0.6150 and an RMSE of 0.2778 m. More importantly, under realistic full-sample scenarios (comprising both positive and negative samples), the cascade framework achieved an NSE of 0.4969, Pearson’ s r of 0.7996, RMSE of 0.3176 m, and MAE of 0.2523 m, outperforming the three direct-regression alternatives.The attribution and ablation results indicate that multiscale rainfall features provide useful information for inundation-depth estimation, while combining static spatial context with dynamic rainfall evolution improves estimation performance. Overall, the cascaded strategy reduces depth underestimation associated with severe class imbalance.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and lifecycle dynamics of soil-atmosphere compound droughts in Central Asia: A three-dimensional perspective
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ping Jiang, Yue Zhang, Xinguo Li, Keremu Guzainuer, Zhi Wang, Yiran Ding
abstract: Study Region Central Asia, including the five Central Asian countries and northwestern China Study Focus Most assessments of soil–atmosphere compound droughts focus on simultaneous water limitation, overlooking antecedent and residual stages that shape event development and recovery. Here, we extended three-dimensional (3D) event tracking to reconstruct the complete lifecycle of soil–atmosphere compound droughts in Central Asia from 1981 to 2024. Soil-moisture drought (DSM) and vapor-pressure-deficit drought (DVPD) clusters were independently identified and then linked within a lifecycle-oriented framework that distinguishes initiation, compound, and decay phases, as well as simple and complex pathways. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: DSM behaved as a stationary–persistent stressor with longer durations and localized clustering, whereas DVPD acted as a mobile–expansive driver with larger spatial footprints and higher intensities. Both drought types increased markedly after 2000, accompanied by earlier DSM onset in spring and summer. Only 13.6% of compound events began with simultaneous DSM and DVPD onset; 51.1% were DSM-initiated with longer propagation lags, whereas 35.2% were DVPD-initiated and developed more rapidly under strong atmospheric moisture demand. Moreover, 63.6% of compound events ended only after delayed dissipation of soil-moisture deficits, highlighting soil-memory effects. Although simple one-to-one pathways accounted for 65.9% of events, complex pathways substantially enlarged and prolonged the compound phase. This lifecycle perspective provides a process-oriented basis for interpreting soil–atmosphere drought interactions and improving drought early warning in drylands.

title: Analysis of the evolution of dominant attributes and composition reconstruction of flood risk from dam failures in parallel reservoir groups
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chunxin Sun, Jinjun Zhou, Jiahong Liu, Ruirui Sun, Chenrui Qin, Songyun Jin, Hao Wang, Yingdong Yu
abstract: Study region The parallel reservoir groups in Zhaotong City, Yunnan Province, China. Study focus Based on Monte Carlo simulation, identify Local Failure Scenarios (LFS) and construct Global Failure Scenarios (GCS); simulate dam-break flood processes using DB-IWHR–HEC-RAS; and, combining improved projection pursuit, Attribute Pattern Dominance Identification, and compositional data analysis methods, analyze the risk organizational characteristics and their evolution for different scenarios and risk areas from the perspective of relative composition of Hazard (H), Exposure (E), and Vulnerability (V). New hydrological insights for the region Multi-source dam-break flood convergence triggered by overall failure leads to scale-dependent reconstruction of the risk structure and reorganizes the relative compositional relationships of H–E–V. At the regional scale, newly inundated areas shift the overall risk composition in a hazard-dominated direction; within the commonly inundated areas, as flood hazards tend to saturate, the risk composition mainly shows relatively increased vulnerability. The Aitchison distances at the regional and inundation zone scales are 1.514 and 7.807, respectively, indicating that risk reconstruction is mainly concentrated within the flood-affected areas. The evolution path of risk-dominant attributes changes from EH_mix–EHV_mix–EHV_mix under LFS conditions to H–EHV_mix–E under GCS conditions, and risk organization evolves from a multi-attribute coordination pattern to a single dominant attribute pattern.

title: Dynamics of coupling between rainfall and groundwater signals under climatic and anthropogenic stressors
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ishita Bhatnagar, Mehdi Rahmati, Harrie-Jan Hendricks Franssen, Akhil Jnanadevan, C.T. Dhanya, B.R. Chahar
abstract: Study region The Ganges Basin (referred to as the Ganga Basin in our study) Study focus The response of shallow groundwater tables to drought events under long-term anthropogenic stress is critical for mitigating water scarcity. In this study, wavelet coherence analysis is applied to seasonally aggregated rainfall and groundwater time series to identify spatial and temporal rainfall-groundwater signal coupling patterns before and after major drought events across regions characterized by varying pumping intensities, recharge-to-pumping ratios, and groundwater depths. New hydrological insights Findings indicate regions with higher aquifer storativity and historically high groundwater extraction exhibit fast initial groundwater response to post-drought rainfall but a slower overall recovery, likely due to hydrogeological properties, lagged recharge through thick unsaturated zones, and long-term system memory. When groundwater tables deepen beyond the 90th percentile (about 9.4 mbgl in heavily developed alluvial aquifers), rainfall-groundwater coupling progressively weakens, indicating an empirical transition in groundwater behaviour and possible delays in the natural rejuvenation cycle. These aquifer systems took nearly a decade to recover to pre-drought levels after the major drought event of 2002. Additionally, regions with pumping less than the 5th percentile (11 mm/y) of pumped depths from the Ganga Basin may display an illusion of stronger monsoonal recovery, possibly sustained by inflows from adjacent sources, though this mechanism was not directly evaluated.

title: Diurnal cycle of summer precipitation in the Eastern Tarim Basin and surrounding mountains using the WRF-NJU model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Kai Zhang, Abuduwaili Abulikemu, Ali Mamtimin, Junqiang Yao, Chenglong Zhou, Kefeng Zhu, Zulipina Kadier, Zhiyi Li, Chunyang Li, Abidan Abuduaini
abstract: Study region Eastern Tarim Basin and its surrounding mountains (Bayingol Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang, China), with focus on the core Eastern Tarim Basin (ETB), Southern slope of Tianshan Mountains (STM), and North slope of Altun-Kunlun Mountains (NAKM). Study focus Utilizing high-resolution WRF-NJU model data, multi-source observations, and reanalysis datasets, this study systematically analyses the diurnal cycle of precipitation (DCP) in the region. Emphasis is placed on the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of precipitation amount (PA), frequency (PF), intensity (PI), and peak timing. New hydrological insights for the region WRF-NJU successfully reproduces DCP, confirming its reliability for high-resolution simulations in arid regions. PA and PF show single afternoon peaks, while PI exhibits dual peaks at dawn and dusk. Mountain precipitation peaks mainly during 14–16 LST, whereas basin precipitation displays nocturnal dominance. PF is the principal driver of diurnal precipitation variability across the region. High coefficients of variation (CV) reveal extreme PF fluctuations in the basin. Overlapping CV-PA and CV-PI values in mountains indicate persistent rainfall elevating hydrological hazards. Precipitation peaks exhibit elevational delays (10–22 LST), transitioning from bimodal to unimodal afternoon patterns above 4500 m. Forests, water bodies, and grasslands show dominant afternoon precipitation, while impervious surfaces and croplands peak pre-dawn, demonstrating urbanization and agricultural impacts on local DCP. This work provides critical scientific foundations for understanding spatiotemporal precipitation mechanisms and water-resource risk management in arid zones.

title: Seasonal low flow regimes reveal compound drought processes and catchment heterogeneity across New Zealand
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sameen Bushra, Svenja Fischer, Markus Pahlow, Céline Cattoën
abstract: Study region: New Zealand shows strong climatic and hydrological gradients, ranging from humid, snow-influenced alpine catchments to temperate lowland and groundwater-dominated systems. This diversity produces distinct seasonal low flow regimes, making New Zealand an ideal setting for investigating the climatic controls and seasonality of low flow extremes. Study focus: This study investigates seasonal low flow behaviour across 227 catchments in New Zealand by comparing summer and winter low flow frequency characteristics. Seasonal low flow frequency analysis was performed using a mixed distribution approach, and the dominant season at each catchment was identified. To investigate climatic controls on seasonal low flows, drought drivers were classified using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), and Temperature Index (STI). New hydrological insights for the region: Seasonal low flow behaviour varies substantially across New Zealand, demonstrating that annual analyses can mask important differences in low flow generation processes. Summer was identified as the dominant low flow season in most catchments. The dominant climatic drivers differed between seasons. Compound drought events were the most common driver category in summer. In contrast, winter low flow events showed no dominant relationship with the selected indices, suggesting a stronger influence of hydrological storage and lagged catchment processes. These findings demonstrate the value of seasonal frequency analysis for identifying distinct low flow-generating mechanisms and improving climate-informed water resource management in New Zealand.

title: Faster autumn recession and increased abundance of Geese after 2003 in Poyang Lake: Temporal cascading effects from water to mudflats and grasslands
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiaobo Liu, Jie Wang, Zhen Han, Shiyan Wang, Long Sun, Aiping Huang, Mingmei Guo
abstract: Study Region Poyang Lake, a river-connected floodplain lake in the middle and lower Yangtze River, is a major wintering area for Greater White-fronted Geese (Anser albifrons) along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. Study Focus We examined how post-2003 changes in autumn recession affected goose abundance and habitat formation. Goose surveys (1998–2022), daily water levels, generalized additive models, EFDC inundation–exposure simulations, and Hill-type Logistic analysis were combined to identify hydrologically sensitive stages, characterize habitat cascade transformation, and determine the hydrological opportunity window. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Under Study After 2003, water levels below 10 m occurred 28 d earlier and persisted 45 d longer. Goose abundance was associated with October water level and November recession rate, with responses concentrated during September–November. Earlier recession propagated through the water–mudflat–grassland cascade, advancing sparse-grassland formation during early recession but reducing its persistence later. The principal rapid-expansion range narrowed from approximately 9.5–12.0 m to 10.0–11.5 m, while EC(50) remained near 10.7 m. This narrowing was consistent across alternative percentile bounds, with the post-2003 interval approximately 40% narrower. The 10.0–11.5 m range therefore defines a multi-year hydrological opportunity window under post-2003 mean conditions and provides a quantitative basis for linking autumn recession, habitat formation, and goose response.

title: Hydrochemical assessment and monitoring priorities in anthropogenically affected arid urban groundwater systems of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ayman Alrehaili, Obaid Alharbi, Abdulaziz Alquwaizany, Faisal K. Zaidi, Oumar Allafouza Loni, Musaad Aleid, Muneer Baata, Mohammed Almoiqli
abstract: Study Region This study investigates arid urban groundwater in metropolitan Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where limited recharge, intense evaporation, urbanization, agriculture, treated-wastewater reuse, industry, and landfills may alter carbonate and alluvial aquifers. Study Focus Forty-one groundwater samples from accessible wells were assessed to characterize dry-condition hydrochemistry and identify spatial response domains for targeted monitoring. Physicochemical parameters, major ions, trace metals, carbon fractions, and water-table depth were evaluated using inferential statistics, multivariate ordination, pollution and exposure indicators, bootstrap confidence intervals, and hydrochemical process screening. The analysis considered natural mineralization, aquifer context, and human pressures without assigning a single contamination source. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Multivariate analysis separated salinity–metal and carbon-related gradients and confirmed group differences (PERMANOVA R² = 0.388, p = 0.0001). Wadi Sulay showed the strongest salinity and trace-metal enrichment and the highest pollution-index and exposure-indicator values. Wadi Hanifa exhibited a carbon-fraction-dominated carbonate-system signature, whereas deeper Southern Riyadh displayed a buffered urban-mixed response. Process indicators suggested a transition from rock weathering to evaporation-controlled conditions, with stronger Ca–Cl–SO₄ mineralization in Wadi Sulay and lower chloride dominance with higher HCO₃⁻calc/Na⁺ ratios in Wadi Hanifa. Mean total hazard quotients remained below 1 under the adopted scenario. Monitoring should therefore follow hydrochemical responses, aquifer vulnerability, and land-use pressures rather than a uniform parameter set. This framework supports targeted monitoring in data-limited arid aquifers but requires independent seasonal validation.

title: A novel sensitivity-driven multistage feedforward inverse modeling approach for source identification of organic-contaminated aquifer
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zeyu Hou, Mengqi Li, Shicheng Yu, Ke Zhao, Yifan Fu, Wenxi Lu
abstract: In the present study, a sensitivity-driven multistage combined search system was established to improve the search capability and accuracy of inverse modeling for the simultaneous identification of DNAPL contamination sources and contaminant transport (CTR) parameters. The system was assisted by a biomimetic intelligence stochastic search process and a homotopy-variational deterministic search process. A Bayesian hybrid learning machine (BHLM) model, designed for accurate surrogate modeling of DNAPL transport numerical simulation, was also embedded in the combined inversion system, thereby reducing the computational burden of iterative likelihood evaluations. The results revealed that BHLM was highly successful in approximating the forward simulation input-output mapping, with a mean relative error (MRE) of 1.1784% for the prediction of contaminant concentrations. The sensitivity-driven whale optimization stochastic search algorithm (SD‑WOSSA) employed swarm intelligence to achieve a multi-chain parallel stochastic search process and incorporated a sensitivity‑driven multistage feedforward mechanism to enhance the differentiated search capability for source characteristics and CTR parameters. The SD-WOSSA approach provided refined prior information and high-quality starting points, which constrained the search space and search paths for the subsequent homotopy-variational deterministic search process. The homotopy-variational search mechanism was effective in reasonably partitioning the search space and transforming the global search problem into several linked local search stages, with the relative identification error remaining below 5%.

title: Event-specific flood extent prediction using ensemble machine learning and multi-source geospatial data
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fatemeh Alishahi, Behzad Ghiasi, Mohammad Hossein Niksokhan
abstract: Study Region The Kashkan River Basin in western Iran is characterized by complex topography and diverse environmental conditions that contribute to spatial variability in flood occurrence and extent. The basin is therefore a relevant case for developing high-resolution approaches to flood extent assessment and spatial flood-risk analysis. Study Focus This study developed a machine-learning framework for predicting the spatial extent of flooding by integrating 11 environmental raster variables on a common 10 m spatial grid with two ensemble machine-learning algorithms, Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). The predictor variables included topographic factors, vegetation cover, land use, precipitation, soil moisture, and hydrological indices derived from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery, together with complementary geospatial datasets. Model performance was evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation based on the 2019 flood inventory. RF achieved an accuracy of 0.9877, F1-score of 0.7426, and recall of 0.9982, whereas XGBoost achieved an accuracy of 0.9977, F1-score of 0.9346, and recall of 0.9344. ROC-AUC and confusion-matrix results further indicated strong discrimination during internal validation of the 2019 flood event. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The results demonstrate that high-resolution, spatially consistent environmental datasets can effectively support event-specific flood extent prediction in the Kashkan River Basin. XGBoost provided substantially better overall classification performance than RF, particularly in terms of F1-score, while RF showed higher recall. Feature-importance analysis identified elevation and vegetation cover as the most influential predictors of the observed flood extent. These findings highlight the potential of integrating multi-source remote-sensing and geospatial data with ensemble machine-learning methods to improve spatial flood assessment and support flood-risk analysis in the basin.

title: Study on spatiotemporal variation characteristics of regional extreme precipitation and its driving factors in geography and atmospheric circulation: Case study of Poyang Lake Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yinxin Ge, Shanghong Zhang, Qingqing Fang, Bohang Yin
abstract: Study region The Poyang Lake Basin, the largest freshwater lake system in China. Study focus Using the CHM_PRE daily precipitation dataset for 1961–2022, this study investigates the spatiotemporal variability and periodicity of extreme precipitation in the Poyang Lake Basin and examines its associations with geographical factors and large-scale atmospheric circulation, untangling non-stationary circulation relationships, and spatial explanatory factors. New hydrological insights for the region Extreme precipitation in the Poyang Lake Basin exhibits marked spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Spatially, intensity- and threshold-based indices generally decrease from northeast to southwest, whereas high values of frequency-based indices are concentrated in the northwest. Geographic Detector results show that the circulation-response factor and longitude have relatively strong single-factor explanatory power, while the interaction between longitude and elevation yields the highest explanatory power for RX5day (Q = 0.96). Temporally, most extreme precipitation indices exhibit fluctuating upward trends and a dominant 2–4 year interannual periodicity. ENSO, AMO, and NAO show distinct statistical associations with extreme precipitation: El Niño conditions and warm AMO phases are associated with higher extreme precipitation, whereas NAO exhibits predominantly anti-phase relationships at interannual timescales. Collectively, the results suggest a cross-scale pattern in which large-scale ocean–atmosphere variability is linked to temporal fluctuations in extreme precipitation, while geographical interactions contribute to its spatial heterogeneity. From a regional hydrological perspective, the contrasting spatial patterns of precipitation intensity and frequency imply differentiated rainfall-driven flood risks across the Poyang Lake Basin, while the identified large-scale climate associations provide foundation for seasonal hydroclimatic risk assessment and preparedness.

title: An exposure-aware graph neural network for peak flood depth prediction in New Jersey urban watersheds
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ahmad Ibrahim, Firas Gerges, Viravid Na Nagara, Abul Hassan Fatemi, Christopher Testa, Michel Boufadel
abstract: Study region This study evaluates flood prediction for three northern New Jersey watersheds. The municipalities, Englewood, Irvington, and Paterson, New Jersey, are susceptible to flooding, but vary in watershed size and extent of riverine influence. Study focus This study develops a spatio-temporal neural network that accurately infers overland and riverine flow dynamics from rainfall. Instead of conventional gridded approaches, this study utilizes unstructured graph representation of hydraulic computation points to preserve physical connectivity. A novel, importance-weighted loss function increases emphasis on high-priority areas while mitigating high-value dominance from channel regions. Incorporating synthetic rainfall patterns exposes the model to irregular storm sequences, bridging historical events and normalized design storms. New hydrological insights for the region The results indicate that the FloodMAGNet effectively predicts peak flood depths aligned with risk assessment objectives. Training with synthetic rainfall sequences established strong predictive capacity for non-monotonic events, demonstrated by an R2 of 0.975 and a 3.3 cm RMSE on high-priority nodes for an observed hyetograph in Englewood. Evaluation of design storms in Irvington yielded an RMSE of 8.3 cm across the full domain and 5.8 cm in prioritized areas. Furthermore, evaluating the larger, river-dominated watershed in Paterson resulted in a baseline RMSE of 29.3 cm, which improved to 14.4 cm after loss function recalibration, demonstrating the framework’s methodological generalizability to distinct topographies and hydrologic responses.

title: A hybrid DeepGR4J and regionalization framework for lake water balance assessment in data-scarce regions: Application to Lake Tana, Ethiopia
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Temesgen T. Mihret, Fasikaw A. Zemale, Abeyou W. Worqlul, Ayenew D. Ayalew, Margaret Chen, Seifu A. Tilahun, Nicola Fohrer
abstract: Study region Lake Tana, the largest freshwater lake in Ethiopia and the headwater of the Blue Nile River, is located in the northwestern Ethiopian Highlands and is vital for water supply, hydropower, irrigation, and ecosystem services. The basin has strong rainfall seasonality, complex topography, and many ungauged catchments, making hydrological assessment difficult due to limited observations. Study focus This study develops a hybrid hydrological framework integrating the DeepGR4J rainfall-runoff model with regression-based regionalization to improve lake water balance estimation under data-scarce conditions. DeepGR4J combines the conceptual GR4J model with LSTM-based error correction to enhance runoff simulation, while regionalization transfers parameters from gauged to ungauged watersheds using physiographic and remote sensing descriptors. The framework is applied for 2000–2020 using CHIRPS precipitation, ERA5 temperature, and Hargreaves evapotranspiration estimates. New hydrological insights for the region Results show a mean annual inflow of 12.61 km³ yr⁻¹ and a combined water-balance outflow term of 12.67 km³ yr⁻¹, resulting in a net storage decline of −0.20 km³ yr⁻¹ and a residual imbalance of 0.06 km³ yr⁻¹. The model reproduces observed lake levels with high accuracy (R² = 0.94, NSE = 0.94, RMSE = 0.18 m). Findings highlight the strong contribution of ungauged catchments and demonstrate that hybrid conceptual-deep learning models with regionalization improve water balance estimation in data-scarce lake basins.

title: Variability and patterns of surface water levels during dry season under environmental change: A case study at the Gan River-Poyang Lake-Yangtze River confluence area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ming Tang, Qianchun Wu, Mingdi Zha, Zhao Tang, Sijuan Chen, Jiechen Yuan, Yaxuan Cui, Lin Li
abstract: Study Region Gan River-Poyang Lake-Yangtze River confluence area (GRPLYR), China. Study Focus Changing environmental and river–lake conditions complicate the interpretation of dry-season water-level records. This study assesses the velocity of water level descending (VWD), a window-based indicator of water-level recession, and tests whether recession information is more consistent than absolute water levels. Daily water levels from six stations during 2010–2021 were used to construct VWD series at 3-, 5-, 7-, 10-, 15-, and 30-day scales. Mann–Kendall trend and mutation tests were applied to water-level and VWD series. Four candidate theoretical probability distribution functions were fitted to VWD samples. Parameters were estimated using particle swarm optimization (PSO), maximum likelihood estimation, and L-moments. The optimal distribution-estimation framework was selected using goodness-of-fit metrics and information criteria. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Absolute water-level series showed contrasting trends: Nanchang declined significantly, Xingzi, Hukou, and Pingfeng increased significantly, and Ganjiang Wucheng and Xiushui Wucheng showed no significant trend. In contrast, VWD series showed no significant trend or clear mutation point across the tested scales. PSO performed best, and the PSO-fitted Pearson type Ⅲ distribution was selected as the most suitable distribution. VWD provides a more consistent probabilistic description of dry-season water-level recession and supports low-water-level risk assessment and urban water-supply management.

title: Continuous spatiotemporal variations of riverine dissolved organic carbon in the Yangtze River Basin revealed by a river-reach-scale machine learning-based model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Menghan Chen, Lei Cheng, Yue Wu, Mingshen Lu, Shiqiang Wu, Lu Zhang, Pan Liu
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Basin (YRB), China Study focus Riverine dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is critical to the global carbon cycle, while its continuous spatiotemporal variations remain poorly understood in large rivers. This study developed an estimation model at the river-reach scale using interpretable machine learning to simulate long-term (2000–2020) monthly riverine DOC concentration (CDOC) in the YRB, identifying its continuous spatiotemporal variations, export characteristics, major predictors, and their effects. These findings highlight the increasing trends and transport-limited characteristics of riverine DOC in the YRB, which are important for understanding the riverine carbon cycle processes. New hydrological insights for the region Seven major predictors representing geography, vegetation, climate, and river attributes had nonlinear effects on spatiotemporal variations in riverine CDOC. Elevation showed dominant negative effects with local low-elevation positive impacts. Generally, riverine CDOC responded positively to vegetation productivity, precipitation, and air temperature, but negatively to river attributes. Annual riverine CDOC averaged 4.69 ± 0.44 mg/L, higher in midstream small tributaries of the YRB. Approximately 23.6% of river reaches exhibited significant CDOC increases, primarily in the up-midstream regions. Riverine DOC export to the ocean was 2.02 ± 0.35 Tg C/yr, with a transport-limited regime. Moreover, mainstream CDOC showed an initial decrease from the source followed by a fluctuating increase and a final decrease toward the estuary, whereas most of its major tributaries generally exhibited fluctuating downward trends.

title: Climate warming and intensified precipitation extremes triggered regime shifts in Lake Ayakkum, East Kunlun Mountains
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yongxiao Zhu, Junqiang Yao, Yang Wang
abstract: Study Region Ayakkum Lake on the Kumukuli Basin. Study Focus This study utilizes the meteorological and lake-level data to analyze climatic and hydrological change in the Ayakkum Lake region during 1961–2023, elucidating the driver mechanisms through which climate variablity and extreme weather events have influenced water level change of Ayakkum Lake. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The results indicate that the Mann–Kendall abrupt change analysis reveals a more pronounced warming–wetting and extreme trend in the Kumukuli Basin and its surrounding areas during 1995–2023. The climatic warming–wetting have led to a significant rise in the water level of Ayakkum Lake at a rate of 0.209 m·year⁻¹ (p < 0.01) during 1995–2009, with the rate accelerating to 0.438 m·year⁻¹ (p < 0.01) during 2010–2023. Random Forest analysis identified extreme precipitation (26.26% contribution) and temperature-driven glacial ablation (45.58% contribution) as the primary drivers of lake water level (LWL) rise, jointly explaining 71.84% of the increase. Between 1995–2009, the rise in LWL was predominantly driven by temperature-induced snow and ice melt. In contrast, the marked acceleration of LWL after 2010 was primarily attributed to increased extreme precipitation. These findings provide a significant scientific basis for water resource management in Lake Ayakkum.

title: Graph neural network surrogates for simulation of urban drainage systems containing orifice actuators
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chutian Zhou, Pan Liu, Yang Liu, Qian Cheng, Xinran Luo, Kang Xie, Jun Zhang, Kunming Wu
abstract: Study region The urban drainage system (UDS) in central Yueyang city, China. Study focus Surrogate models for UDSs can reduce computational costs. Graph neural networks (GNNs), which capture the topological structure and intrinsic relationships within UDSs, are natural candidates for constructing surrogate models. However, existing GNN surrogate models fail to incorporate orifice actuators, which are critical components in UDS management. To address this, the study develops physics-guided surrogate models based on GNN. For complex hydraulic relationships caused by orifice actuators, physics-guided surrogate models are established to enhance the hydraulic simulation by incorporating conduit capacity. Thus, two model architectures are developed: graph convolution with seq2seq (GC-S2S) and graph attention with transformer (GAT-Trans). These models are compared with the non-physics-guided GC-S2S and long short-term memory network with seq2seq (LSTM-S2S). New hydrological insights for the region (1) Compared with the non-physics-guided GC-S2S, the physics-guided model increases the NSE of conduit and orifice flow from 0.85 to 0.90 and 0.75 to 0.85, respectively. (2) The proposed GAT-Trans model demonstrates superior performance, achieving NSE of 0.94 for conduit flow, compared with 0.90 and 0.85 for GC-S2S and LSTM-S2S, respectively. (3) Compared to the Storm Water Management Model, the GAT-Trans model completes each simulation in 124 ms, corresponding to an 83-fold speedup. The proposed method can be utilized for orifice actuator application of UDS surrogate model, enhancing real-time prediction and control efficiency.

title: Multivariate spatiotemporal patterns and propagation characteristics of meteorological and hydrological compound hot-drought events in the Yangtze River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ziying Zhu, Kang Xie, Chang Yu, Yan Li, Zhangkang Shu, Junliang Jin, Cuishan Liu, Yanli Liu, Zhenxin Bao, Jianyun Zhang, Peng Liu, Guoqing Wang
abstract: Study area The entire Yangtze River Basin, China. Study focus Compound hot–drought events pose increasing risks to water resources, ecosystems, and socio-economic systems under global warming. However, their hydrological manifestations remain insufficiently understood compared with meteorological characteristics. This study identifies compound hot–meteorological and hot–hydrological drought events in the Yangtze River Basin using long-term observations and a joint-threshold approach. New insights for the region Findings show that: (1) compound hot–drought events in the YRB have intensified since the 2000s. Meteorological compound events show increasing event days at most stations, with the largest trend at Hukou (0.19 yr⁻¹). Hydrological compound events also strengthened, with drought intensity reaching 2.36 at Datong and drought severity exceeding 14 at Yichang. (2) Spatially, meteorological compound events increase from western to central–eastern regions, whereas hydrological compound events are stronger in the middle and lower reaches. (3) The propagation time from meteorological to hydrological compound events varies among stations, with the longest lag (8 months) at Yichang. (4) ENSO, PDO, and IOD also exhibit notable associations with compound event characteristics. These findings enhance the understanding of compound hot–drought dynamics and support climate risk assessment and water resource management in the Yangtze River Basin.

title: Spatiotemporal changes of glaciers in the Bosten Lake Basin using object-based classification from multi-source satellite imagery
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Weiwei Wang, Fei Zhang, Ngai Weng Chan, Zia Ahmed, Mou Leong Tan, Lifei Wei, Xu Ma, Zhenzhou Zhu, Shuai Yuan
abstract: Study region The Bosten Lake Basin, located in Northwest China, serves as a regional water resource distribution hub, a crucial ecological barrier, and a major source of water for the Tarim River. Study focus The Bosten Lake Basin is characterized by complex topography and heterogeneous surface conditions, while its glacial environment is highly sensitive to climatic variability. These characteristics make the basin particularly susceptible to climate-driven changes in glacier dynamics. However, reliable estimates of glacial change in this area remain insufficient due to the complexity of debris-covered glaciers and the persistent cloud cover that limits the availability of remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this study develops a classification framework that combines hierarchical object-based methods with rule-based analysis. By integrating multi-source remote sensing data with detailed topographic information, this approach enables the separation of objects with similar spectral signatures. The multi-level classification provides new insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of glaciers in the Bosten Lake Basin. New hydrological insights for the region The findings reveal a significant decline in glacierized water area across the Bosten Lake Basin, accompanied by increasing fluctuations, highlighting pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in glacier dynamics. Between 2010 and 2025, the total glacier area in the Basin decreased by 880.309 km². This decline occurred in three phases: 432.279 km² from 2010 to 2015, 220.553 km² from 2015 to 2020, and 227.477 km² from 2020 to 2025. Glacier retreat varied markedly with slope orientation, with the most pronounced losses occurring on southern and eastern slopes. This spatial heterogeneity was closely associated with regional variations in precipitation and solar radiation. By applying a multi-level object-oriented and rule-based classification, this study effectively captures the complex glacial environment of the basin. These findings not only document patterns of glacial change but also enhance understanding of the broader environmental consequences of climate change in one of Central Asia’s most sensitive regions.

title: Multi-scale SPI drought forecasting and threshold-based early warning using optimized machine learning models: A case study of Sharjah, United Arab Emirates
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mohamed Elkollaly, Ahmed Sefelnasr, Assaad Kassem, Abdel Azim Ebraheem, Mayed Almemari, Mahmoud E. Abd-Elmaboud, Ahmed El-Shafie, Mohsen Sherif
abstract: Study region: Sharjah, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Arabian Peninsula Study focus: Drought forecasting in arid environments is constrained by sparse, intermittent rainfall and abrupt transitions between wet and dry states. This study develops a multi-scale machine learning (ML) framework for one-month-ahead Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) forecasting in Sharjah, UAE, using monthly precipitation and temperature data from 1995 to 2024. SPI-3, SPI-6, and SPI-12 were forecast under three predictor configurations: antecedent SPI combined with climatic variables, SPI-only, and climate-only. Seven model families were evaluated: Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with eXogenous inputs (ARIMAX)/Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). These models were tested under standard tuning, Genetic Algorithm (GA), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and Hybrid FOX–Tree-Seed Algorithm (HFTA) optimization, with optional ARIMA residual correction. Performance was assessed using continuous metrics, threshold-based drought classification, permutation-based predictor importance, and Taylor diagrams. New hydrological insights for the region: This study provides a systematic separation of drought memory and meteorological forcing as SPI predictors across three accumulation scales in an arid environment. Forecasting skill improved consistently from SPI-3 to SPI-12. The best SPI-3 result used SVR + HFTA + ARIMA under the combined configuration (R² = 0.808, RMSE = 0.295). For SPI-6, the climate-only XGB + PSO model achieved the strongest performance (R² = 0.891, RMSE = 0.266), demonstrating that seasonal drought can be forecast from meteorological predictors alone, without prior SPI records. The highest overall skill was obtained for SPI-12 using SVR + GA + ARIMA under the SPI-only configuration (R² = 0.943, RMSE = 0.222), highlighting the dominant role of drought memory at annual scales. Threshold-based classification showed that SPI-6 < 0 was detected most reliably by the climate-only XGB + GA model, with 98.33% balanced accuracy and zero false alarms. SPI-12 ≤ −1 was best detected by LSTM + PSO, reaching 94.44% balanced accuracy. Predictor importance showed that antecedent SPI governs long-scale forecasts, while precipitation drives climate-only models. The framework supports multi-scale drought early warning and water-resource planning in arid regions, contributing to SDG 2, SDG 6, and SDG 13.

title: An integrated physics-based–machine learning framework for groundwater head prediction in a highly managed multi-aquifer watershed
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Rajesh Khatakho, Ernest W. Tollner, David E. Stooksbury, Adam M. Milewski, Ritesh Karki, Nandita Gaur
abstract: Study region Lower Apalachicola–Chattahoochee–Flint (ACF) Basin, Southwestern Georgia. Study focus Predicting hydrogeological processes in complex, heterogeneous multi-aquifer systems remain challenging, especially where intensive agricultural pumping strongly alters groundwater dynamics. This study developed an integrated MODFLOW–machine learning (ML) framework to simulate and forecast spatiotemporal groundwater head variations, drought occurrences under varying climatic and anthropogenic stress conditions. New hydrological insights Among the evaluated ML models, the MODFLOW-XGB exhibited superior performance across 85 observation wells, achieving an RMSE of 0.92 during the testing phase less than one-fourth of the standalone MODFLOW RMSE (3.77). Based on validation metrics, the ML models were ranked in descending order of performance as XGB, RF, GPR, DT, SVM, and ANN. The optimized MODFLOW–XGB model forecasted maximum seasonal groundwater declines ranging from 0.23 to 5.26 m across 30 observation wells, with the largest drops (>2 m) observed in regions of intense irrigation underscoring strong anthropogenic influence. Groundwater drought index revealed spatially variable drought frequency (15–20%) in confined areas with limited recharge, driven by low-conductivity Upper Semi-Confining Layer (USCU). Wells beneath thin USCU experiencing sharp short-term declines during periods of intensive abstraction and limited recharge. Modified Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator depicted that no significant long-term trend in groundwater drought but seasonal decline in groundwater was observed. The research reveals the prospective of the coupled framework for real-time groundwater forecasting, early drought warning, and targeted watershed management.

title: Improved multi-class drought classification through climate data analysis and advanced imbalanced data handling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Razieh Taraghi Delgarm, Mehdi Ahmadi, S. Jamshid Mousavi
abstract: Study region The Urmia Lake Basin, a terminal endorheic system in semi-arid northwestern Iran, faces severe hydrological decline. 51 years of monthly precipitation records (1971–2021) from four upper sub-basin rain gauges are analyzed alongside 11 climate teleconnections. Study focus Detecting rare, extreme drought events in terminal basins is frequently hindered by class imbalance in historical hydroclimatic records, biasing machine learning classifiers toward normal conditions. We benchmark a complete ladder of nine data-augmentation methods, including SMOTE, ADASYN, stand-alone CTGAN and VAEs, and two novel hybrids, to improve multi-class Standardized Precipitation Index nowcasting (3–12-month scales) under an identical, strictly leakage-free chronological evaluation protocol. New hydrological insights Under chronological validation, three-class nowcasting yields a moderate operational baseline of approximately 0.42 macro-F1. This exposes a massive temporal leakage gap from the artificial 0.90 F1-score obtained via conventional shuffled splitting, which fits the strong temporal autocorrelation of cumulative SPI. While simpler adaptive oversamplers maximize macro-F1, the hybrids achieve the highest minority-class recall and G-mean on the rare dry states. This trade-off is mathematically explained by CTGAN learning the non-convex probability manifold, whereas SMOTE is geometrically restricted to the minority class’s convex hull. Longer scales function as low-pass filters, smoothing synoptic noise and isolating persistent planetary signals. This nowcasting tool can be directly translated into regional water governance through an operational Traffic-Light Policy Roadmap at Bukan Dam.
